docs.text: section what it settles The data model dims, multi-dims, properties, attributes and the schema that declares them Layers the tree of layers, removing labels, and how a read resolves Using a record reading, editing with WorkingRecord, and writing a layer Storage the parquet format, workspaces and stores, threads and processes Frameworks tools, and the PyPSA tool The package where the code lives, and the one-way dependency Open questions what is deliberately unsettled

docs.title: Whether partial should ever be per attribute
docs.text: The schema puts it on the axis because it is true of every attribute varying over that axis. A counter-example would be an attribute whose series a consumer can accept in pieces while others cannot. None is known. Permitting it would make the fold's key vary per attribute, and the owner-map key is fixed.

docs.title: Whether results should be invalidated by a later input edit
docs.text: A result is an attribute and inherits, so a child that edits an input holds results computed from its parent's inputs, describing a record that no longer exists. Dropping them on the next input edit was considered and rejected: it silently discards work the caller may have wanted, and a record that guesses which of the two the caller meant to keep is worse than one that keeps both and says so. Coherence is the caller's business. If this bites in practice, a pending-level warning is the cheap next step.

docs.title: Detecting intermediate results that no longer fit their inputs
docs.text: A results layer replaces the SubNetworks of its base, but a child editing the topology keeps its parent's until the next solve. Telling them stale needs provenance of which inputs each came from.

docs.title: Filtering a record before build
docs.text: Selecting one period or chosen outputs is a separate feature. It has no design yet.

docs.title: Whether a WorkingRecord over an open record stages against a snapshot
docs.text: Writing into an open record invalidates its owner-map cache. A mutable record would need the same invalidation per edit, or to stage against a snapshot taken at construction. The second is simpler and arguably more correct, since an edit sequence should not see another writer's changes mid-flight. It means a record can go stale.

docs.title: Registering a record's relations as named views
docs.text: A frontend issuing ad-hoc SQL needs names in a catalog, which CREATE VIEW against a file-backed catalog provides. Each view's definition is the resolved overlay and materialises nothing. Creating a view binds its schema, so registering N attributes costs N footer reads. Catalog reopen cost is linear in view count, which argues for one catalog per record.

docs.title: What else a Record should answer about its labels without handing over a frame
docs.text: flags sets the shape: cheap derived metadata a consumer plans against before opening a file. It answers only per attribute. entity -> ctype is a column of the resolved axis, so it is one frame across all categories. "Which categories have live labels" and "how many labels a category has" are still frames to collect. What is open is the granularity: those are the same kind of question, and a protocol growing one method per question is worse than the frames it replaces. Whatever is chosen, it has to be answerable off the fold, which is where a record's membership already lives.

docs.title: Whether a property referring to a dim without one_of may categorize a partial dim
docs.text: entity.carrier refers to carrier, and a default_by keyed on it would make a vocabulary that is data: a category that a layer adds and removes. Today a category is a label of a dim with one_of.

docs.title: Whether a multi-dim in partial may have categories
docs.text: A default_by on connection.role would give each role of a connection its own default. The schema refuses it: a multi-dim is never categorized, even in partial and by a property referring to a dim with one_of. Whether the categories rule extends to a multi-dim is open.

docs.title: Whether a multi-dim may be over another multi-dim
docs.text: Each coordinate of a multi-dim draws on a dim that is no multi-dim, and the schema refuses one that does. Nothing needs a tuple of tuples yet; the refusal stands until something does.

docs.title: Whether a functional mapping over two coordinates justifies a dim
docs.text: A zone per plant and period is a multi-dim plant_period with the property zone. The multi-dim exists only to carry zone, and its tuples must be added before the property can be set.

docs.title: How the published package depends on mathspec
docs.text: Core reads its dtypes from mathspec.program, and the environment pins mathspec at a commit of a pull request branch, which lasts only while the commit exists on GitHub. Before a release the pin moves to the merged commit. A PyPI release cannot declare a git pin as a dependency, so the package metadata names none until mathspec is published.

docs.title: How a property that refers to a dim maps onto mathspec
docs.text: mathspec spells it as a mathspec relation, carrier_of: { key: generator, values: carrier }, a declaration of its own beside the dims. datarecord declares one_of: carrier on a property of generator. Unifying the two is left for later.

docs.title: Whether a default must name a live label
docs.text: bus.carrier defaults to AC in PyPSA's schema, and a default is never stored, so nothing checks that AC is a label of carrier.

docs.title: Whether bus earns its place in the fold key
docs.text: PyPSA's partial gains bus so a layer patches one bus's v_nom, and every partial coordinate is paid for by every read (keep it small). Measuring it on a pypsa-eur-sized record would settle it.

docs.title: Whether a custom bus column can be a property
docs.text: It is an attribute over bus today, so custom Bus.country beside custom Generator.country is one attribute over two dims and refused. Placing it as bus.country would dissolve the one remaining custom-column clash, but needs a rule telling a custom property from a custom attribute.

docs.title: Whether selector keywords need a qualified form
docs.text: A bare selector naming a property of two dims one attribute reaches is refused. The only way to say which is meant is setting per dim.

docs.title: Whether Schema should declare a dim with its mapping property in one call
docs.text: A snapshot mapped to its period is a dim and a property that refers to the period, two declarations a helper could make one.

docs.title: What PyPSA#1474 lands as
docs.text: Upstream making buses and carriers indices may turn an unlisted carrier into an error, or stop "" meaning none. The tool adds the one and stores the other as NULL today (PyPSA).

docs.title: What a pointwise set leaving one of two dims outside partial NULL reaches
docs.text: Every label of the dim it leaves NULL, at the label it names. The rest of the series keeps the parent's values, staged, committed or over a materialised parent (a dim outside partial).

docs.title: Whether a broadcast survives materialisation
docs.text: It does. The owner map holds keys as written and the fold reads no axis, so a NULL reaches every label the axis holds at the node read: one added below a materialised revision and one staged in a WorkingRecord alike (what a row reaches). A map materialised before partial changed is no cache, and the read folds from the layers again (materialised node caches).

docs.title: Whether flags needs a record-level counterpart
docs.text: It is one. flags() answers per record, every attribute included, and flags(**categories) per category, restricted to the rows reaching its labels (flags). An attribute over an axis alone or a multi-dim outside partial is reachable through the first.

docs.title: What a NULL multi-dim struct reaches
docs.text: Every tuple, as a NULL on the dim itself reaches every label (the broadcast rule). A constant efficiency lands on generators' connections too. One for links alone is set("efficiency", 0.7, ctype="Link").

docs.title: What build does with a value its type does not take
docs.text: It leaves the value out and reports it in Requirements.ignored, as an unknown type is reported. build does not raise (tools).

docs.title: What a connection value staged without its bus should mean
docs.text: Nothing. The call is rejected. {entity: dc, bus: NULL} is no multi-dim value, a multi-dim value being a whole tuple or NULL, so it is refused wherever a row comes in. The alternative, "every connection of this entity", would broadcast over part of a tuple. A multi-dim's column broadcasts only whole, and a NULL struct means every tuple.

docs.title: The package
docs.text:
The package is a core of subpackages that import each other in one direction at runtime, and a tools/ subpackage beside it. Nothing in the core names a modelling framework. Each framework lives in one tool module under datarecord/tools/, which a caller imports explicitly.

datarecord/
├── __init__.py        # every public name; where a user imports from
├── duck.py            # relation helpers
├── protocols.py       # RecordLike, LayerData, Relations, LazyRelations, EMPTY, Flags
├── schema/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Schema, Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec
│   ├── dtypes.py      # DUCK_TYPES, enum_type, enum_labels, takes
│   ├── specs.py       # Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec
│   ├── schema.py      # Schema, flag_type, LAYER_COLUMN, LONG_TAIL, DERIVED
│   └── categories.py  # selecting a categorized dim's labels, and their defaults
├── resolve/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Record
│   ├── fold.py        # Fold
│   ├── sources.py     # LayerSource, ParquetLayer, DirectorySource
│   ├── coords.py      # resolve_coords, resolve_one, Coords, mortal
│   ├── owner_map.py   # fold_attributes, the owner-map fold over keys as written, and its shared tables
│   └── record.py      # Record, PinnedRecord
├── mutable.py         # WorkingRecord, StagedSource
├── settle.py          # settle, the broadcast rule over long rows
├── store/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Workspace, Store, Revision
│   ├── store.py       # Workspace, Store, Revision, ancestry
│   ├── files.py       # Files, LocalFiles, RemoteFiles
│   ├── cache.py       # materialised node caches
│   ├── manifest.py    # read_schema, reconcile_schema
│   └── write.py       # write_layer, layer_data
└── tools/
    ├── base.py        # Tool, Schema, Attr, Requirements, UnsupportedRecordError
    └── pypsa.py       # PyPSA

docs.title: The import order
docs.text:
Runtime imports follow the order duck → schema → protocols → resolve → mutable → store → tools. A module imports at runtime only from modules earlier in that order or in its own subpackage. Nothing outside tools/ imports tools/. An import under TYPE_CHECKING may point the other way, as when resolve/ names Workspace in an annotation.

A subpackage's __init__.py re-exports its user-facing names, and datarecord/__init__.py imports them from there, so a user imports from datarecord alone. Code inside the package imports a name from the module that defines it, so no internal import runs through an __init__.py.

Workspace, Store and Revision share store/store.py because they need each other at runtime. Revision is a pydantic model with a field of type Store, and it attaches to Workspace.process() when it loads from its serialised form. Store constructs Revisions. The modules in resolve/ take a Workspace and look up workspace.con on each call, so they reach the calling thread's cursor (a cursor per thread). store/ decides where a connection and a location come from, so duck.py holds no state. mutable.py is one module because StagedSource reads the private members of WorkingRecord.

The protocols live in protocols.py because several modules consume them. A tool both implements and consumes RecordLike, and WorkingRecord satisfies it. The writer takes a LayerData, the write-side protocol a layer source answers, and wraps a RecordLike in an adapter where a tool hands one over. The protocols cannot sit beside Record either: the fold in resolve/ imports Flags, so a module that held both would import the fold back.

docs.title: Core and tools
docs.text:
One question decides on which side code lives: does it name a modelling framework? Nothing in the core may. This is how the core depends on duckdb, pydantic and mathspec alone.

A tool lives under datarecord/tools/<name>.py, one module per modelling framework. A caller imports it explicitly, as in from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSA. datarecord.tools itself imports no tool module, and the package's own __init__.py imports nothing under tools/. The dependency runs strictly one way, so importing the record layer pulls in no framework, and importing one tool pulls in no other.

docs.title: Removing labels
docs.text: A layer removes a label by restating the axis without it. Removing a label also removes its values on every attribute and the tuples of every multi-dim that name it. A property that still holds the label blocks its removal. The writer checks every layer against its final axes, a multi-dim's tuples included, so every value and tuple names a label that is there. Sibling branches keep a label that one branch removes.

docs.title: Restating an axis
docs.text:
A layer that changes an axis writes dims/<dim>.parquet whole: every label the axis has at its revision, with their properties, in order. A layer removes a label when its axis file omits a label that its parent's axis holds.

A layer removes a multi-dim's tuple the same way, by restating dims/<multi-dim>.parquet without it. An axis loses a label or tuple only where its own file omits it.

A hand-written layer whose axis file holds only a few labels is a restatement too, so it removes every label it omits.

docs.title: What a removal reaches
docs.text:
Removing the entity e1 removes its p_nom, its p_max_pu at every snapshot and scenario, and its value in every other attribute.

The fold removes the values. fold_attributes drops the parent's owner-map rows that name a label or tuple the layer removes. A key whose label or tuple was removed is then absent from the resolved map. A row that leaves the coordinate NULL names no label and stays. A dim outside partial, multi or not, is in no key, so its rows are dropped at read against that coordinate's dead labels.

A removed tuple takes its values with it. The labels it names keep their other rows, so removing a connection leaves the entity it attached.

Removing a label is one cascade, the same for every dim. remove(dim, labels) restates the axis without the labels, and every multi-dim with a coordinate over dim without the tuples that name one, in one layer. The tuples' values go with them. Re-adding a label or tuple in partial brings back the label and no value that named it below the removal. Every broadcast covering it, written before or after the removal, reaches it again. Re-adding one outside partial brings back its values, since the read only hid them.

docs.title: What the writer checks
docs.text:
The writer refuses a layer that adds a tuple naming a dead label. It refuses a layer that stores a dead label in a property that refers to a dim. It refuses a layer that removes a label which a tuple or such a property still names. A property that holds a label must be cleared before the label goes, and remove refuses the label until then.

The writer checks two kinds of subject, each whole and in its final state:

  • each subject whose rows name a label the layer removes;
  • the properties of each subject the layer restates.

It checks them against the dead labels at the layer's revision. The labels a layer removes are its parent's axis minus its restatement. A restated multi-dim's tuples are held to the layer's final axes, which hold no dead label. A reference that an ancestor left dangling therefore fails the next write that touches its subject. That write restates the subject whole, so it can drop or repair the row.

A layer's attribute rows name only labels of its final axes and tuples of its final multi-dims. Its multi-dims' tuples name only labels of its final axes. The writer checks both, so a value or a tuple names only a label that some layer added and this layer keeps.

docs.title: A layer from elsewhere
docs.text: A layer may be a parquet directory that this package did not write. Each of its dims/ files must restate its axis whole and hold each key once. Each such file carries its key and its subject's declared properties, and no other column.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: The owner map records each layer's attribute keys as the layer wrote them, with removals applied. Where a deeper layer's row crosses a parent row, the map adds one overlap row, owned by the deeper layer. For axes, a multi-dim's tuples included, the deepest file for each one is the answer. Reading an attribute joins the owning layers' files to the map with one hash join and returns the owned rows as written. The read then drops rows that name a removed label outside the key. A consumer settles each coordinate by the broadcast rule. A single directory folds as a tree with one layer. A revision can materialise its owner map and resolved axes under resolved/, and a read then stops at that revision.

docs.title: Owner map
docs.text:
The owner map is one relation over every attribute. An attribute's winning key and its winning value live in different files, since its ownership spans every layer's attributes/<attr>.parquet. The map names the owning layer per key, and a read then goes to that layer's file for the value. Every axis is a single keyed file that a layer restates whole, so it needs no map and resolves to a resolved relation.

The map's columns, keys first:

# owner map
<partial dims>          -- the fold key: exactly the partial dims, multi-dims included, NULL as written
  <owned_per coordinates> -- e.g. entity, scenario; a partial multi-dim as one STRUCT: connection STRUCT(entity, bus)
attribute
layer_uuid              -- the owning layer
varies      STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)   -- a field per dim, multi-dims included
broadcast   STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)
breakpoints BOOLEAN

The map holds no value, no value of a varying dim and no breakpoint, so its size is independent of the series data and of the length of a curve. It holds no depth either: the fold settles ownership across layers, so a read needs none.

The key derives from the schema: it is partial_dims plus attribute. A coordinate that an attribute's own file lacks reads as NULL, so the key is one fixed tuple across attributes whose columns differ. A multi-dim is one column, so the map itself shows which columns name a multi-dim's tuple. A multi-dim outside partial is in no key, as any dim outside it is in none. A layer that touches one connection's value restates the attribute's whole extent along that multi-dim. An attribute over such a multi-dim and no other partial coordinate has the key (attribute) alone, the grain of a record-level weighting.

The map holds one row per layer and per distinct key the layer wrote, a NULL key column left NULL, and the overlap rows of crossing rows. The fold builds it along the path from the root: the parent's map minus removals and the rows the layer covers, union the layer's own keys and its overlap rows. A revision whose caches are materialised persists the map and its resolved axes. A read then needs the ancestry only back to the nearest materialised revision, which is what lets a deep tree scale.

The fold applies removals to every key column. fold_attributes drops the parent rows that name a label of a partial dim, or a tuple of a partial multi-dim, which the layer's restatement omits and the previous restatement held (removing labels). A multi-dim's removed tuples are one NULL-safe anti-join on its struct column, its file's own key, which is the shape every dim's removal takes. A layer's removals apply to its parents' keys. Its own rows pass through. A plain dim's anti-join matches its top-level column only. A label inside a struct is reached through its tuple, since removing a label restates each multi-dim without the tuples naming it in the same layer. A row that leaves a key column NULL is not addressed by it, and the NULL-safe anti-join keeps it. Only a row that names a removed label or tuple is dropped.

docs.title: Crossing rows
docs.text:
A row names a partial dim where its key holds a label, and any other dim where it varies along it, so a series over snapshot names snapshot. Only the dims the attribute uses count: its dims and the coordinates' dims of its multi-dims. Two rows cover a common key where, on each partial coordinate, they hold the same label or one of them holds NULL. They cross where they cover a common key and neither names every dim the other names.

A layer folds onto its parent's map in four steps, none of which reads an axis:

  1. The parent rows naming a label or tuple that the layer removes are dropped, and a row NULL there never is.
  2. A parent row is dropped where a row of the layer covers it and names no partial dim the parent row leaves NULL.
  3. For each parent row and row of the layer that cross on partial dims, the layer gains an overlap row naming every label either names. The crossed parent row stays as written, as does a parent row naming strictly fewer dims than a row of the layer covering it.
  4. The layer's rows and its overlap rows are added.

An overlap row carries the owning layer's varies and broadcast, so the layer's value row finds it by the same NULL-safe join as its own key and reads the overlap row's labels. To a later fold it is an ordinary row, which that fold drops, crosses or removes like any other. The pairs are found by one equi-join per pair of named sets, over the dims both name, so no join compares every row with every other.

docs.title: Why the map holds keys as written
docs.text:
Two rules decide which row gives a value. Within one layer, the more specific row wins (the broadcast rule). Across layers, the deeper layer wins. The two disagree only where rows of two layers cross. There an overlap row, owned by the deeper layer and naming the labels of both, makes them agree. Everywhere else the rows stay as written, and the broadcast rule alone gives every answer.

Take partial = {entity, scenario}, a root layer that sets p_nom per entity, and a child that sets it for one scenario:

root layer                     child layer
entity  scenario  value        entity  scenario  value
gas     NULL       50          NULL    high      999
wind    NULL      100

At (wind, high) the root's row names entity and the child's row names scenario, so neither row is more specific. The child is deeper, so 999 wins there, while (wind, low) keeps the root's 100. The fold adds an overlap row for each crossing pair:

# owner map                          # attributes["p_nom"]
entity  scenario  attribute  layer   entity  scenario  value
gas     NULL      p_nom      root    gas     NULL       50
wind    NULL      p_nom      root    wind    NULL      100
NULL    high      p_nom      child   NULL    high      999
gas     high      p_nom      child   gas     high      999   -- overlap rows
wind    high      p_nom      child   wind    high      999

At (wind, high) the overlap row names every dim the other two name, so the broadcast rule gives 999. A child writing (gas, NULL) = 60 instead names no more than the root's (gas, NULL), and step 2 drops the root's row. A child writing (gas, high) = 70 names more and leaves the root's rows as written, and the broadcast rule gives (gas, high) to the child.

The map grows with the rows layers write and the pairs that cross, not with the labels a broadcast reaches. A depth per row would let the read settle ownership instead, but every read would then pay what the fold pays once, and a consumer would have to know about layers.

docs.title: What a row reaches
docs.text:
A NULL on a partial coordinate reaches every label of that coordinate's axis, or every tuple of its multi-dim, as resolved at the node read. The fold reads no axis and splits no row, so a label added below a materialised node is reached, as is a label staged in a WorkingRecord and the first label of an axis that was empty when the broadcast was written. Adding the scenario mid below the child above reads (gas, mid) as 50.

A row reaches every coordinate that no more specific row covers, whichever layer wrote it. A deeper layer thus owns only the coordinates its rows reach. With partial = {entity, scenario} and x also over snapshot, a root writing (gas, NULL, 1) = 1.0 and a child writing (NULL, high, 0) = 2.0, (gas, high, 1) reads 1.0 from the root.

A label removed and added again takes every broadcast covering it, written before or after the removal, and no row that named it below the removal (what a removal reaches).

docs.title: A dim outside partial
docs.text:
An overlap row cannot settle a crossing on a dim outside partial, since the key has no column to name its labels. A WorkingRecord settles it as it stages: a staged row leaving such a dim NULL, over a base row naming it, is also written out along the base row's labels there, with the staged value. With partial = {entity}, a root writing a series over snapshot for every entity and a child setting wind to 0.9:

root:             (NULL, 0) = 0.2   (NULL, 1) = 0.5
child as staged:  (wind, NULL) = 0.9
child as written: (wind, NULL) = 0.9   (wind, 0) = 0.9   (wind, 1) = 0.9

The child's rows at wind name entity and snapshot, a strict superset of the root's, so nothing crosses and the root's series stays as written. The fold refuses a layer written otherwise that leaves such a crossing, naming the layer, the attribute, the dim and the key.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
The fold computes the flags of each map row in the group-by that builds the layer's rows, so they cost nothing beyond it. It computes them per key, so per entity: whether this entity's p_max_pu sets timestep differs from whether any entity's does. An overlap row carries the flags of the layer's row it comes from. flags() aggregates the map's rows per attribute, bool_or over each field of varies and broadcast and over breakpoints. It describes the rows the map keeps, so a broadcast that deeper rows shadow at every label still counts.

Each struct has a field per coordinate: every declared dim, multi-dims included. A dim that a multi-dim draws on has its own field, so a marginal_price constant over buses reports bus as broadcast.

The flags are two structs because which dims exist is declared. A column per dim would make the map's column set depend on the schema. Versioning calls adding a dim compatible, and that has to hold for a map persisted at a materialised revision too. In a struct, the new dim is a missing field, which UNION ALL BY NAME fills with NULL as it would a missing column. The new dim then reads as unset, which is true, since no row mentions it. The map's columns stay fixed, and only the fields change.

breakpoints sits outside both structs, since a breakpoint is no dim (wide and long rows). The dim namespace lives entirely inside varies and broadcast, so a dim named breakpoints collides with nothing.

Record.flags() unions the flags over the record. flags(**categories) unions them over the rows reaching the labels of those categories, a row NULL on the coordinate reaching every label. Reading says what the union means to a consumer.

docs.title: One fold for every axis
docs.text:
Every dim's axis is one construct: a keyed relation that a layer restates whole. A plain dim's key is the column named for it, and a multi-dim's key is its one struct column. Every axis resolves by one path. A revision's resolved relation for an axis is the deepest file for it on the path from the root. Each row carries its properties, such as ctype on the entity axis and role on connection, and no layer_uuid. The fold refuses a file that holds a key twice, or that carries a column other than its key and its subject's declared properties.

The resolved relation comes in member order, which is the deepest file's row order. A revision's caches persist it in that order, so a reader recovers member order from the resolved file's own row number. A key that one layer removes and a later layer adds again is a row of the later layer's file, and sits where that file puts it. Member order is the file's row order and is no stored column. A consumer that wants positional ports numbers an entity's connections by this order. So the writer refuses a restatement that orders its parent's labels differently, naming the first label out of place, which prevents the positional-keying failure. A new label may sit anywhere among its parent's. A WorkingRecord appends one, so a layer it writes renumbers no existing port. The order holds across a materialised parent, whose resolved file is a copy of the deepest layer file at or below it, read in its own row order.

Every property is a column of its subject's file, so the resolved axis holds everything a per-category read needs. One category's labels are properties[dim] filtered on its categorizing columns.

Over the unmaterialised tail of an ancestry, the fold runs live and caches its results in the workspace's database as shared tables. Layers are write-once, so such a cache never needs invalidating.

docs.title: Resolving a relation
docs.text:
A resolved relation joins the owning layers' files to the owner map and keeps only owned rows:

SELECT u.timestep,
       COALESCE(u.scenario, o.__owned_scenario) AS scenario,   -- one per owned_per coordinate, entity likewise
       u.attribute, u.breakpoint, u.value
FROM ( -- one arm per distinct layer the map names for this attribute
  SELECT ?::UUID AS layer_uuid, * FROM read_parquet(<layer>/attributes/<attr>.parquet)
  UNION ALL BY NAME
  ...
) u
JOIN ( -- the map keyed as its owning layer stored each key
  SELECT * EXCLUDE (scenario), scenario AS __owned_scenario,
         UNNEST(list_concat(
           CASE WHEN COALESCE(varies.scenario, false)   THEN [scenario] END,
           CASE WHEN COALESCE(broadcast.scenario, true) THEN [NULL] END
         )) AS scenario
  FROM owner_map
) o
  ON o.attribute  = u.attribute
 AND o.layer_uuid = u.layer_uuid
 AND o.scenario   IS NOT DISTINCT FROM u.scenario  -- owned-per coordinates: as stored, NULL included

The query projects the attribute's own coordinates (the long schema). That is connection for an attribute over that multi-dim, entity for a per-entity one, and none of them for a record-level weighting. The join conditions follow from the key columns the attribute's file carries, so the schema derives the query's shape. A coordinate outside the key, here timestep or a multi-dim outside partial, is in no join condition and passes straight through.

The map already names the winning layer per key, so resolution reads only the owning layers' files. A read runs no MAX or group-by of its own. It returns the owned rows as written: a key NULL on a dim stays NULL, an overlap row reads its labels, and no row is expanded or dropped by depth. The row order is unspecified. A consumer settles each coordinate by the broadcast rule over the full coordinates, partial or not, and needs neither depth nor the list of partial dims. Wherever two rows cross, the fold or the staging has written a row naming both, so the rule finds one winner wherever a row reaches. Its only filter of removed labels covers what the map cannot see (below).

The join condition for each owned-per coordinate is NULL-aware. A stored NULL means every value. The row joins its own map row, where it stays NULL, and each overlap row of its layer that names its key, where it takes that row's label in the output. The plain condition u.scenario IS NULL OR u.scenario IS NOT DISTINCT FROM o.scenario is no hash key. DuckDB would join on the other columns and filter the dim afterwards, which costs the square of the dim's length per key.

So the map is keyed as its owning layer stored each key, which its flags record. A map row keeps its value where the layer's row set the dim (varies), and holds NULL where the row left it NULL (broadcast), with the owned value carried beside it. A layer row then finds its owned keys by its stored values, NULLs included, on NULL-safe equality. That is one hash join, which scans the layers and the map once each. A flag field missing from a map folded before the dim was declared counts as broadcast here, since the layers' rows hold NULL there. The flags a consumer reads count it as unset.

An overlap row reads its labels, so a layer that also wrote a row naming those labels answers that coordinate twice. Where a layer holds rows of an attribute naming different sets of partial dims, the read keeps at each coordinate the row that names every partial dim another row there names, the more specific one, through a window over the attribute's coordinates. A coordinate with no such row, or with two at one breakpoint, fails the read, naming the attribute and the coordinate. breakpoint is no coordinate, so the window keeps or drops a curve whole. An attribute whose layers each name one set of dims, the common case, skips the window.

A staged layer has not met the write's refusal of two rows neither more specific. So the read of a WorkingRecord fails where two staged rows cross and no staged row names both, naming the attribute and the coordinate.

A partial multi-dim column such as connection joins NULL-aware exactly as scenario does, and a NULL there reaches every tuple of the resolved multi-dim. DuckDB hash-joins IS NOT DISTINCT FROM on a STRUCT key directly. A dim the multi-dim draws on, such as bus beside it on a per-bus attribute, is a coordinate of its own and joins NULL-aware where it is partial.

The query projects breakpoint and does not join on it, since it is no part of the key. A curve is owned whole (wide and long rows), so every breakpoint of a key comes from the winning layer. Dims outside the key pass through unchanged, because the rows of one key come from one layer.

An attribute that no layer wrote is absent from the map. Its relation is empty, and the consumer applies the schema's default.

docs.title: A label outside the key
docs.text:
The fold prunes removed labels from every key coordinate, so a row whose label of a partial dim or tuple of a partial multi-dim was removed is already gone from the map. A dim outside partial, multi or not, is in no key, so the fold cannot see its labels. With connection owned whole, a connection attribute's map row is (attribute) alone and owns every tuple's value.

The read drops those rows instead. It anti-joins each such coordinate against its dead labels: the labels that some layer removed and the final axis lacks. A multi-dim's dead labels are its dead tuples, so a removed tuple's values go whichever way the multi-dim is keyed. The fold computes dead labels for each coordinate outside the owner-map key, and for each dim that a multi-dim's coordinate draws on or a property refers to. They are the base's dead set, the base's resolved axis and every restatement above the base, minus the final axis. The fold keeps them beside the resolved axes. A materialised revision caches them, since its resolved relations hold only live labels and a read above it would otherwise miss a label removed below. The set is usually empty, and the join against it cheap.

docs.title: One record over one fold
docs.text:
There is one Record, and it is the fold itself. Its mappings hand over the folded axes, multi-dims included, and each attribute as the owner map resolves it. Workspace.at(uri) folds over a single DirectorySource. Over one source the fold is a scan of it: every key is owned by the one layer, and the anti-join has nothing to evict.

A directory therefore has the same properties as a revision:

  • flags come from the ownership group-by in the same scan. They need a real aggregate in any case, since parquet's footer statistics are per row group. A file that mixes one label's series rows with another label's constant says nothing about either in its footer.
  • Member order is the file's row order, the general rule over one source.
  • schema.partial sets the granularity of a patch, and one layer patches nothing, so partial is inert there.

The fold requires a layer layout, and a record directory is one. A directory copied out of any tree, with no revision file, reads identically.

docs.title: Materialised node caches
docs.text:
A revision's owner map and resolved axes may be materialised under layers/<id>/resolved/. The schema is not, since there is one for the whole record and nothing per revision to resolve.

Where a materialised map exists, a read stops there. The map is already folded over everything above it, so a read walks the ancestry back to the nearest materialised revision and no further. That truncation keeps a deep chain cheap. The same rule decides where resolved axes come from: a revision's own resolved/dims/ where materialised, and its raw dims/ otherwise. The presence of the cache answers this, and no recorded state is involved. A map whose key columns are not those the schema's partial gives is no cache: one persisted before a dim joined partial holds NULL there for a row varying along it, so the read folds from the layers as if nothing were materialised. The two are distinct paths within one directory, so a record read as an ancestor and the same record read as itself never alias. resolved/dims/ holds copies of the deepest layer file for each axis, a multi-dim's included, at or below the revision, so a read of an axis stops there too.

Beside them, resolved/dead/<coord>.parquet holds the dead labels of each coordinate outside the owner-map key, and of each dim that a multi-dim's coordinate draws on or a property refers to. It is written only where there are any. A read above the revision seeds its dead labels from these files, since the copied axis files hold only live labels. resolved/dead/ and owner_map.parquet are folds, since no layer file holds either.

Materialising is a policy: every N layers, at a branch point, or on demand. It only adds files under resolved/, so it changes no answer, only how many layers a read touches. The persisted map is the fold's result, and a NULL in it reaches the labels of the node read, so a label added below the node is reached as it would be without the cache.

docs.title: A tree of layers
docs.text:
A revision adds one layer on top of its parent, and the revisions form a tree. A layer's data is written once, so any revision can be a parent and every cache stays valid. Reading a revision folds its ancestry from the root, and a deeper layer's row wins where it crosses a shallower one. A layer restates each axis it touches as a whole, a multi-dim's tuples included. For attributes, partial sets what one layer may override. Along a partial dim, a layer overrides one value per label. Along any other dim, it restates the whole extent of each key it touches.

class Revision(BaseModel):
    id: UUID
    parent: UUID | None  # None for a root
    store: Store  # serialised as its location

A revision's layer sits at <location>/layers/<id>/. The path derives from the id and the revision's store, so the revision stores no path. Branching is several revisions sharing one parent. The children point at the parent, so they share its layer and all further ancestry. Each revision's (id, parent) is a file beside the layers, so the location alone resolves a revision id to its ancestry and its layers.

The fold reads the layers in ancestry order along the path from the root, and the revision's own layer comes last. Resolution is how it settles each key, and removing labels is a restatement of the axis without them.

docs.title: A layer's data is write-once
docs.text:
A revision has no mutable state. One act creates a layer's data: store.root or rev.child. rev.child is also how a WorkingRecord's edits become a layer. The write refuses an existing directory and stages into a sibling path, so a layer is complete when it first becomes visible. Its revision file is written last, and that file makes the layer reachable. Editing needs no mutable layer: edits accumulate in the staging area until they are written as a child.

After that act, the only thing written into a layer directory is its resolved/ cache, so the invariant covers the layer's data. A cache derives from immutable layers, so writing one changes no answer, and no read takes it for data. Every glob the read path issues into a layer is single-level: attributes/*.parquet and dims/*.parquet. No glob reaches resolved/, so a reader pointed at a layer directory sees exactly what that layer wrote.

Two things follow. Any revision may be a parent, since an immutable base cannot shift under its descendants. A cache never needs invalidating, since a cache derived from immutable layers cannot go stale.

docs.title: partial: the granularity of an override
docs.text:
A layer exists to override, and every value is overridable. partial decides how finely a layer overrides along each axis. That question differs from the one AttributeSpec answers, because each belongs to a different thing:

  • Which dims may an attribute vary over? This belongs to the attribute, as AttributeSpec.dims. p_max_pu varies over scenario and snapshot, and p_nom over neither.
  • May a layer patch single values along an axis, or must it restate the axis whole? This belongs to the dim, as schema.partial. A layer patches scenario value by value, and restates snapshot whole for every attribute.
partial = {"scenario"}  # snapshot absent, so a patch restates the series

A layer that touches one value along a dim outside partial restates that key's whole extent along the dim. Overriding one snapshot of p_max_pu therefore carries the entity's entire series, which a WorkingRecord stages beside the edit. Ownership itself follows reach: a row reaches every coordinate no more specific row covers, whichever layer wrote it (what a row reaches). A partial series would resolve into a mix: the layer's values at the snapshots it wrote, and its parent's at the rest. A framework that splits constant from varying data cannot receive half a series. That holds for every attribute over the axis, so the rule belongs to the axis.

The dims a layer owns an attribute per follow from the declarations:

owned_per(attribute) = attribute.dims ∩ partial_dims
partial_dims         = the dims in schema.partial, multi-dims included

partial_dims is the fold key: the dims that partial names, multi-dims included, in declaration order. A schema that patches entity by entity lists entity, as PyPSA's {entity, bus, scenario, connection} does. A layer that patches a per-bus marginal_price one bus at a time needs bus in partial. A layer that patches one connection's efficiency needs connection there, and the connection's bus is patched with it inside the connection column. Under PyPSA's partial, p_max_pu is owned per entity and per scenario, so a patch to one hour restates that entity and scenario's whole series. marginal_cost is owned per entity and scenario, and p_nom per entity, once across everything else.

Splitting the two questions lets the schema tell p_max_pu from p_nom. A flag on the dim alone would make every attribute owned per scenario, including the ones a scenario must not change. A p_nom row that carries scenario is refused at write, since p_nom is not addressed by scenario (the long schema). A first-stage decision turned into a per-scenario one is the error worth catching.

The owner-map key is (*partial_dims, attribute), one fixed tuple for every attribute. An attribute that does not vary over a key coordinate writes NULL there, and the key compares NULL-safe. A multi-dim in partial sits in the key as its struct column, so a per-connection attribute is owned per connection. With the multi-dim outside partial, a patch to one connection's efficiency restates every connection's value. A tuple is keyed by its labels, so an ancestor that inserts a tuple earlier cannot redirect a patch.

breakpoint (wide and long rows) is outside the overlay key. A layer owns a whole curve, as it restates a whole extent along a dim outside partial. So a resolved curve never mixes a parent's breakpoints with a descendant's.

partial governs attribute ownership alone. A layer that touches an axis file restates it whole, every label with its properties in order, whatever partial says (removing labels). The properties an axis carries are no reason to add it to partial, with one exception. A property categorizes its dim only when the dim is in partial.

Keep partial small. Every partial coordinate widens the fold key, and every read of every attribute pays for the key. Leaving a coordinate out costs once per edit, bounded by the size of the axis. Putting it in costs every read. PyPSA's partial names only the dims a layer patches value by value: entity, bus, scenario and connection. snapshot and carrier stay out. A layer patches one bus's v_nom, and restates every carrier's co2_emissions, a few dozen rows.

docs.title: Attributes and the broadcast rule
docs.text: An attribute is data: long rows of coordinates, a breakpoint and a value, one file per attribute. Its dims name the dims that address it, multi-dims among them. A NULL coordinate means every label of that dim (the broadcast rule). A solve's results are attributes like any other. A child layer inherits its parent's results, and after an input edit the caller keeps them coherent (open questions). Which attributes a framework computes is its tool's knowledge (PyPSA).

docs.title: AttributeSpec
docs.text:
An AttributeSpec declares what one attribute may do over the record's axes:

attributes = {
    # a capacity to build: one decision, evaluated against every scenario
    "p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity"}),
    # an availability profile: varies over time, and per scenario
    "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity", "scenario", "snapshot"}),
    "marginal_cost": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="float", dims={"entity", "scenario"}, breakpoints=True
    ),
    # addressed by a multi-dim
    "efficiency": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"connection", "snapshot"}),
    # addressed by an axis alone: a weighting belongs to no entity
    "objective_weighting": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"snapshot"}),
}

One attribute is one spec, one file and one value dtype.

dims is the only addressing mechanism. It names a multi-dim as it names any dim, and a multi-dim's labels are tuples. The declaration and the storage of the attribute stay the same.

dims also makes a scenario-varying p_nom a schema violation. A capacity is a first-stage decision, one value taken before the scenario is known, and stochastic scenarios differ only in dispatch.

dims says which coordinates address a value. It says nothing about what kind of value it is. p_nom over entity alone is data an optimiser decides, and carrier describes the entity, so carrier is a property.

breakpoints declares whether the attribute may carry a piecewise-linear curve. The write refuses a curve on an attribute that takes one value (wide and long rows).

Every attribute is long rows in attributes/<attr>.parquet, whatever its dims. The section a name is declared in decides where a value lives. Widening dims adds a column to the same file.

default and default_by give the value for a coordinate that no row covers.

docs.title: The broadcast rule
docs.text:
A row's value applies to every combination of its NULL dim columns, enumerated from the axis frames in dims. A NULL dim means all labels of that dim. A constant p_max_pu is one row with snapshot = NULL, and a varying one is a row per snapshot.

set("p_max_pu", 0.9) is one row with entity = NULL that reaches every entity, loads and entities added in a later layer included. A tool that does not take the value for a load leaves it out. A value for some categories is written per label, set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator").

A multi-dim's column broadcasts too, over its resolved tuples. A NULL connection means every connection, expanded against dims/connection.parquet as a NULL snapshot is expanded against dims/snapshot.parquet. The dims a multi-dim draws on broadcast on their own: a connection's bus is a field of the connection column, so a per-bus marginal_price with bus = NULL holds one value for every bus.

Within one layer, the more specific row wins. Two rows of one layer may cover one coordinate, such as a p_nom row with entity = NULL beside one that names a. A row that names a label of a dim is more specific than one that leaves that dim NULL. Where one row names every dim the other names and more, it wins at every coordinate both cover. Two rows may cover one coordinate where each names a dim the other leaves NULL, or where both name the same dims at one breakpoint. Neither row is then more specific. The write refuses such a layer, and a read of a layer written another way fails. Both errors name the attribute and the coordinate. Rows of two layers meet at a coordinate too, and the rule decides between them the same way. Where a deeper layer's row crosses a shallower one, the fold adds a row naming both, owned by the deeper layer, so the rule finds one winner wherever a row reaches.

A coordinate that no row covers takes the attribute's default from the schema. That includes every coordinate of an attribute with no rows. The default is the default_by entry for the label's category where one exists, else default.

The read preserves broadcast form. A value held once is answered once, so a consumer can tell a constant from a varying value by the shape it gets back. The read returns the rows as written, NULL included, along every dim, and the consumer applies the rule over the full coordinates. It needs neither the layers nor the partial dims to do so.

docs.title: Wide and long rows
docs.text:
A record hands over its data in two shapes.

dims and properties are wide, one row per label or tuple:

dims["entity"]                     entity                              key columns only
dims["connection"]                 connection STRUCT(entity, bus)      key columns only
properties["entity"]               entity | ctype | carrier | ... stored values
properties["connection"]           connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role

dims[dim] is the axis's key, the label, in axis order; a multi-dim's is its one struct column. Reading covers properties and categories.

attributes are long, one row per value, keyed by the attribute's name:

attributes["p_nom"]        entity | attribute | breakpoint | value
attributes["p_max_pu"]     entity | <one column per coordinate> | attribute | breakpoint | value
attributes["efficiency"]   connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | <...> | attribute | breakpoint | value

A row names what the value belongs to, the coordinate it sits at, and the value there.

The coordinate columns are the attribute's own, which its dims declare, with a multi-dim carried as one struct column named for it. efficiency over the connection multi-dim carries connection, flow over a corridor carries corridor, and objective_weighting over snapshot alone carries no entity column. A consumer that wants a multi-dim's coordinates flat takes connection.bus in SQL, or unnests. A numpy-backed pandas frame has no struct dtype, so a pandas consumer unnests on the DuckDB side first. union_by_name lets the fold union files of differing shape, and it supplies NULL for a coordinate that a file does not carry.

An attribute row holds no property columns, so attributes["p_max_pu"] holds every entity's p_max_pu together. A consumer that wants one category's rows joins properties["entity"], filtered on the category, on entity.

breakpoint is NULL in the ordinary case. It carries the abscissa of a piecewise-linear value: a curve is one row per breakpoint, with value the ordinate at each. The record never checks or records convexity, which is a framework's judgement.

properties and attributes answer stored values only and apply no default. A NULL property is one that no layer wrote, and a coordinate that no row covers is absent. The consumer applies a default, a property's or an attribute's, through Schema.default_for.

docs.title: Dims and labels
docs.text:
A dim is a set of unique labels, declared with a dtype from mathspec. The row order of a dim's file is its order. A dim with one_of allows only the labels its one_of names. The axis holds the labels that layers have added. A property may map each label to a label of another dim, such as a snapshot to its period (mapping labels to another dim).

Every dim is declared in the schema, so a record with region, technology or vintage needs no code change. A Dimension declares the axis's type and, optionally, its one_of, unit and description (the schema). A dim declaring over instead is a multi-dim, whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels. Which dims an attribute varies over is declared per attribute. The patch granularity is partial. What describes or classifies a label is one of the dim's properties.

docs.title: Axis order
docs.text:
An axis's order is the row order of its frame in dims. The labels of an axis, a multi-dim's tuples among them, come in the row order of the deepest layer file for that axis (one fold for every axis). A label or tuple that one layer removes and a later layer adds again sits where the later layer's file puts it.

Writers need to ensure data is not inadvertently reordered from its parent's labels, since the order may carry meaning, such as port numbering, which follows from the connection order.

docs.title: A dim with one_of
docs.text:
A dim with one_of: [labels] allows only those labels, as a mathspec dimension does. Its dtype is str, the default. A one_of on any other dtype is refused at load. So is an empty list, a label listed twice, a label that is no string, and a dim name in place of the list. The dim's column is an ENUM of the labels (dtypes).

The list bounds the axis. add refuses a label outside the list. The axis file holds the labels that layers have added and not removed. remove works as on any dim. A property that refers to the dim holds a live label like any other. A tool may write the whole list, as PyPSA's does for ctype and role. That is the tool's convention.

docs.title: Mapping labels to another dim
docs.text:
A dim's labels may map to labels of another dim, such as each snapshot to its period. A property that refers to the other dim holds that map, with at most one label per label of its subject. mathspec declares the same map as a mathspec relation, {key: snapshot, values: period}. PyPSA's multi-period (period, timestep) snapshot is a dim snapshot with two such properties, snapshot.period and snapshot.timestep. A snapshot label is unique across the dim, so a source that repeats its timesteps in every period gives each snapshot a label of its own (PyPSA). A level above the period is a property of period, such as period.horizon (a chain is a join). A selector keyword such as period=2030 picks the snapshots of that period (set).

properties = {
    "snapshot": {
        "period": PropertySpec(one_of="period"),
        "timestep": PropertySpec(one_of="timestep"),
    }
}

docs.title: Multi-dims
docs.text:
A multi-dim is a dim whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels, which is a sparse subset of their product. It is declared under dimensions with over and has its own table in dims/, as any dim does. A record carries a multi-dim as one struct column named for it, in its table and in every attribute row over it. The value of that column is a whole tuple or NULL. A multi-dim's property may refer to a dim, such as a bus's country per scenario.

dimensions = {
    "entity": Dimension(dtype="str"),
    "bus": Dimension(dtype="str"),
    "scenario": Dimension(dtype="str"),
    "connection": Dimension(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}),
    "corridor": Dimension(over={"from": "bus", "to": "bus"}),
    "bus_country": Dimension(over=["bus", "scenario"]),
}

A dim without over declares an axis of labels. A multi-dim declares which combinations of labels exist, which no single axis can say because the product is sparse: an entity attaches to two buses out of a thousand. A multi-dim has its own order, as any axis has (axis order).

over maps each coordinate name to the dim it draws its labels from. Two coordinates may draw on the same dim: a corridor between two buses is (from, to). A list is short for the dict with identical keys and values, so over=["bus"] is over={"bus": "bus"}. Each coordinate draws on a declared dim that is no multi-dim. A multi-dim has no dtype and no one_of, and the schema refuses one declaring over beside either. Schema.dimensions holds every dim, multi or not, and Dimension.over holds the map.

docs.title: One struct column
docs.text:
An attribute over a multi-dim carries it as one struct column named for it, with a field per coordinate in over order:

attributes/efficiency.parquet       connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value
attributes/flow.parquet             corridor STRUCT("from", "to")  | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value
attributes/marginal_price.parquet   bus | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value

The column's name says which multi-dim constrains the row, so two multi-dims may share a set of coordinates. A coordinate stays inside its struct: bus inside connection is a field, and the dim bus is a separate column beside it.

A multi-dim's table is keyed by the same column. dims/connection.parquet is connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role, as dims/bus.parquet is keyed by bus, so a row and the tuple it names meet on one column. A layer that changes its tuples or their properties writes it whole and in order, as it writes any axis (one fold for every axis).

The other columns of the table are the multi-dim's properties, declared under its name. PyPSA's role on a connection is properties: {connection: {role: ...}}, which the tool declares. An attribute over the multi-dim is long rows in attributes/ keyed by the struct (where a value lives).

A multi-dim's property may refer to a dim, as any dim's property may. One value per tuple is what a property is. A mapping that varies along another dim needs a multi-dim: a bus's country per scenario is the multi-dim bus_country over [bus, scenario] with the property bus_country.country: {one_of: country}, stored as dims/bus_country.parquet with columns bus_country STRUCT(bus, scenario) | country. A mapping that does not vary is a property of the dim, bus.country. A multi-dim is never categorized: a property of it that refers to a dim with one_of categorizes nothing, whether partial lists the multi-dim or not (categories). A property refers to a dim that is no multi-dim.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
connection.bus names the bus of each tuple, wherever a dotted subject.name stands, as a property is named. Schema.resolve("connection.bus") answers the multi-dim and the dim the coordinate draws on. A coordinate is part of the key, not a value, so set refuses set("connection.bus", ...) and points at remove and add, and a default_by keyed on a coordinate is refused, a multi-dim having no categories. A property of a multi-dim named like one of its coordinates is refused at load (names).

A selector keyword stays bare: bus="north" on an attribute over connection selects the tuples whose bus is north.

docs.title: Attributes over a multi-dim
docs.text:
An attribute names a multi-dim in its dims as it names any dim:

"efficiency": AttributeSpec(dims={"connection", "timestep"}),  # connection | timestep
"co2_budget": AttributeSpec(dims={"country"}),  # country

The attribute has one coordinate for the multi-dim: its struct column. The tuples are that coordinate's labels, as an axis's labels are a dim's. A NULL struct means every tuple (the broadcast rule). Any other value is a whole tuple. A struct with some fields NULL, such as {entity: dc, bus: NULL}, names no tuple, and set, add and the writer refuse it. The dims a multi-dim draws on broadcast on their own, so a per-bus marginal_price with bus = NULL holds one value for every bus.

Removing a label that a tuple names removes the tuple and its values (removing labels). A declared multi-dim with no rows reads back as an empty relation.

partial may name a multi-dim as it names a dim, and then a layer overrides one tuple's value at a time. Otherwise a layer restates the attribute's whole extent along it. The fold's key is the same for every attribute: partial_dims is one fixed tuple of exactly the dims that partial names. Schema.coordinates_of lists an attribute's multi-dims first, then its other dims in the schema's declaration order.

An attribute may not name a multi-dim beside a dim that shares a name with one of its coordinates, since a keyword such as bus= in set would address both. dims={"connection", "bus"} is refused for that reason. A multi-dim whose coordinate draws on bus under another name, such as port, may sit beside bus.

docs.title: Properties and categories
docs.text: A property holds one value per label of its subject, which is a dim, a multi-dim's tuples being its labels. It describes the label, so it has no dims of its own. A caller names a property as subject.name, and a plain name means an attribute. A property may refer to a dim, and then each value is a live label of that dim. If that dim has one_of and the subject is in partial and no multi-dim, the property categorizes the subject. Categories select labels and key per-category defaults.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Properties are declared per subject:

dimensions = {
    "ctype": Dimension(one_of=["Generator", "Line", "Load"]),
    "carrier": Dimension(dtype="str"),
    "country": Dimension(dtype="str"),
    ...,
}
properties = {
    "entity": {
        "ctype": PropertySpec(one_of="ctype"),
        "carrier": PropertySpec(one_of="carrier"),
        "sign": PropertySpec(
            dtype="float", default=1, default_by={"entity.ctype": {"Load": -1}}
        ),
    },
    "bus": {
        "carrier": PropertySpec(one_of="carrier", default="AC"),
        "x": PropertySpec(dtype="float", unit="°"),
        "country": PropertySpec(one_of="country"),
    },
    "carrier": {"color": PropertySpec(dtype="str", default="")},
    "connection": {"role": PropertySpec(dtype="str")},
}

A property is a column of its subject's own file, dims/<dim>.parquet, a multi-dim's included (where a value lives). ctype is a column of dims/entity.parquet because it is declared under entity.

An attribute is data: what a model reads as part of its problem and what a layer varies. Whether a name is a property or an attribute is the author's declaration. A tool reads it from its framework's registry where it can (PyPSA). Each section decides the file a value is stored in, so widening an attribute's dims to [entity, scenario] is a compatible change that keeps its rows where earlier layers wrote them.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
A property's name belongs to its subject. An attribute name is one spec record-wide, with one file and one value dtype (AttributeSpec). A property name is unique within its subject's file only. x on bus sits beside an attribute x, a line's reactance, and carrier is a property of entity, a property of bus and a dim. The schema refuses at load a property named like a column of its subject's key, which is the dim's column, a multi-dim's struct column. It also refuses a multi-dim's property named like one of its coordinates, since those are the keywords that address a tuple and the names a coordinate is addressed by. Two spellings that differ only in case are refused record-wide (names).

A caller addresses a property as subject.name, such as entity.ctype, bus.x or connection.role. This holds wherever a caller names one: in set, as a default_by key, and in default_for. A plain name is always an attribute, however few subjects declare a property of that name. Its meaning stays the same when another subject declares the name later. Schema.resolve(name) returns the AttributeSpec, or the subject and the PropertySpec, or for a multi-dim's coordinate such as connection.bus the multi-dim and the dim the coordinate draws on. For an unknown plain name it raises an error that lists the dotted forms of the properties of that name.

A column keeps its plain name. The frames of properties[subject], and the categories that flags and default_for take, are each read against one subject already. A selector keyword is bare: it matches a coordinate of the attribute first, else any property of a dim the attribute reaches.

docs.title: Referring to a dim
docs.text:
A property may refer to a dim with one_of: <dim> in place of dtype. Its values are that dim's labels, typed as the dim (dtypes). Above, entity.carrier and bus.carrier refer to carrier, and bus.country to country. Any subject, a multi-dim or not, may declare such a property. The schema refuses at load a property that refers to an undeclared dim or to a multi-dim.

A stored value that is not NULL must be a live label of the dim. The record checks it where it checks a multi-dim's coordinate. set and add refuse a label that the record as staged lacks. The writer refuses a layer that stores a label the layer removes. remove refuses a label that a property still holds. NULL is no label.

A property of a dim holds one value per label, so a classification of a dim's label is single-valued. A many-to-many classification is an ordinary multi-dim. A multi-dim's property is one column of its tuple's row in the same way. It may be NULL, so a tuple may carry no label (open questions).

A chain of classifications is stored as a chain of properties. bus→state→country is two properties, bus.state and state.country, and the chain is a join over two axis files.

An attribute over country reads back keyed by country. A consumer that needs it per bus joins through the classification.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
A property categorizes its subject when both of these hold:

  • The subject is a dim in partial, and no multi-dim. Only there is a dim owned per label, and a default per label needs that. A multi-dim is never categorized.
  • The property refers to a dim with one_of. The one_of is a declared list, so the schema checks each category that a default or a selection names.

entity.ctype: {one_of: ctype} with ctype: {one_of: [Generator, Line, ...]} is one. Its values are the subject's categories along that property. A default_by keys on them, and a selector keyword selects by them. Schema.categorizing(dim) lists a dim's categorizing properties in declaration order. A dim may have several: a technology property that refers to a dim technology with one_of categorizes entity beside ctype. The schema refuses a default_by key on a property that fails a condition, and the error names the property and the reason.

A label's categories are its values of the categorizing properties. An entity with ctype = Generator has the category Generator, which is itself a label of the dim ctype.

Categories do two things:

  • They select labels. flags(ctype="Generator"), a selector keyword and a consumer's per-category frame all pick the labels with that category.
  • They pick a default. default_for(name, ctype="Generator") gives the default of an attribute or property for such a label.

The keyword is the property's plain name, ctype, not entity.ctype. A category in the one_of that no label holds is valid and selects no label.

A label's category can change, because set patches a categorizing property like any other. The label keeps its attribute values, and a per-category read uses its current categories.

docs.title: default_by: a default per category
docs.text:
default is the fallback. default_by maps a categorizing property, written as subject.name, to overrides per category. Attributes and properties both take it:

"p_min_pu": AttributeSpec(
    dtype="float", dims={"entity", "snapshot"}, default=0,
    default_by={"entity.ctype": {"StorageUnit": -1}},
)

An unset value takes the first default_by key, in declaration order, whose map lists the label's category. Otherwise it takes default.

  • Each key must categorize a dim the value reaches. Such a dim is one the value names directly, such as entity, or one a coordinate of its multi-dim draws on, such as the entity coordinate of connection.
  • The schema refuses a category that is not in the one_of of the dim the key refers to.
  • A categorizing property takes a plain default and no default_by, since a category defaulted by a category is circular.
  • Only the default varies. dtype, unit and description belong to the spec, which keeps one name to one column and one attributes/ file.

A default is never stored. record.properties and record.attributes hand over stored rows, and a consumer applies a default through default_for. The PyPSA tool does so when it builds a component's static frame.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
A record has one schema, written as manifest.json beside its layers. It declares the record's dims, properties and attributes, maps each dtype to one DuckDB type, and limits which names may become columns.

class Dimension(BaseModel):
    """One axis attribute data may vary over."""

    over: dict[str, str] | None = None  # a multi-dim: coordinate -> dim
    dtype: DimensionDtype | None = "str"  # float, int, str or datetime
    one_of: tuple[str, ...] | None = None  # the labels a str dim allows
    unit: str | None = None  # what the labels measure, if anything
    description: str | None = None  # what the axis is, in prose


class AttributeSpec(BaseModel):
    """What shape one attribute's data may take."""

    dtype: ParameterDtype  # float, int, bool or str
    dims: frozenset[str] = frozenset()  # what addresses it: dims, multi-dims among them
    default: Any | None = None
    default_by: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}  # subject.name -> category -> default
    breakpoints: bool = False  # may carry a piecewise-linear curve
    unit: str | None = None  # what the values measure
    description: str | None = None  # what the attribute is, in prose


class PropertySpec(BaseModel):
    """One value per label of its subject, describing the label."""

    dtype: ParameterDtype | None = None  # float, int, bool or str
    one_of: str | None = None  # the dim it refers to, in place of dtype
    default: Any | None = None
    default_by: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    unit: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None


class Schema(BaseModel):
    id: UUID | None = None  # a standalone record's layer id
    version: int = 1  # bumped by any change to the declarations

    dimensions: dict[str, Dimension] = {}  # every dim, multi-dims among them
    attributes: dict[str, AttributeSpec] = {}  # one attribute, one spec
    properties: dict[str, dict[str, PropertySpec]] = {}  # subject -> name -> spec

    partial: frozenset[str] | None = None  # dims a layer may patch value by value

    meta: dict[str, Any] = {}  # stored, never interpreted

Dims, multi-dims, properties and attributes each have their own page. partial is the one part specific to layering, and so the one optional part. It is None for a record with no layers, since nothing overrides anything there (partial).

meta holds a framework's own top-level data, such as network attributes, a coordinate reference system or free-form metadata. The package stores it and never interprets it, since none of it describes the dimensioned data.

docs.title: Dtypes
docs.text:
A dtype is mathspec's: DimensionDtype and ParameterDtype from mathspec.program, stored as the plain string a mathspec model declares. The manifest and the model that a record feeds share one vocabulary. Each declaration maps to one DuckDB type, one constant in schema/dtypes.py that every typed column reads:

declares declaration DuckDB type dim, attribute, property dtype: float DOUBLE dim, attribute, property dtype: int BIGINT attribute, property dtype: bool BOOLEAN dim, attribute, property dtype: str VARCHAR dim dtype: datetime TIMESTAMP (no time zone) dim one_of: [labels] ENUM of the labels property one_of: <dim> that dim's type

A dim with one_of is a str dim whose column is an ENUM of its labels.

A property declares exactly one of dtype and one_of. A property with one_of: <dim> refers to that dim, whether its subject is a multi-dim or not, and takes the dim's type: an ENUM for a dim with one_of, TIMESTAMP for a datetime dim (referring to a dim). The schema refuses at load a property that declares both or neither, a list of labels in place of the dim, and a multi-dim as the dim.

A multi-dim declares over and neither dtype nor one_of; the schema refuses it beside either, and a coordinate drawing on an undeclared dim or on another multi-dim.

An attribute declares no one_of, as a mathspec parameter has none. No property is datetime. A property that holds a time refers to a datetime dim, such as snapshot.

Struct columns are derived from the declarations. A multi-dim's column is a STRUCT with a field per coordinate, each typed as its dim, and an owner flag is a STRUCT of BOOLEAN. The fixed columns are attribute VARCHAR, breakpoint DOUBLE and breakpoints BOOLEAN.

The manifest writes a dtype as its string, "dtype": "float". A dim with one_of carries "one_of": [...] beside it. A multi-dim carries "over": {...} and no dtype. A property that refers to a dim carries "one_of": "<dim>" in place of dtype.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
A declared dim, multi-dim coordinate, attribute or property name becomes a column, beside the columns datarecord writes itself. Schema refuses at load a name that cannot stand there, and the error names it and the reason:

  • A name that contains " or .. A name reaches DuckDB as a column reference, which reads a.b as column b of table a and cannot spell a " at all. A space, mixed case, a keyword or a leading digit is fine, since DuckDB quotes those.
  • A column the format writes, compared ignoring case as DuckDB resolves a column name. These are attribute, breakpoint and value on every long row, varies, broadcast, breakpoints and layer_uuid in the owner map, and order_key on a resolved frame. A collision would be silent: a dim named value would give the long file two columns of one name.
  • A name with a leading _. Every scratch column that a fold adds and drops starts with _, so that set can grow and this list stays the same.
  • Two spellings that differ only in case. DuckDB resolves Country and country to one column, so one would read the other's values. One spelling declared twice, as when a multi-dim's coordinate is named after the dim it draws on, is a single column and is fine.

Labels are data, and none of these rules constrain them. Beyond these columns, no name is special: entity or bus is a name like any other. The properties page says where a name may appear twice.

docs.title: One schema per record
docs.text:
A record has one schema. A directory record's schema is manifest.json in the directory. A layered record's schema lives beside the layers, and no layer holds one:

record-root/
├── manifest.json               # the schema, one for the whole tree
└── layers/<uuid>/              # a layer: dims/, attributes/
    └── resolved/               # caches (owner map, resolved dims)

The schema is not layered data. A layer cannot change what p_nom means, its dtype or the dims it varies over. The schema is known without walking the ancestry, and the record can validate it before anything is read. Adding an attribute amends the root schema, so a new attribute is visible at the top of the tree. A layer directory holds only data, which keeps it a plain parquet directory that a tool knowing nothing about layering can read.

A standalone record carries its own manifest.json. Workspace.at(uri) reads that file, so the record answers the same through any workspace, and at refuses a directory without one. A standalone manifest also carries an id, a UUID that ws.write mints, as the schema's optional id field, so the file stays flat and validates whole. The id is the record's layer id, which keys the fold tables a workspace shares. An id derived from the URI would serve stale folds to a record deleted and written again at that URI, or to a relative path read from another working directory. at refuses a manifest without an id. Rooting a schema into a tree clears its id. A tree's manifest needs none, since its revisions name its layers. A single layer directory carries no manifest, so it is read through its store, store.layer(id), under the manifest of the tree it belongs to.

An edit changes neither kind of schema. A WorkingRecord is one more layer over its base. A layer declares nothing, so a working record reads under its base's schema, standalone or not.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
One schema outlives many layers, so a change to it meets data written under the previous one. version records which schema a record's layers were written against. What matters is which changes existing layers survive.

A compatible change keeps old layers readable. version bumps and nothing else happens:

  • adding an attribute or a property, since neither changes the key of the owner map, which only partial widens
  • adding a dim that no existing attribute varies over, a multi-dim among them; until a layer writes a new multi-dim, it has no tuples
  • widening an AttributeSpec.dims, since an unset dim is NULL and NULL means every label (the broadcast rule)
  • adding to partial, which makes ownership finer while an existing layer's rows stay owned at the coarser granularity they were written with; a materialised owner map keyed before the change is no cache, and the read folds from the layers again
  • changing a unit or description, which decides how no row decodes

An incompatible change makes existing rows decode differently, or not at all:

  • narrowing dims, since a row that sets a dim no longer declared has no valid reading
  • changing a dtype or one_of, which includes dropping a label from a dim's one_of
  • moving a name between properties and attributes, or between subjects, which moves the file its value is read from
  • removing from partial, after which a layer that patched one value along that axis is a partial override of an axis owned whole, which partial forbids

The compatible changes are those where NULL already means what the new schema needs, so the broadcast rule absorbs them and no row changes. schema.compatible_with(other) returns one reason per incompatibility.

An incompatible change needs the layers rewritten. For a layered record that means flattening it to a standalone directory under the new schema. A reader that meets a version it was not written for should refuse, since every failure above is silent.

docs.title: unit and description
docs.text:
A Dimension, an AttributeSpec and a PropertySpec may each carry a unit and a description. The package stores them, reads them back and hands them to whatever displays or documents the record. It interprets neither: there is no unit conversion, no dimensional analysis and no check on adding MW to kW.

They describe the dimensioned data, so they belong in the schema. meta holds what does not describe it. A unit belongs to an attribute as its dtype does, and a consumer finds what p_nom is and what it is measured in from the schema alone.
