The type-scoping (semi-join the map to that type's entities) needs the entity axis, which a Fold has via coords.axes["entity"]; so flags belongs on Fold, the one object holding both the map and the axes, rather than on a map-only OwnerMap that would have to be handed an entities relation from outside. owners(attribute) is the map-only read relation joins against; attributes() is the map-only enumerator. flags_from_rows stays a module function flags calls — it is schema logic, not map logic.

Fold.read and Fold.compute are the two tenses: a materialised node's resolved/ read back, versus a fold computed over sources. The same object shape either way, which is what makes a computed fold able to start from a read one as its base.

docs.title: NodeCache becomes Resolver, LayerData routing into its Fold
docs.text:
The rename says what the class is: it resolves a node's layers into the answer a Record presents. "Cache" named an implementation detail (the frozen-prefix materialisation) as if it were the identity; "resolver" names the job.

class Resolver:
    revision_id: UUID
    sources: list[LayerSource]    # the whole (frozen-truncated) ancestry as sources; no `base` field
    con: DuckDBPyConnection
    schema: Schema                # a plain field (see below), resolved by the caller

    @cached_property              # stable-gated as `coords` is today
    def fold(self) -> Fold: ...   # base = deepest materialised source; compute the rest over it

    # LayerData surface — routes into `fold`
    def axes(self): ...           # set(fold.coords.axes)
    def axis(self, dim): ...      # fold.coords.axes.get(dim)
    def attributes(self, kind): ...    # fold.attributes() for inputs; own-layer listing for outputs
    def attribute(self, name, kind): ...   # relation(name)/outputs(name), via fold.owners + source_for
    def entity_types(self) / entity_type(self, ct): ...   # was entity_types / entity_type_frame
    def groups(self) / group(self, g): ...                # was (from schema) / group_frame

    # routing reads that need the fold's members by name
    def owners(self, attribute): ...   # fold.owners(attribute)
    def flags(self, entity_type=None): ...   # fold.flags(entity_type)  (was attributes_of)

    # extras a single fold-product cannot answer
    def source_for(self, layer_uuid) -> LayerSource: ...   # dispatch a winning key to its layer
    def with_source(self, source) -> Resolver: ...         # append one more layer (staging)
    @property
    def frozen(self) -> bool: ...   # all(s.frozen for s in sources)   (was `stable`)

inputs (the raw map relation) and entity_axis stay as thin routing properties — fold.owner_map and axis("entity") — because white-box tests and mutable.py read them by those names; they are owners and axis("entity") without the argument.

Resolver.frozen (the LayerData member) is today's NodeCache.stable: all(s.frozen for s in sources), whether the whole source list is write-once. Distinct from frozen_prefix, which counts how far the leading run is frozen to decide the in-memory cache boundary.

schema becomes a plain field (deferred to its own commit): today it is a property returning declared if set else read_schema(con), threaded through with_source. Every fold reads the schema, both construction sites already hold it (the tree node reads the root schema, Record.over has the manifest), and the resolver is lazy, so the fallback buys nothing. Moving read_schema(con) to the one tree-node construction site makes schema a plain field, deletes declared and the property, and lets with_source pass self.schema already resolved.

docs.title: The base is a Fold, discovered from the sources, not stored
docs.text:
The base is not a stored field. sources is the whole ancestry (frozen-truncated for the in-memory cache, unrelated to materialisation) as plain LayerSources, and the fold discovers its base from among them:

def materialised(self, con) -> Fold | None: ...  # on LayerSource


# ParquetLayer: Fold.read(self.revision_id, con)   — a resolved/ dir, or None
# DirectorySource / StagedSource: None

Resolver.fold walks sources from the deepest, asks each source.materialised(con), and the first hit is the base: everything at or below it is skipped, everything above folds on top via Fold.compute(above, con, schema, base=hit). No materialised ancestor → base=None, fold the whole list.

This is why frozen and materialised are two questions, not one. frozen = "these rows cannot change under a reader" — a source-type flag (False only for StagedSource) gating the in-memory, connection-scoped fold cache (frozen_prefix/_frozen_table). materialised = "this node has a resolved/ directory on disk" — a filesystem fact, set only by an explicit .materialise(), gating the fold-shortening base. Every materialised node is frozen; almost no frozen node is materialised. So the base comes from the deepest materialised source, which the walk finds by testing source.materialised(con), never from "the last frozen source".

ResolvedLayer is deleted. Its fold-role becomes the base Fold.read(...) a source offers via materialised(con); its own-rows role, where source_for reaches a winning layer's rows, becomes a plain ParquetLayer. source_for resolves an owner id to a source and never to the base. The fold-result stops being an entry in the fold-input list.

docs.title: Sequenced commits
docs.text:
This lands as three tested-green commits:

  1. Read-path split ✅ done — kill the masquerade: source.materialised(con) -> Fold | None, Resolver.fold takes its base from the deepest materialised source, sources is plain ParquetLayers, ResolvedLayer deleted, NodeCache -> Resolver rename (and .stable -> .frozen). This is the piece a-member-file-holds-values is blocked on.
  2. Fold object ✅ done — extract coords + owner_map and the reads (owners, flags(entity_type=None), attributes, per-type/group frames) into Fold; Resolver routes into it. Orthogonal to (1); a clean second diff.
  3. LayerData + write path ✅ done — define LayerData, make Resolver and LayerSource both satisfy it (source gains entity_types/groups/attributes enumerators), rename the fold-named readers to the shared vocabulary, write_record takes a LayerData, _Written/staged_only() deleted, both commit callers pass the object they hold.

[!NOTE] Commit 1 as landed (departures from the sketch above, and facts for commits 2–3):

  • Fold lives in its own module datarecord/layered/fold.py, not in resolve.py, to break the import cycle a source.materialised() -> Fold return would otherwise create (resolve.py imports sources.py; a source returning a Fold from resolve.py would close the loop). In commit 1 it is a minimal seed struct — axes/groups/entity_types dicts + owner_map, and Fold.read — depending only on duck. Commit 2 moves the reads (owners/flags/attributes) onto it and folds the four dicts into coords: Coords.
  • _base_and_above(sources, con) in resolve.py is the split helper: it scans sources[:-1] deepest-first for the first materialised(con) and returns (base_fold, sources_above). The last source is never the base — a node resolves from its own layer, never its own cache — which is also what stops materialise (which writes owner_map before dims) from reading its own half-written cache back as a base.
  • The base seeds the fold as depth 0 of each fold_axis/fold_inputs call (its resolved, tombstone-free relation prepended), so a layer above still wins per key and its tombstones still evict a base key — behaviourally identical to the old ResolvedLayer-as-first-source seed. This touches resolve_dims, resolve_groups, _fold_map, entity_type_frame, and _materialise_dims.
  • The invariant guard test_resolved_reads_same_as_unresolved (in test_overlay.py) landed first, green before and after: it folds one node through the base and one from the root (via an _Unmaterialised ParquetLayer subclass forcing materialised() -> None) and asserts they agree on the owner map, entity axis, and every attribute relation.

Commit 2 as landed (the Fold object):

  • Fold grew into the real object in fold.py: schema + axes/groups/entity_types dicts + owner_map, plus the map reads attributes() (was attribute_names), owners(attribute), and flags(entity_type=None) (was attributes_of, now whole-record when None). flags_from_rows moved to fold.py beside its only caller.
  • Fold.compute is a resolve.py concern, not a Fold classmethod. The folding that builds a live Fold needs Coords' broadcast algebra and the DuckDB expression machinery, both in resolve.py; relocating them into the light fold.py would invert the layering. So Resolver.fold assembles a live Fold from dims (the folded Coords) and _map("inputs") (the folded owner map) — both of which keep their own frozen-scoped connection cache, so fold re-wraps rather than re-folds and no cache moved. Fold.read (the base tense) stays a Fold classmethod.
  • The live Fold carries entity_types={}: it is never another fold's base, and its reads never touch the per-type frames (those go through Resolver.entity_type_frame, which folds per call). Coords is unchanged — Dims renamed, holding axes+groups+the broadcast algebra.
  • materialised(con, schema) gained the schema argument, since Fold.read needs it to cast the read-back map; every implementation and _base_and_above thread it through.

Commit 3 as landed (LayerData + the write path):

  • LayerData lives in record.py beside RecordLike, the neutral protocol module both the write path and mutable.py already import. Its enumerators return Iterable[str], not set[str] — a Resolver.attributes orders its keys (a Record over it needs a stable order) while a source's are a set, and Iterable is the covariant type both satisfy without either re-wrapping.
  • Every source carries a schema reference, so a LayerSource is a LayerData. The reference is passed in at construction — sources_to_read, source_for, Record.over/Record.at and WorkingRecord all thread the one schema they already hold down into each ParquetLayer/DirectorySource/StagedSource — never re-read from disk. This is the "schema becomes a plain field" step the commit-2 note deferred: Resolver.schema stops being a lazy declared or read_schema(con) property and becomes a required field resolved by the caller, and the same reference sits on every source in the fold. A file layer's schema is never read by anything (the writer only ever gets a StagedSource or Resolver), but carrying it is what lets commit hand self.resolver.sources[-1] straight to write_record with no cast.
  • A LayerSource's new enumerators take no schema argument and do not filter by declaration — entity_types/groups/attributes are plain directory listings, as axes() already is. The ∅-not-{None} schema-governance the proposal makes an acceptance test of is a property of the objects write_record actually receives (StagedSource, Resolver), whose staged/folded state is already declaration-scoped.
  • Resolver keeps relation/outputs as private _relation/_outputs behind the shared attribute(name, kind), and returns a non-None relation (an empty one where no layer wrote the attribute) — a valid narrowing of LayerData.attribute's | None. group_frame and entity_type differ: entity_type_frame renamed to entity_type (the shared name, no collision), but group_frame stayed, being the Record-presentational read (member order, empty→None) that Record._group_frame alone uses; the shared group(name) is the raw fold Resolver already had.
  • isinstance(x, LayerData) decides the adapter, and @runtime_checkable checks only member names. A RecordLike producer (_NetworkSource) has dims/entity_types where LayerData wants axes/axis/entity_type/frozen, so it correctly fails the check and routes through _RecordLikeAsLayerData in write.py — a thin adapter reading its Frames mappings through the enumerate-and-read pairs (as_relation for the one non-DuckDB backend boundary). write_record takes LayerData | RecordLike.
  • commit hands the fold's last source straight over: self.resolver.sources[-1] (the StagedSource) for NewChild, self.resolver for Directory, both already a LayerData with no cast needed. _Written, staged_only(), and the _staged_axes/_staged_entities/_staged_attributes Frames builders are deleted; _staged_groups stays for StagedSource.groups()'s key set.
  • write.py is raw-relation throughout: _validate_frame/_write_frame/_require_unique take DuckDBPyRelation, nw.concat/.unique/.group_by became union_all_by_name + a self-join count, and as_relation is reached only inside the RecordLike adapter.

docs.title: The interface Resolver and a layer share
docs.text:
A Resolver and a LayerSource answer the same questions — "the keys of kind X" and "the rows for one key of kind X" — one over a fold, one over a single layer. That is a shared read protocol; call it LayerData. Each is that protocol plus its own extras.

the shared question LayerData member a layer answers (own rows) a Resolver answers (folded) the schema in force schema — the writer supplies it schema which axes exist axes() axes() ✓ keys of coords.axes one axis's rows axis(dim) axis(dim) ✓ coords.axes[dim] which types exist entity_types() new: list member files; ∅ if the schema declares no type axis entity_types() ✓ one type's rows entity_type(name) entity_type(name) ✓ entity_type_frame → renamed which groups exist groups() new: list group files; only what the schema declares from schema → made explicit one group's rows group(name) group(name) ✓ group_frame → renamed which attributes exist attributes(kind) new: list attr files attribute_names/output_names → renamed one attribute's rows attribute(name, kind) attribute(name, kind) ✓ relation/outputs → renamed

schema heads the table but governs it: which of the pairs below it are populated depends on what the schema declares — see schema governs which pairs are live.

So LayerData is: schema, frozen, axes/axis, entity_types/entity_type, groups/group, attributes/attribute — the enumerate-and-read pairs (each an enumerate() -> set[str] and a read(key) -> Rel | None) plus the two members that mean the same over a layer and a fold. all_attributes stays source-only (see all_attributes is source-only). A LayerSource gains the three enumerators it lacks (entity_types, groups, attributes — directory listing for a _FileLayer as axes() already is, the staging tables for StagedSource); a Resolver renames its fold-named readers (entity_type_frame → entity_type, relation → attribute, and the coords.axes keys become axes()) so the two answer under one vocabulary.

frozen is on LayerData; all_attributes(kind) is not (source-only, below). frozen is a real property of a fold, not a convention-constant: a Resolver can hold a StagedSource (this is what WorkingRecord is), so it is over a mix of frozen and unfrozen sources, and its frozen is all(s.frozen for s in sources) — whether its whole source list is write-once. (Distinct from frozen_prefix, which counts how far the leading run is frozen to decide materialisation, not whether all of it is.)

Beyond the shared protocol, each keeps what only it has:

  • LayerSource also has layer_id — the per-source key source_for dispatches a winning layer_uuid back through — and uri on the file-backed ones. layer_id stays source-only because a fold has no single one: it spans many layers, keyed by revision_id and routed by the owner map, so "the last layer's layer_id" is not a value source_for could dispatch on.
  • Resolver also has the fold machinery a single layer has no answer for, held in its Fold object: with_source, source_for, owners (over the one owner map), flags, fold/coords/entity_axis (the folded state), and revision_id in place of a layer_id. (stable is now frozen on the shared protocol; the base is a Fold discovered from the sources, not a stored field.)

Resolver fulfils LayerData; so does LayerSource. write_record takes a LayerData — a single StagedSource for the NewChild commit, a Resolver for the Directory commit — and _Written is deleted, being the adapter that filled the gap LayerData now closes.

The discipline that keeps this from becoming "one protocol for two unlike things": LayerData holds only the enumerate-and-read members that mean the same for a layer and a fold. A method only one has — all_attributes on a source, with_source on a Resolver — stays off the shared protocol. The shared names are for the shared idea; the rest are each type saying it is not the other.

docs.title: schema governs which pairs are live, it is not a peer of them
docs.text:
The table above lists schema as one shared member among the enumerate-and-read pairs, but it is not their peer — it is what decides which of them exist. a-member-file-holds-values establishes that the entity-type axis is optional: where a schema declares no type axis (entity_type_dim is None), there are no member files, no entity_type column, and a component's attribute values live on dims/entity.parquet directly. So the entity_types()/entity_type(name) pair is not universal — it is populated exactly when the schema declares the axis, and groups() reflects only the groups the schema declares.

LayerData therefore reads through schema, not alongside it: schema is the one member the other pairs are conditional on, and a LayerData for an untyped record is a first-class shape, not the typed shape with types nulled out. The new source enumerators inherit a-member-file-holds-values's own acceptance test on this — the failure mode is an enumerator answering {None} rather than ∅:

  • entity_types() on a source whose schema declares no type axis returns the empty set, not {None}. entity_type(name) is then never a valid question — a direct call is a caller error, mirroring Resolver.entity_type_frame on the same record.
  • groups() returns only the groups the schema declares, and no more.

This is the point where the two proposals are the same work at two altitudes. a-member-file-holds-values is the read/write-path consequence of entity_type being optional, and it names the ResolvedLayer axis-means-one-thing fix as its prerequisite — which is the base/source split above. The two land together: this note gives LayerData the enumerators, and the untyped case is where those enumerators must answer ∅ rather than carry a phantom type.

docs.title: axis is layer-local on every LayerSource, no exception
docs.text: ResolvedLayer's axis/axes overrides go; it is deleted, and every source inherits the layer-local _FileLayer ones. The folded read moves to the base Fold a source offers via materialised(con), which is not a LayerSource. The test of correctness is a-member-file-holds-values's own: sources.py needs no branch, because a file-backed source no longer has to know whether it is being read as a layer or as a fold.

docs.title: The writer takes a LayerData, and _Written disappears
docs.text:
_Written is not a second shape of StagedSource — it is a RecordLike, because write_record(source: RecordLike) speaks the record dialect and StagedSource speaks the source dialect. _Written is the adapter: staged_only() rebuilds the staged layer's rows as per-kind Frames so the writer can eat what the fold already reads as a source. It exists only because the writer's input was spelled as neither of the two things that can supply it.

But the writer needs exactly LayerData. It uses schema and, per kind, enumerates the keys this thing holds and reads each — which is the enumerate-and-read protocol above, no more. (It never touches flags, and outputs is attributes(kind="outputs").) So write_record takes a LayerData: the NewChild commit hands it the StagedSource, the Directory commit hands it the Resolver, each the object it already is. _Written is deleted, not collapsed — it was the adapter for a gap LayerData closes.

This is why LayerData earns its three new enumerators. The reader never needs them — the fold learns which keys exist from the schema and the owner map, so a LayerSource was point-accessor. The writer must enumerate what a layer actually holds, where the schema over-declares. Adding entity_types/groups/attributes to the source is what lets the reader's interface serve the writer too.

The Directory case proves the interface rather than excepting it. It writes the resolved record — base and staged flattened — which is not one layer's rows, so it cannot be a StagedSource; but "enumerate what I hold, hand each over" is exactly what a fold answers, where "what I hold" means every folded key. That is this proposal's thesis on the write path: one interface, the object deciding whether it means a layer or a fold.

This is the larger of the two halves and the most safely deferred, since it moves write_record's contract and reconciles names across the fold and the source. It belongs to the same idea: _Written is the write-path twin of a resolved_axis prefix — a third spelling of a thing the common interface should already carry.

docs.title: What this buys
docs.text:
No object answers axis two ways. The overload that a-member-file-holds-values has to route around disappears at the source, so that proposal's prerequisite section reduces to "already true".

A file-backed source needs no branch. _FileLayer/ParquetLayer/DirectorySource read whichever columns a file has and never learn which configuration they are in — the strongest single signal the layout is carried by the format, not by the readers.

One vocabulary for "the rows of this thing". axis, entity_type, attribute, group mean "the rows of the object I hold", whether that object is a single layer or a fold. A reader learns the interface once.

The WorkingRecord and resolved-node mechanisms become one pattern. Both are "a fold-object over sources, with a distinguished own-rows source for the layer that is also the fold's boundary". Today they rhyme; after, they are the same construct.

The writer takes LayerData, the interface a source and a Resolver share. write_record's input is the enumerate-and-read surface both fulfil, so both commit callers pass the object they already hold and _Written, the adapter that existed only because the input was spelled as neither, is deleted.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
It reshapes the Resolver's (NodeCache's) source list. The head stops being a LayerSource that is secretly a fold; the base becomes a Fold the deepest materialised source offers via materialised(con), and source_for stops returning it. sources_to_read, the fold construction (now Fold.compute), resolve_coords, and source_for all move together. This is the change a-member-file-holds-values deferred as a prerequisite, taken at its root — the masquerade — rather than papered with a resolved_ prefix.

A shared interface across a source and a fold invites isinstance where a method belongs. The discipline that keeps it honest: if the fold-object needs a method a source does not have (a map has no entity_type; a source has no map), that is the interface telling you they are not the same type — the shared members are the ones that mean "my rows", and the rest stay apart. This proposal is not "one protocol for both"; it is "the same names for the same idea where the idea is shared".

Teaching the writer to take LayerData touches its contract. write_record moves from RecordLike to LayerData, LayerSource gains the three enumerators, and _Written and its staged_only() builder go. _Written has callers in the tests and one in commit, and the Directory path hands over a Resolver under the new contract rather than the record it built. A real change to the write path, not only a read-path cleanup, and the part most safely deferred.

docs.title: What it settles
docs.text:
The base is a Fold, discovered from the sources. It is not a stored field. Fold.read(revision_id, con) reads resolved/ and folds nothing; a source offers it via materialised(con), and Resolver.fold takes the deepest materialised source's Fold as the base for Fold.compute. Same object shape either tense — read or computed — which is what lets a computed fold start from a read one.

LayerData is a Protocol both types satisfy structurally, with layer_id the sole source-only member. LayerSource is LayerData plus layer_id (and uri on file-backed ones) and all_attributes (source-only); Resolver is LayerData plus the fold machinery and revision_id. frozen is on LayerData, not source-only (above). Neither type inherits from LayerData — each satisfies it by shape, as LayerSource implementations already satisfy that protocol.

The untyped case keys on entity_type_dim is None, enum or not. An enumerator answers ∅ exactly when the schema declares no entity-type axis — not when schema.entity_types is empty, which is also true for a declared String-typed axis whose labels are data. A declared-but-non-enum axis is still a declared axis: its member files exist and entity_types() lists them. a-member-file-holds-values leaves whether those two cases should ever converge open; this note does not, keying only on declaration.

docs.title: What it opens rather than settles
docs.text: How far the name reconciliation reaches. The write-path half already reconciles the rows interface a fold and a source share (entity_type_frame/entity_type, relation/attribute, dims/axes become one vocabulary the writer reads). Left open is whether Record's public narwhals surface joins it — Record.dims returns Frames, not the relation a source's axis does, so it is a presentation over the same idea rather than the idea itself. Whether the resolved-and-own pair should share the outward name too, or only the internal rows interface does, is the larger claim this page does not force.

docs.title: all_attributes is source-only, for now
docs.text:
all_attributes(kind) — a source's <kind>/*.parquet unioned by name, unfolded, values intact — stays a LayerSource member and off LayerData. It reads like the fold's owner map's raw input, and the temptation is to give a Resolver a folded all_attributes so the pair attributes/all_attributes is complete on both. Two facts hold it back:

  • No fold-side caller. Both callers read it on a source: fold_inputs on each source to build the map, and the outputs bulk read on the last layer (sources[-1].all_attributes("outputs")). Nothing asks a Resolver for its own all_attributes, so a fold-side one would be a method with no reader.
  • The per-layer aggregate that looks separable is not layer-local. A layer's contribution to the owner map (aggregate all_attributes to (input_key, layer_uuid, varies/broadcast/breakpoints)) needs expand_dims against the resolved axes to fan a broadcast NULL out to every value on its axis — a record-wide fact a single layer's files cannot supply. So the clean fault line is all_attributes (raw rows, coords-free, source) | expand+aggregate+recurse (coords, fold), not one row higher where a source.owner_map(coords) would sit.

Whether a later Store-shaped refactor makes a Resolver.owner_map(kind) and an all_attributes folded read worth having — so the two are the same enumerate-and-read pair on both types — is reopened then, not settled here.

docs.title: How to know it worked
docs.text:
ResolvedLayer is gone; the base is a Fold. The single assertion the resolved-node half is downstream of: the persisted fold is a Fold.read(...) the live fold starts from, not a source in its input list. def axis in sources.py is found only on _FileLayer, and nothing folded-answer-shaped is typed as a source.

A resolved record reads the same as an unresolved one. Materialise a node, read a component's value through the resolved node and through the same node read from its own layers unmaterialised; they agree. This is the invariant the whole split protects, and it belongs in the suite before the change, not after — it is what says the base carries the fold correctly once axis stops doing so.

Resolver.sources holds only LayerSources, and the base is a Fold. The masquerade is over exactly when no ResolvedLayer appears in a sources list — every entry is a plain ParquetLayer, and the fold-to-here the head stood for is the Fold the deepest materialised source offers. source_for then always hands back an own-rows source, never the base. Assertable on the source types and on what source_for returns.

sources.py is untouched but for deletion. As in a-member-file-holds-values: if the file-backed sources need no added branch, the layout is carried by the format. A diff that adds a conditional to _FileLayer means the fold is leaking into the source again.

A source's new enumerators answer ∅, not {None}, for an untyped record. entity_types() on a LayerSource whose schema declares no type axis returns the empty set, and groups() only the declared groups — the same ∅-not-{None} check a-member-file-holds-values makes on the owner map. A test that materialises an untyped node and asserts entity_types() == set() on both the base Fold and a ParquetLayer of the head is what says schema governs the pairs rather than the pairs carrying a phantom type.

_Written is gone and write_record took the StagedSource directly — once that half lands. The NewChild commit passes the staged source to the writer, the Directory commit passes the resolved record, and both satisfy one input contract. Until it lands, _Written standing unchanged is the marker that this is the deferred part, not a regression.

docs.title: DEP 9: A Workspace and a Store
DEP 9: a Workspace holds the connection, a Store holds a location
docs.text:
DEP 9 Title a Workspace holds the connection, a Store holds a location Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented 2026-10-10 Created 2026-10-09 Version Unreleased

Landed in four steps (landing) on layers, writing, the working record, the read path, consuming a record and the module layout; this page is kept as the argument for the change rather than as the current description, and those pages are authoritative where the two disagree.

The departures are all in the remote Files. boto3 uses path-style addressing whenever AWS_ENDPOINT_URL is set, as DuckDB's secret does, since a self-hosted server has no bucket-subdomain DNS. A failure setting up httpfs raises rather than leaving a workspace that fails on its first remote read. A 403 on a read or an exists counts as a miss, since S3 answers one for an absent key the caller may not list, and a 409 counts as a refused write alongside 412, since that is how a server reports a racing conditional write.

One claim: what a process now gets from duck's module globals is two objects' state, not one. A Workspace holds the DuckDB connection and the means to reach files, local or remote, which is all a standalone directory needs. A Store holds one store location — the directory with its manifest, its revision tree, its layers — and works through a workspace, which several stores share. Every Revision, Record and WorkingRecord reaches its connection and its paths through the object it came from, and a revision crosses a process boundary as its store's location.

Changes layered resolution, writing a whole record, the working record, the read path, consuming a record, the module layout and what a data record is, for the optional remote dependency.

docs.title: What starts it
docs.text:
Each claim below was checked against 49b7268; the last three rows were found while checking the others.

claim holds? default_connection() is a process singleton Revision attaches lazily, deserialisation included Yes, and worse than stated. The default connection is :memory:, and the revisions table lives only in it. A revision deserialised in a new process reattaches to an empty tree: Revision.model_validate_json(child.model_dump_json()).ancestry() returns []. The serialised form ({"id", "parent"}) does not even say which store it belongs to. the base URI is DEFAULT_BASE_URI (from DATARECORD_BASE_URI) plus _BASE_URIS keyed by connection; tests monkeypatch it Yes, and the two disagree. Only the schema consults base_uri_of(con) (read_schema, _reconcile_schema). Layers and caches use the process default: write_record calls layer_dir(revision_id), sources_to_read and Resolver build ParquetLayer(uid, schema, con) with no base_uri, and _map_uri/materialise call resolved_dir(revision_id). A connection opened with connect(base_uri=X) therefore writes its manifest under X and its layers under DEFAULT_BASE_URI. an empty base makes layer_dir, schema_uri and the layer_dir macro fall back to the working directory Yes. DEFAULT_BASE_URI is "" unless the env var is set, so any path that misses the fixture's monkeypatch writes layers/<id>/ into the cwd. The layer_dir SQL macro is registered by connect but called from nowhere. _NetworkSource builds relations on duckdb.default_connection() unless write_record calls on_connection(con) Yes. write.py checks hasattr(source, "on_connection"); PyPSA.results(n) builds _NetworkSource(model) with no connection, so its frames land on DuckDB's own default. as_relation passes any DuckDBPyRelation through, and the next union or replacement scan on the record's connection fails ("Cannot combine LEFT and RIGHT relations of different connections", "created by another Connection"). WorkingRecord.set(..., kind="outputs") reaches that through _incoming. revisions cannot be listed Yes. No API reads the table as a whole, and in a new process there is nothing to read. a remote location works No. read_json opens a URI with urlopen, which has no s3:// handler, so a remote manifest is unreadable. write_schema writes with open(), and write_record writes a standalone directory's manifest only if local, so a remote manifest is unwritable too. Only the parquet goes through DuckDB's httpfs. A remote write_record also has no staging directory, so a failed write leaves part of a layer behind. a connection may be shared between threads No. Eight threads querying one DuckDB 1.5.5 connection: seven fail with "Attempting to execute an unsuccessful or closed pending query result". default_connection() hands every thread the same one. a node's materialised caches are complete once materialised() says so No. materialised() takes resolved/<id>/owner_map/inputs.parquet to stand for the whole cache, but materialise() writes that map first and the resolved dims and groups after. A reader in another process can see a node as materialised and fold from half its cache, and a failed materialise() on a remote location leaves it that way for good.

The second row is the root of the third: every path helper takes base_uri: str | None = None and treats None as "the process default", so forgetting to pass one is silent. A store makes its location unavoidable rather than defaulted.

One object holding both the location and the connection would fix those rows, but at a cost: a location is needed only by the tree, and a connection by everything. Reading or writing a standalone directory would have to name a location it never uses, and two locations would each own a connection, so records from them could not be joined. So the two are split.

docs.title: The construct
docs.text:
class Workspace:
    con: DuckDBPyConnection  # the calling thread's cursor

    def __init__(self, database: str = ":memory:") -> None: ...
    @classmethod
    def process(cls) -> Workspace: ...  # the process's, created on first use

    def store(self, uri: str) -> Store: ...
    def at(self, uri: str) -> Record: ...  # a standalone directory
    def write(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike, uri: str) -> Record: ...
    def close(self) -> None: ...


class Store:
    uri: str  # the store location: absolute, never empty
    workspace: Workspace

    def root(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike) -> Revision: ...
    def revision(self, id: UUID) -> Revision: ...
    def revisions(self) -> list[Revision]: ...
    def layer(self, id: UUID) -> Record: ...  # one layer, read alone

    def layer_dir(self, id: UUID) -> str: ...
    def resolved_dir(self, id: UUID) -> str: ...


class Revision:
    def child(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike) -> Revision: ...

    # record, ancestry(), materialise() as now

ws = Workspace()
store = ws.store("/data/a")

root = store.root(PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con))  # a new root with this layer
child = root.child(other_record)  # a new child of root with this layer
rev = store.revision(rid)  # look one up
out = ws.write(rev.record, "out/")  # a standalone directory, read back

Three calls make something, one per place it can go, and each is named for what it returns:

you hold call you get Store store.root(src) a new root Revision Revision rev.child(src) a new child Revision Workspace ws.write(src, uri) the directory's Record

What needs the workspace named, and what does not. A call reaches the workspace explicitly only where nothing in hand carries one: ws.store, ws.at, ws.write, and the con a tool converting a framework object is handed. Everything built from something takes the connection from it — WorkingRecord(record) from the record, rev.child and rev.record from the revision's store. Naming the workspace there as well would be a second name for one thing, which can disagree, and a check to catch it; taking it from the source makes the disagreement unrepresentable.

docs.title: The workspace
docs.text:
• The connection, on database, :memory: by default — see the location is authoritative, the database is disposable.
  • Files, local and remote — see files, local and remote. Both DuckDB's httpfs and boto3 read the AWS environment, and are set up the first time the workspace is handed a :// URI, whether a store's location or a directory's; today httpfs is loaded only for a remote base URI, so an s3:// directory read through a connection with a local base has no httpfs. A purely local workspace still never pays PROVIDER credential_chain's metadata probe.
  • Standalone directories. at(uri) reads one and write(source, uri) writes one. Both need only the connection and files. at requires the directory's own manifest.json and raises if it has none: a directory without one is a tree layer, read under its store's schema through store.layer(id). Today Record.at falls back to the connection's base URI for that case, which is the coupling this split removes.
  • Its stores. store(uri) returns this workspace's store at uri, the same object for the same normalised location, so two calls do not hold two views of one tree. The map is filled with dict.setdefault, which is atomic, so two threads asking for a new location at once still get one store.
  • A cursor per thread — see a cursor per thread, a relation per thread.

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
• The location. Required and non-empty: ws.store("") raises ValueError. A local path is resolved to an absolute one, so neither a later chdir nor a process with another cwd moves it. That ends the working-directory leak by construction — there is no fallback left to fall back to.
  • The tree. Persisted at the location, not in the connection — see the tree lives beside the layers.
  • Paths. layer_dir, resolved_dir and the manifest's location derive from the location and nothing else.

What it hands out:

  • Revisions, from root, revision and revisions, and from child on a revision. A revision carries its store, and child, record, materialise() and ancestry() reach the connection and paths through it. Revision.create/Revision.get and their con= go.
  • Records, from revision.record and store.layer(id). A Record keeps exposing con — the calling thread's cursor, read through its Resolver — because that is how a tool building from one reaches DuckDB SQL.

A store holds no connection of its own and has no close; closing is the workspace's.

docs.title: A revision exists only by writing its layer
docs.text:
write_record(revision_id, source, con, *, uri=None) splits by where the result goes:

  • store.root(source) and rev.child(source) create a revision and write source as its layer, in one call. There is no empty revision: Revision.create and the source-less child() go, and branching is writing a child.
  • ws.write(source, uri) writes a standalone record carrying its own manifest, and returns it as ws.at(uri) would. It is the one call taking a URI, because a directory hangs from no tree.

child lives on the parent rather than as store.write(source, parent=…), which would name the store twice — a parent is always its own store's. It is not rev.write, which would read as changing rev when layers are write-once. And a call per destination, rather than one taking a NewChild | Directory target, because the destinations need different things — a tree write the location and the tree, a directory write only a connection — and return different things, which a target union could only express through overloads.

The revision file is written last, and its existence is what makes the layer real. Locally, a failed write leaves nothing: the layer is staged into a sibling and renamed, as now. Remotely there is no rename, so a failed write can leave part of a layer behind — but without a revision file no revision(), revisions() or ancestry reaches it. A remote write becomes atomic in what any reader can see, and its leftovers are unreachable rather than half-read. Sweeping orphaned layers is a follow-up.

So a tree write runs in three steps: the layer, then the manifest, then the revision file. The manifest check comes after the layer rather than before it as today, so a layer whose schema turns out incompatible, or whose write fails, leaves the manifest untouched as well as unreachable; the manifest is never widened for a layer that does not exist.

materialise() follows the same rule: the maps other than inputs, the resolved dims and groups, then owner_map/inputs.parquet, the file materialised() reads. Locally each file is written under a temporary name and renamed, because to_parquet creates the file at its final path before it is complete and a reader meeting it mid-write fails rather than misses. Two writers materialising one node then write the same content, so that race is harmless.

A standalone directory has no revision file, so there the manifest is written last: ws.at requires one, which gives ws.write the same property, and a directory whose write failed reads as no record rather than part of one. Before any COPY, a remote ws.write refuses a URI under which Files.list finds anything, as the local write refuses an existing directory. Unlike a layer's UUID the caller picks this URI, and DuckDB's COPY would overwrite an existing record's files before the Absent manifest write could fail, leaving a mix of both under the old manifest. The check and the write are two steps, so two writers racing to one new URI can still mix; a standalone directory has one writer.

The tests that create a revision and hand-write its layer files keep doing so through a helper in tests/fixtures.py over the store's private revision-file write; no public API makes an empty revision.

The write path itself — staging into a sibling locally, the refusal of an existing directory, validation — is otherwise untouched (writing).

docs.title: A WorkingRecord does not write
docs.text:
WorkingRecord(record) takes no con: it stages on record.con, and _base_resolver's "base reads through another connection" check has nothing left to check. It loses commit, and NewChild, Directory and Target go with it. What it gains is edits, its staged layer as the LayerData it already is (StagedSource, staging as a layer):

w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.set("p_nom", 100.0, entity=["gen1"])
edited = rev.child(w.edits)  # the delta, as a child layer
ws.write(w, "out/")  # base plus edits, flattened
w.rollback()

commit did three things, and each now has one owner. Which rows to write — the delta for a child, the flattened record for a directory — is the caller's choice of w.edits or w, where commit chose it by target. Which parent — NewChild() defaulted to the base's revision, looked up by revision_id in _base_revision with its own error for a base that is no node — is named by the caller, who built w from it. Clearing the staging area is rollback(), called or not: a WorkingRecord still holding its edits after a write reads exactly what it did before.

The cost is one mistake nothing catches: rev.child(w) writes the whole resolved record as a child layer rather than the delta. It reads back correctly, just larger, and there is no cheap guard, a resolved record being a valid layer source too. edits is the name that has to carry it.

The other mistake is caught. other.child(w.edits), with w built over a different revision, would write a delta computed against the wrong parent — an axis edit carries its base's sibling columns — and read back wrong. NewChild() made that impossible by defaulting the parent; child keeps it impossible by comparing a staged source's base revision with its own id and raising on a mismatch.

A WorkingRecord still needs a base, so there is no empty start. Building one from a schema alone would have nothing to take a connection from, so it would be the workspace's (ws.new(schema)); that is a follow-up, not part of this change.

docs.title: The tree lives beside the layers
docs.text:
A store that serialises as its location is only useful if the location is enough to find the tree, and today it is not. Each revision becomes one file, written once, right after its layer:

<location>/
├── manifest.json
├── revisions/<id>.json        # {"id": ..., "parent": ...}
└── layers/<id>/

Beside layers/ rather than inside a layer: a layer directory stays exactly what the layer wrote, which is what lets a foreign reader consume it (deletion), and listing the tree is one listing over small files rather than a probe into every layer. One file per revision rather than one table because a file named by a fresh UUID is write-once like a layer, so two processes creating revisions in one location never write the same object — which a shared DuckDB file or a single revisions.parquet could not promise on S3. Written create-only through files, so write-once is enforced by the store rather than assumed. JSON rather than parquet because it is one small document, like the manifest beside it, read and listed through Files as the manifest is. The UUID is drawn in Python rather than by gen_random_uuid(), since the layer directory is named by it before any row exists.

The workspace's revisions table stays, as a cache of those files for every store on it: (location, id, parent), so revisions() and revision(id) filter by location — a revision of another store on the same workspace is not this store's — while ancestry, a walk from a revision already found, needs none. It cannot go stale, only incomplete, for the same reason a node cache never needs invalidating: a revision's parent never changes. So it is only ever added to:

  • revisions() lists revisions/ once through Files.list, compares the names against the table, and reads only the files it does not hold — one listing per call rather than one read per revision, which on S3 is one request per thousand revisions rather than one per revision.
  • revision(id) that misses the table reads revisions/<id>.json, then each parent the table does not hold, until it reaches one it does; KeyError where the first file is absent.

Two cursors adding one row at once conflict: DuckDB fails the second with TransactionException, even under ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The row is the same whoever wins, so the insert catches it and moves on.

revisions() returns every revision, unordered; a created field is for whoever first needs chronology.

Existing locations. A location written before this change has layers but no revisions/, so it reads as an empty tree. The project holds no compatibility promise, and the fix is one-off: export the revisions table of any DuckDB file used with connect(database=…) as one JSON file per row. A location only ever opened on :memory: has no tree to recover — which is the first row of what starts it.

docs.title: Files, local and remote
docs.text:
Two kinds of I/O, with one owner each:

  • Tables go through DuckDB, as now: reading and writing parquet and globbing it, over httpfs for a remote URI.
  • Everything else goes through the workspace's Files — the manifest, the revision files, listing them, and whether a layer exists:
class Files(Protocol):
    def read_text(self, uri: str) -> tuple[str, Version] | None: ...  # None on a miss
    def write_text(
        self, uri: str, text: str, *, expect: Version | Absent | None
    ) -> Version: ...
    def list(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]: ...  # names directly under prefix
    def exists(self, uri: str) -> bool: ...

expect is the precondition: Absent writes only if nothing is there, a Version only if the object is unchanged since it was read, None unconditionally. It replaces read_json's urlopen, write_schema's open(), and the if local around the standalone manifest. list returns names, not contents; remotely it follows S3's pages of a thousand keys.

Two implementations, picked by the URI's scheme: s3:// is remote and a URI without :// is local. Any other scheme raises, naming those two; reading over https:// is for whoever first needs it.

  • Local, on pathlib, which the code already uses. A local location keeps core at duckdb, narwhals and pydantic. Absent is open(…, "x"), which the OS makes atomic. A Version is the SHA-256 of the content, checked and replaced while holding a lock on a sibling <name>.lock (fcntl.flock, msvcrt.locking on Windows, both stdlib), with the new content written to a temporary file and renamed over the old one. The lock is what makes the check and the write one step; without it two local writers race exactly as two remote ones would on a server that ignores the headers.
  • Remote, on boto3, behind an optional extra, datarecord[remote] = ["boto3>=1.35.69"]. put_object is what expect maps to: IfNoneMatch="*" for Absent (botocore 1.35.2) and IfMatch=<etag> for a Version (botocore 1.35.69, hence the floor); either fails with 412 PreconditionFailed. A Version is the object's ETag.

boto3 because it is what Manta already runs on: the playbook[s3] extra its blocks install, the backend's S3FileStorageService, and prefect-aws in the runner are all boto3, so one S3 library serves the whole stack and the block images already carry it. Its conditional writes guard the two small files a store coordinates through: revision files become create-only by the server's guarantee rather than by trusting that a UUID never collides, and the manifest compare-and-swap. They do not guard the layer: its parquet is written by DuckDB's COPY over httpfs, which sends no condition, so remotely nothing refuses an existing layer directory. A fresh UUID makes that collision a non-event, and a failed write's leftovers are unreachable without a revision file (above). Removing them is cleanup, a separate concern. fsspec/s3fs has no create-only write, and obstore, which does, would be a second S3 client beside Manta's. The cost is boto3's size and S3 alone, which is every store Manta targets.

The manifest race closes too. Two processes writing the first layers into a new location, or widening one location's schema at once, race on manifest.json today. With expect, the first write is Absent, and widening, after the layer is written, reads the manifest with its version, checks compatibility, and writes expect=<that version>; a writer that lost re-reads and checks again. _reconcile_schema is the one caller that changes.

Only as far as the server honours the headers. A server that ignores them accepts every write, so create-only and the manifest check would silently become last-writer-wins. For SeaweedFS, which Manta deploys (chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.05 in docker/compose-dev-services.yaml), the source says:

SeaweedFS If-None-Match / If-Match on PutObject before 3.97 ignored 3.97 – 4.17 honoured, but checked once when the request arrives, before the upload: two writers racing on one key can both pass, and the later overwrites (#7154) 4.18 and later checked again under the object's write lock as the entry is committed, so exactly one of two racing writers succeeds (#8802, "make conditional mutations atomic and AWS-compatible")

On Manta's 4.05 the revision files are safe in practice — two writers never race on one UUID — but the manifest's compare-and-swap can lose a widening inside that window. So Manta's pin moves to 4.18 or later; that is Manta's change, and this proposal names it rather than working around it. AWS S3 itself has honoured If-None-Match since August 2024 and If-Match since November 2024.

The remote tests run against SeaweedFS in a container at that version, the server Manta deploys, rather than against a mock: a mock that ignores the headers would pass exactly the tests the headers exist for.

One configuration, two consumers. The configuration is the AWS environment and config files, following playbook's convention, and there is no datarecord-specific one. boto3 reads all of it itself: the AWS_* variables, profiles, session tokens, roles, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL. DuckDB gets CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, PROVIDER credential_chain, …), which resolves credentials the same way; the workspace adds only what the chain does not supply, ENDPOINT and URL_STYLE 'path' from AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, since SeaweedFS and MinIO need path-style addressing for want of bucket-subdomain DNS. With an endpoint set it also passes CHAIN 'env;config': such a server has no instance-metadata service, and probing for one is the two-minute hang connect avoids today. A secret built by hand from KEY_ID and SECRET would lose session tokens and roles. There is no remote= override: a setting passed to one workspace would not reach the Workspace.process() a deserialising task builds, while the environment does.

docs.title: The location is authoritative, the database is disposable
docs.text:
database may name a DuckDB file, and what lives in it is a workspace, never the record: deleting it loses at most uncommitted edits. The tree cannot live only there — a DuckDB file takes one writer at a time, so parallel tasks would serialise on its lock, and it cannot be written to S3 — and a tree in two places is two sources of truth that can disagree, the split this proposal removes for the base URI.

Within that rule a file earns its place three ways:

  • Staged edits outlive the process. A WorkingRecord's staging tables are tables on the connection, so on a file they survive a crash. Resuming one needs a handle back to its tables, which are keyed by a random _layer_id today; that handle is a follow-up, not part of this change.
  • The revisions cache persists. It cannot go stale (above), so keeping it across runs is safe, and it saves re-reading every revisions/*.json of a remote location on open.
  • Room to spill. A file-backed database gives DuckDB somewhere natural to page out a larger-than-memory plan.

A location is not reused. Every cache keyed by id — the revisions rows, the shared fold tables — assumes what an id names never changes. A revision keeps that by construction, a fresh UUID over write-once files. A location wiped and written again does not, nor does a standalone directory rewritten at the same URI, its fold being keyed by uuid5 of the URI: a persisted database would serve the old tree or fold. Rewriting one means a fresh database, or a fresh location.

docs.title: A cursor per thread, a relation per thread
docs.text:
A DuckDB connection is not safe to use from two threads at once (what starts it). DuckDB's answer is a con.cursor() per thread, and measured on 1.5.5 it holds: eight threads, each on its own cursor of one database, querying one table concurrently, all succeed. Tables are shared between those cursors, so are the revisions cache, the staging tables and the folded owner maps. A DuckDBPyRelation is not: it is bound to the cursor that built it, and scanning or unioning it on another fails exactly as across connections.

So the line runs around relations alone:

  • ws.con is the calling thread's cursor, made from the workspace's database on first use in that thread. One workspace serves every thread, and their work shares one database.
class _Cursors(threading.local):
    def __init__(self, db: DuckDBPyConnection) -> None:
        self.con = db.cursor()  # rerun by threading.local in each new thread

A threading.local subclass reruns __init__ with its original arguments in each thread that first touches it, so there is no existence check and no lock; sixteen threads taking their first cursor at once, fifty times over, all succeed on 1.5.5. A thread's cursor is dropped with the thread. A dict keyed by threading.get_ident() would do neither, ids being reused, and a ContextVar is copied into the workers of a task runner, which would share the parent's cursor.

  • Nothing but a relation holds a cursor. Store, Revision, Resolver, ParquetLayer and DirectorySource hold their workspace — a layer through its store — and look up workspace.con per call, so every relation they build lands on the calling thread's cursor. A Record is then usable from any thread, and Revision._resolver keeps caching its Resolver. What they cache besides is plain values any thread computes the same, so two threads racing on one cost a duplicate, not a wrong answer.
  • A relation, and a narwhals frame over one, belongs to the thread that built it, and so does a WorkingRecord, whose staging is one writer's. A relation reaching another thread's as_relation is rejected as one from another connection is.

There is no thread check: concurrent misuse hits DuckDB's own error, and a check on workspace methods would miss the calls a frame makes on its own cursor.

What a fold caches is shared, not held. Two caches hold relations today, and both stop:

  • Resolver._cached_dims keeps a frozen node's folded axes and groups as relations. They become tables, dims_{dim}_{id} and group_{name}_{id}, beside the owner_map_{kind}_{id} that _frozen_table already keeps. The unfrozen tail is folded on top per access, as now.
  • Record.dims captures that dict of axis relations. It builds each frame per access through resolver.axis(dim) instead, as the other _stable_cache members already do; what those cache is the name tuples, plain data.

{id} is the node whose frozen layers were folded: a revision's id, the base's for a WorkingRecord, uuid5 of the URI for a standalone directory. The schema is not in the key, so a table is read through cast_declared(schema, …) as a materialised cache already is. Today _frozen_table returns it uncast, so a Resolver reading under a manifest widened since the fold lacks what the wider schema adds.

A fold one thread builds serves every thread. Two threads that miss at once both fold and both create, and DuckDB fails the second with TransactionException ("Catalog write-write conflict"), not a name clash; the miss path catches that and CatalogException alike and reads the winner's table. The duplicate fold is wasted, not wrong.

Re-issuing a relation on another cursor, so that frames could move too, was considered. A relation over files and tables re-issues from its sql_query(), but one over a Python object (the PyPSA melt, Index.of, as_relation's arrow landing) serialises as a memory pointer and cannot. Asking the record again costs only the plan.

docs.title: Crossing a process boundary
docs.text:
Revision serialises its store as its location:

{ "id": "050c…", "parent": "8db9…", "store": "s3://bucket/my-record" }

A new process has to attach that to some workspace, and the code deserialising it — Prefect, between tasks — has none to pass. So it validates back through Workspace.process().store(uri).revision(id), which reads the revision file and each parent the cache lacks, so ancestry() answers in a fresh process; Store.__reduce__ does the same for pickle.

This is the one default that survives, and it is the same idea as default_connection(), narrowed. Nothing reaches it implicitly but deserialisation: every constructor takes an explicit workspace, and Workspace.process() is reached by name. It is created on first use on :memory:, its remote access comes from the environment like every workspace's, and its database does not travel — a second process could not open the same file for writing anyway.

Revisions deserialised in one process share its workspace, and frames built from their records in one thread join. Code that also builds records of its own and wants them joinable with deserialised ones uses Workspace.process() rather than Workspace() — an opt-in by name rather than the first workspace silently adopted. One that does not gets the foreign-relation error, stated at the boundary.

docs.title: Record moves to layered/record.py
docs.text:
Record lives in layered/revision.py today because its builders did: Record.at builds a DirectorySource and reads the schema, and Revision.record constructs one. With Record.at gone to ws.at and store.layer, and Record.over — the other place a Resolver is assembled — gone with it as a private helper in store.py, nothing ties it there.

It is the Resolver-backed implementation of RecordLike, so it moves beside its backing, into its own layered/record.py, taking _stable_cache with it. Module layout's rule is the reason: protocols live with their implementations rather than with a consumer, and an implementation lives with what it is built over. Its own module rather than resolve.py, so that file stays the DuckDB fold alone rather than also carrying the narwhals face over it. The dependency runs one way — resolve.py, sources.py and fold.py name Record only in docstrings — so layered/record.py imports Resolver and nothing imports back.

What stays:

  • datarecord/record.py keeps its name and contents — RecordLike and LayerData, and the vocabulary their members speak in: LazyFrames, EMPTY, Flags, Frames, Kind. Not protocols.py: most of those are value types, and a tool building frames imports LazyFrames from it. The two record.py modules are the record's vocabulary and its one implementation, told apart by package.
  • LayerData stays in datarecord/record.py, not mutable.py. Its implementations are spread over layered/sources.py, layered/resolve.py and mutable.py, and its one consumer is layered/write.py; in mutable.py the core write path would import from the edit layer above it.
  • layered/revision.py keeps Revision and ancestry, which is what its module docstring already says it is.

mutable.py, datarecord/__init__.py and the tests importing Record from datarecord.layered.revision import it from datarecord.layered.record.

docs.title: Tools take the connection; on_connection goes
docs.text:
Tool.to_datarecord(model, con) and Tool.results(model, con) take the connection their frames are planned on, required. A tool is handed con, not a workspace or a store: it plans relations and has no business with directories, locations or the tree. build(record) is unchanged: it reads record.con as _connection does now. So _NetworkSource.con becomes required, and _melt_con, its duckdb.default_connection() fallback and on_connection go, and write.py loses its hasattr hook. Core names no tool before or after: the connection is now an argument of the tool protocol in datarecord/tools/base.py, not a structural hook in the write path (module layout).

The call sites that broke now read:

root = store.root(PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con))
w = WorkingRecord(root.record)
for attr, frame in PyPSA.results(n, w.con).items():
    w.set(attr, frame, kind="outputs")

docs.title: A relation from another connection is rejected
docs.text:
Copying one onto the target connection would collect it to arrow on its own connection — a full materialisation the caller never asked for, and one that fails anyway if that connection has been closed. Making it impossible by construction covers what this package builds, but a caller can still hand set a relation from a connection of their own.

So as_relation rejects it, and says why: binding con.sql("FROM native") costs no read and raises duckdb.InvalidInputException for a relation from another connection, which it re-raises as a ValueError naming the fix — build the frame on record.con in this thread, or hand over a non-DuckDB frame and let it land. Construction removes the case for every path this package owns; the check turns the case it cannot own from an InvalidInputException three calls later into a sentence at the boundary. The same check catches a frame built on another thread's cursor.

docs.title: What is deleted
docs.text:
• duck.DEFAULT_BASE_URI, the DATARECORD_BASE_URI env var, _BASE_URIS, base_uri_of, default_connection, connect (its body moves into Workspace), and the unused layer_dir SQL macro with _register_macros. A caller wanting the env var writes ws.store(os.environ["DATARECORD_BASE_URI"]).
  • Every base_uri: str | None = None. layer_dir, resolved_dir and schema_uri become Store methods; ParquetLayer holds its store in place of con and base_uri, and DirectorySource its workspace in place of con; read_schema(store), write_schema(schema, store), Fold.read(…, store), resolve.materialise(…, store), materialised(revision_id, store) and sources_to_read(ancestry, store, schema) take one, and _map_uri becomes a Store path. Resolver holds its workspace in place of con; source_for builds a ParquetLayer on the store its sources share, and a standalone record, whose one source is a DirectorySource, never reaches that path.
  • read_json with its urlopen; the manifest and revision files go through Files.
  • Revision.create, Revision.get, the source-less Revision.child(), Record.at, Record.over, and con= on WorkingRecord.
  • write_record as a public name, WorkingRecord.commit, NewChild, Directory, Target and _base_revision. datarecord.write_record, datarecord.layer_dir, datarecord.connect, NewChild and Directory leave __all__; Workspace and Store join it.
  • on_connection, _NetworkSource._melt_con, and _base_resolver's connection check.
  • Resolver._cached_dims, for tables; and the axes dict Record.dims captures.

A con argument stays where a function plans relations — fold_axis, union_all_by_name, try_read_parquet, the fold — since those take the connection they compose on, not a location.

docs.title: The test fixtures
docs.text:
@pytest.fixture
def workspace():
    ws = Workspace()
    yield ws
    ws.close()


@pytest.fixture
def store(workspace, tmp_path):
    return workspace.store(str(tmp_path))

They replace base_uri and con: no monkeypatch, since there is no global to patch. layer_dir(x.id) in the tests becomes store.layer_dir(x.id), Revision.create(con) followed by hand-written layer files goes through the tests/fixtures.py helper, Record.at(layer_dir(x.id), con) becomes store.layer(x.id), and a test needing the connection reads workspace.con. test_two_roots_in_one_process_read_their_own_schema becomes two stores on one workspace, and gains an assertion it could not make before, that each location's layers land under it. The connect(base_uri=…/"unrelated") cases in test_write.py and test_mutable.py read a standalone directory through a second connection, and become ws.at(out); what the test_mutable.py one pins besides — that edits are validated under their base's schema, not a connection's — gets a test of its own.

New tests pin what this adds: a revision round-tripped through model_dump_json into Workspace.process() reads its ancestry back; threads sharing one workspace read concurrently, each on its own cursor, and reuse one folded owner map; two threads missing that cache at once both get it; a store and a standalone directory on SeaweedFS (≥ 4.18, in a container) write and read their manifest and revision files; a second create-only write of one revision file fails; two writers widening one manifest end with both widenings or a reported incompatibility, never one silently lost; a remote write that fails part-way leaves no revision revisions() lists; a remote ws.write to a non-empty URI is refused before it writes; two threads adding one revision row at once both succeed; a fold table built before the manifest widened reads under the wider schema; a Record built in one thread reads in another; and child(w.edits) on a revision other than w's base raises.

docs.title: Landing
docs.text:
1. Workspace and Store, with the tree at the location: the local Files, revisions/<id>.json read back into the revisions table, a revision serialising its store's location, the fixtures, every con=/base_uri path switched over, a cursor per thread with the fold caches as shared tables, as_relation rejecting a foreign relation, and the globals deleted; Record.at and Record.over go, and Record moves to layered/record.py. One commit: the half-honoured base is a bug either side of the change, keeping both would be the alias AGENTS.md forbids, and the tree at the location fixes deserialisation only once a revision carries the location. Until step 2, Revision.create writes the revision file before its layer.
  2. Writing: store.root, rev.child(source) and ws.write replacing write_record and Revision.create, so the revision file, or a directory's manifest, is written last; WorkingRecord(record) with edits, and commit and its targets gone.
  3. Remote files: the boto3 Files behind datarecord[remote], the AWS environment configuring it and httpfs together, and _reconcile_schema on conditional writes. Manta's SeaweedFS pin moves to 4.18 or later before it relies on them.
  4. Tools: the protocol takes con, and on_connection goes.

The design pages follow in the same commits: layers gains revisions/<id>.json beside layers/, the revision file as what makes a layer real, and the store a revision carries; writing documents root, child and ws.write, and the remote write's atomicity; the working record replaces committing with edits; the read path the fold tables shared between threads and read through cast_declared; tools the con parameter; module layout adds store.py for both classes, files.py and layered/record.py for Record, takes Record off the top-level record.py's line, and narrows duck.py to relation helpers; what a data record is names datarecord[remote] as the one optional dependency of core. record.md and the usage pages name write_record(…, con) and WorkingRecord(…, con) and follow too.

docs.title: DEP 10: A group is one struct column
DEP 10: a group is one struct column
docs.text:
DEP 10 Title a group is one struct column Author Jonas Hörsch Status Superseded 2026-10-26 (implemented 2026-10-12, amendment 2026-10-13) Created 2026-10-12 Version Unreleased Superseded-By DEP 20 (its group tombstones anti-joining the owner map), DEP 23 (its groups, which become multi-dims)

Landed in the steps below on the schema, the record, the format, the read path, the working record and consuming a record; this page is kept as the argument for the change rather than as the current description, and those pages are authoritative where the two disagree. What the implementation found records where it departs from or adds to the argument below.

An attribute over a group carries the group as one column, named for the group, of a STRUCT dtype over the group's key — connection STRUCT(entity, bus) — rather than the group's coordinates spread out as columns of their own.

That gives back broadcasting to every dim a group draws on, and makes the owner map key one column per membership, so a group shows up there as itself.

docs.title: What starts it
docs.text:
Addressing expands a group in dims to its coordinates, so inputs/efficiency.parquet is entity | bus | timestep | … and the fold key is the flat union of every group's coordinate names (partial_dims). A column in the fold key is either broadcast or membership, never both, and a group coordinate never broadcasts. So Schema.broadcast_dims drops every coordinate any group is keyed by, schema-wide:

sparse = {c for g in self.groups.values() for c in g.key}

The cost lands on attributes that have nothing to do with the group. Declaring connection over (entity, bus) means no attribute anywhere may hold a value once for every bus: a per-bus marginal_price over {bus, timestep} reads a NULL bus as "no bus", not "every bus". Declaring bus_country over bus into country — a classification, which addresses no attribute row at all — does the same. The broadcast rule is right that a connection's bus has no axis to expand against; it is wrong that the dim bus therefore has none. The two are one column today only because the group was flattened into the dim's name.

The owner map pays the same flattening in legibility. Its key is entity | bus | from | to | <partial dims>, and which of those columns together name a connection, a corridor or nothing is recoverable only from the schema. A group's tombstones are a multi-column anti-join over coordinates that other groups and plain dims share names with.

docs.title: The construct
docs.text:
An attribute row carries a group as one struct column named for the group, with one field per key coordinate, in over order:

inputs/efficiency.parquet   connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value
inputs/flow.parquet         corridor STRUCT("from", "to")  | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value
inputs/marginal_price       bus | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value

coordinates_of("efficiency") is ("connection", "timestep"): addressing still resolves a name in dims to the dim of that name first and to the group otherwise, but a group resolves to itself rather than expanding.

The membership keys are entity and one column per group, and every declared dim but entity and the type axis broadcasts. broadcast_dims loses its sparse exclusion; bus broadcasts like scenario. The fold key stays one fixed tuple, its columns now entity | connection | corridor | <partial value dims>.

A group column does not broadcast, for the reason the broadcast rule already gives: it addresses a sparse subset only the group's table knows. It is compared NULL-safely as one value, which DuckDB hash-joins on directly — checked on 1.5.5, k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM k over a STRUCT key plans a HASH_JOIN, and a NULL field compares equal to a NULL field. So resolving a relation joins o.connection IS NOT DISTINCT FROM u.connection where it joined entity and bus separately, and the address columns still derive from the schema.

A group does not share a dim's name. A group is carried as a column named for it, so country into country would make two columns one name; the functional group is bus_country, and only the entity-type group, which has no file or column of its own, may share its dim's name.

A group file is keyed by its struct column: groups/connection.parquet is connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role, folded like any axis keyed by that one column, exactly as dims/<dim>.parquet is keyed by the column named for the dim — so a row and its group meet on one column with nothing packed between them.

docs.title: The owner map
docs.text:
# inputs
entity        -- never NULL where the attribute addresses an entity
connection    STRUCT(entity, bus)
corridor      STRUCT("from", "to")
<partial value dims>
attribute
layer_uuid
varies        STRUCT(<broadcast dim>: BOOLEAN, ...)   -- now with a `bus` field
broadcast     STRUCT(<broadcast dim>: BOOLEAN, ...)
breakpoints   BOOLEAN

Only the groups a long input row can carry are keyed. A group column belongs in the map where some attribute in attributes names the group beside another coordinate, so that it is long rows in inputs/ — efficiency over {connection, timestep}. Every other group would be a column NULL on every row of the map, widening the key every read pays for to identify nothing:

  • the entity-type group, whose rows are the entity axis and which no attribute names beside entity;
  • a group addressed only alone, whose attributes are columns of its own file — role on connection, were it the only one;
  • a group only results name, outputs/ never overlaying;
  • a group nothing names.

So the map's membership columns are entity and Schema.group_columns, derived like partial_dims rather than declared. Adding an attribute stays compatible though it may add a group to the key: a map folded before has no such column, which is correct — no row there names the group — so a reader takes a missing group column as NULL, as it takes a missing flag field as unset.

Each membership is one column, so reading the map needs no schema to say which columns belong together. A group's tombstones are a single-column NULL-safe anti-join, the same shape as the entity axis's; the no-cascade rule is unchanged. The flag structs gain a field for each dim that now broadcasts, so flags reports a constant-over-buses marginal_price as broadcast over bus rather than not at all.

docs.title: What changes for a caller
docs.text:
Record.attributes["efficiency"] hands back a connection struct column; a consumer wanting flat columns takes nw.col("connection").struct.field("bus"), or unnests. The PyPSA tool does that once, where it reads and builds connections.

WorkingRecord.set keeps coordinate keywords: bus="north" addresses one connection and the stage packs {entity, bus}. A long frame handed to set may carry either the struct column or its coordinates flat; the coordinates are packed on the way in, so the frame a tool already builds keeps working.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
• An on-disk format change. Every inputs/ and outputs/ file over a group is rewritten, and materialised owner maps are rebuilt. The project is pre-1.0 and holds no compatibility promise; no reader for the flat form survives.
  • Struct support at the boundary. narwhals' struct.field works on DuckDB, polars and pyarrow-backed frames; a numpy-backed pandas frame has no struct dtype, so a pandas consumer unnests on the DuckDB side first.
  • A filter by entity on a connection attribute becomes connection.entity = 'g1'. That costs nothing measurable: DuckDB 1.5.5 pushes a struct-field filter into the parquet scan and skips row groups on the field's statistics as it does for a top-level column — over 2M rows in 20 row groups, conn.entity = … and entity = … both read one row group (2.0 ms and 1.8 ms), and a field value outside every range skips all of them.

docs.title: One behaviour that must not move
docs.text: Today a connection attribute row carries a top-level entity, so the fold drops it when the entity is tombstoned even though the connection tuple survives. Under the struct it has no top-level entity, so the entity tombstone matches every entity a row names instead — entity, and each entity inside the group's struct. Removing an entity still drops its connections' values and leaves the tuples, which is the no-cascade rule as it stands: the tuples are a membership of their own, the values belong to the entity.

docs.title: A rule it adds
docs.text: An attribute naming a group and a dim one of its key coordinates is named for — dims={"connection", "bus"} — is rejected: the row would hold the bus twice, free to disagree. It is unexpressible today only because the two land on one column; the struct makes it expressible, so the schema says so instead. It is the same "keyed twice over" rule into already states.

docs.title: Landing
docs.text:
1. Schema: coordinates_of resolves a group to itself; broadcast_dims drops sparse; membership_keys gains the group columns; the rule above.
  2. The fold and the read path: owner-map key and the group tombstone anti-join on the struct column; the resolve join on it.
  3. Staging: pack coordinate keywords and flat frame columns into the struct.
  4. The PyPSA tool packs on to_datarecord and unpacks on build.
  5. Schema, record, format and read-path pages rewritten; this page marked landed.

docs.title: What the implementation found
docs.text:
