1. schema.py: Trait, Schema.traits, _check_trait, attributes_for, properties_for, _carried, _dropped_by_category go. A traits key is refused at load. Docstrings drop the traits links.
  2. __init__.py: Trait leaves the exports.
  3. layered/categories.py: narrowed, label_carriers, carriers, attributes_among, carried_properties go; with_defaults loses _carries_.
  4. layered/resolve.py: the carriers join in the broadcast goes.
  5. layered/fold.py: flags(**categories) filters by matching labels only.
  6. mutable.py: the category check in set validation goes.
  7. tools/pypsa.py: as above; BY_CTYPE stays for default_by.
  8. Tests: trait tests in test_schema.py, test_categories.py, test_mutable.py, test_overlay.py, test_properties.py, test_functional_groups.py are deleted; fixtures.py declares no traits.
  9. Pages: schema loses "Traits" and "switch"; categories, properties and default_by drop trait mentions. record, read path, working record, open questions, usage schema, CHANGELOG.md.
  10. On implementation, DEP 1 and DEP 3 take Superseded-By this DEP.

Checks: no trait in src/; a manifest with traits is refused naming the replacement; a PyPSA network round-trips.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
• Keeping traits as an unenforced bundle for dispatch: a vocabulary no caller asks for.
  • Moving narrowing onto AttributeSpec (carried_by): the same rule under another name, with every branch kept.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
• What build does with a value its type does not take. Recommend reporting it from _verify, as an unknown type is, not raising.
  • Whether a category still needs partial. It guarded per-label narrowing. Recommend keeping it: default_by per label needs a dim owned per label.
  • The committable case DEP 3 raised. Recommend leaving it to the consumer reading the committable attribute.
  • Owner-map size. Recommend measuring the PyPSA example before and after; no change unless it regresses.

docs.title: DEP 17: results are attributes
docs.text: DEP 17 Title results are attributes Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-20) Requires DEP 16 Created 2026-10-20 Version Unreleased Superseded-By DEP 20 (its SubNetwork as an entity, and its tombstones)

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A result becomes an ordinary attribute. A layer has one attributes/ directory, and inputs/ and outputs/ go. Schema.results, RecordLike.outputs, Kind and every kind="outputs" go with them. Only a tool knows which attributes it computes. Tool.results gives way to to_datarecord(model, con, results_only=True, base=record).

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Today a record keeps two vocabularies of one shape. attributes and results are both mappings of AttributeSpec. Each lands in its own directory, inputs/ or outputs/. The split reaches every layer of the code:

  • The schema. Schema.results is a second mapping. Name checks, spec, the column check and compatibility each union the two.
  • The protocol. RecordLike.outputs sits beside attributes. LayerData.attributes(kind) and attribute(name, kind) take a Kind.
  • The read path. outputs/ does not overlay. A node reads its own layer only, so a child loses its parent's results.
  • The working record. set(..., kind="outputs") checks the name against results. It skips the label check and keeps staged results apart.
  • The write path. A result's shape is unchecked beyond attribute, breakpoint and value.
  • The owner map. It is keyed by kind (owner_map_uri(id, "inputs"), owner_map_<kind>_<id>), for a kind that is always inputs.

The distinction belongs to a framework. PyPSA marks an attribute "Output" in its registry. The record layer stores, validates and resolves that distinction, for a vocabulary it never defines. A reader wanting a solved marginal_price must also know which of two mappings holds it.

docs.title: What goes
docs.text: today becomes inputs/<attr>.parquet, outputs/<attr>.parquet attributes/<attr>.parquet, one directory per layer Schema.results gone; a result is declared in Schema.attributes the name check across attributes and results one name, one entry in attributes Schema.spec reading attributes then results attributes alone results in compatibility gone; attributes versions as before RecordLike.outputs, Record.outputs gone; record.attributes[name] Kind, attributes(kind), attribute(name, kind) attributes(), attribute(name) the read path's outputs gone; a result overlays like any attribute, latest layer winning owner maps keyed by kind one owner map: owner_map_uri(id), owner_map_<id> set(..., kind="outputs") set(name, frame) the name check of a result against results the attribute check of set the label exemption for a result gone; every label must resolve staged_outputs_<attr>_<id> the staged attribute table the write path's shape exemption for a result gone; a result's file carries its declared coordinates outputs/ written only when non-empty gone; attributes/ holds whatever the source has Tool.results(model, con) to_datarecord(model, con, results_only=True, base=record)

docs.title: Loading an old layer
docs.text:
A layer with an inputs/ or outputs/ directory is refused when its source is opened:

layer <id> has an `inputs/` directory; a layer holds every attribute in
`attributes/`, results included. Re-export the record.

docs.title: The tool interface
docs.text:
Tool.results goes. to_datarecord takes results_only and base:

def to_datarecord(
    self,
    model: Any,
    con: DuckDBPyConnection,
    *,
    results_only: bool = False,
    base: RecordLike | None = None,
) -> RecordLike: ...

base is the record the model was built from. It is required with results_only=True and refused otherwise.

With results_only=True it presents only what the solve produced. That is the result attributes and the intermediate results they need. It is a thin layer, written as a child of the record the model was built from: rev.child(layer). Nothing is staged through a WorkingRecord. Where inputs were edited first, their edits are committed as a child, and the thin layer goes on top of that child.

docs.title: Intermediate results
docs.text:
A solve derives structure as well as values: PyPSA's SubNetworks, a cycle matrix. Each is an ordinary dim, entity or attribute the tool writes. A SubNetwork is an entity with ctype="SubNetwork", and a line's sub_network an attribute naming one. A cycle matrix is an attribute over a cycle dim and the lines. The tool's schema declares them like any other name.

On every results_only write the tool replaces them. The model does not say what the base held, so the tool reads the intermediate entities and labels in base, such as its SubNetwork entities. The thin layer tombstones those it does not write again, then adds the new ones. A re-solve that numbers SubNetworks differently leaves no stale label behind.

docs.title: The PyPSA tool
docs.text:
• It knows its outputs. _output_attributes(c) still reads PyPSA's registry status "Output". _result_attributes still maps each to its record name.
  • The schema declares them as attributes. _registry_schema adds them to attributes. A name that is an input on another type stays dropped, as today.
  • build incorporates every attribute the record holds. A solved bus's marginal_price is copied into the network, as any attribute is.
  • "Output" is read only on import. It decides what results_only presents. It never drops data from build or a full export.
  • to_datarecord writes outputs as attributes. A solved network round-trips its results through attributes/.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
One mapping, one directory. A result already has a dtype, dims and a description. Its file already has the long schema. Keeping it apart costs a branch at every reader and buys only the overlay rule.

Results inherit. A child that changes nothing a solve reads keeps its parent's solution. A child that changes inputs holds results computed from its parent. That is the same staleness a staged result has today after an input edit.

The tool owns "output". PyPSA's registry already says which attributes a solve fills. Only the tool's import reads that. This matches the module layout, which keeps framework knowledge out of core.

One import, two scopes. A full export and a results layer differ only in what they present. One to_datarecord keeps the rule for each result in one place.

No label exemption. Every row of a record names a declared label. A reader joining a result to dims["entity"] never meets an orphan.

Costs. Every record is re-exported, breaking changes being free. A child of a solved node shows results its inputs no longer support. A results layer meets full validation, so it carries the labels its results name.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Before:

n = PyPSA.build(w)
n.optimize()
for attr, frame in PyPSA.results(n, w.con).items():
    w.set(attr, frame, kind="outputs")
solved = rev.child(w.edits)  # inputs and results in one layer
solved.record.outputs["marginal_price"]  # a child of solved has none
schema.results["p"]

After:

inputs = rev.child(w.edits)
n = PyPSA.build(inputs.record)
n.optimize()
solved = inputs.child(
    PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, w.con, results_only=True, base=inputs.record)
)
solved.record.attributes["marginal_price"]  # a child of solved reads it too
PyPSA.build(solved.record)  # marginal_price is in the network
schema.attributes["p"]

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. schema.py: results, its name, column and compatibility arms go; spec reads attributes.
  2. record.py: Kind and outputs go; attributes() and attribute(name) lose kind.
  3. layered/sources.py: reads attributes/; a layer with inputs/ or outputs/ is refused.
  4. layered/resolve.py: _outputs goes; map_kinds becomes one fold; every kind parameter goes.
  5. store.py: owner_map_uri(id) drops kind.
  6. layered/record.py: outputs goes.
  7. layered/write.py: writes attributes/; the outputs arm and the result exemptions go.
  8. mutable.py: kind on set, _validate_result, outputs and the staged outputs tables go.
  9. tools/base.py: results goes; to_datarecord takes results_only and base.
  10. tools/pypsa.py: as above; results folds into to_datarecord; intermediates in base are replaced as above.
  11. Tests: kind="outputs" and outputs tests in test_mutable.py, test_records.py, test_tools.py, test_overlay.py, test_write.py, test_properties.py, test_owner_map.py are rewritten or deleted; fixtures.py declares results as attributes.
  12. Pages: format, read path, schema, working record, writing, tools, record, layers, open questions, the usage pages, CHANGELOG.md.

Checks: no outputs, Kind or results field in src/; an old layer is refused naming attributes/; a solved PyPSA network round-trips with its results; a child reads its parent's results; a re-solve leaves no stale SubNetwork; results_only without base, or base without it, is refused.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
• A result: bool flag on AttributeSpec: the split again under another name, and still a framework's vocabulary.
  • Keeping outputs/ beside attributes/: two directories for one shape, and every reader still branching.
  • build skipping outputs: it would drop data the record holds, and a solved record would build unsolved.
  • A PyPSA.attach(n, w) staging results: a thin layer from to_datarecord writes them without a WorkingRecord.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
• Stale results after an input edit. They now inherit, so the open question on staged results widens. Recommend leaving coherence to the caller, as today.
  • Detecting intermediates that no longer fit their inputs. It needs provenance of which inputs each came from. Deferred.
  • Filtering a record before build. Selecting one period or chosen outputs is a separate future feature, not designed here.

docs.title: DEP 18: drop narwhals
docs.text: DEP 18 Title drop narwhals Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-20) Requires DEP 17 Created 2026-10-20 Version Unreleased

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: narwhals leaves datarecord, core and tools alike. DuckDB is the one query engine. A record answers bare DuckDBPyRelations, and the write path takes relations and pandas, polars or arrow frames. Dtypes are mathspec's DimensionDtype and ParameterDtype, stored as plain strings, with one fixed DuckDB type map. A dim may list its labels with one_of: [...] beside its dtype, and a property may take its labels from a dim with one_of: <dim> in place of its dtype, which replaces into on properties and groups.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Every record is DuckDB underneath. narwhals is a wrapper a reader passes through on the way:

  • The read path. Record resolves a relation, then wraps it with nw.from_native. A caller wanting SQL unwraps it again with to_native().
  • The write path. set turns any frame into narwhals, then into a relation (as_relation). Two conversions do the work of one DuckDB scan.
  • Private API. duck.py imports narwhals._duckdb.utils and narwhals._utils.Version for its type translation. The >=2,<3,!=2.21.0 pin guards that.
  • Two dtype vocabularies. The manifest stores narwhals class names ("Float64", {"Datetime": "us"}). A mathspec model declares float, int, bool, str and datetime, and a dimension's labels with one_of. Every consumer translates between them.
  • A wider vocabulary than any consumer reads. Date, number widths and time zones are expressible. Nothing downstream distinguishes them.
  • Tools. tools/base.to_relation exists because narwhals has no PIVOT. The PyPSA tool wraps every pandas frame in narwhals to hand it back.

The footprint is 175 lines in 9 files under src/, and 219 lines in 13 test files.

docs.title: mathspec
docs.text:
datarecord pins mathspec at 9f180255a180ce7cc1f046fdc75020cdbfc9d90e, the head of energy-models/mathspec#915. There a dimension may write one_of: [labels] beside dtype: str, and dtype defaults to str. program.Dimension carries dtype: DimensionDtype (float, int, str, datetime) and one_of: tuple[str, ...] | None. ParameterDtype is float, int, bool, str, and a parameter takes no one_of.

A git pin to a PR branch lasts only while the commit exists on GitHub. Before a release, the pin moves to the merged commit.

docs.title: Dtypes
docs.text:
declares declaration DuckDB type dim, attribute, property dtype: float DOUBLE dim, attribute, property dtype: int BIGINT attribute, property dtype: bool BOOLEAN dim, attribute, property dtype: str VARCHAR dim dtype: datetime TIMESTAMP (no time zone) dim dtype: str, one_of: [labels] ENUM of the labels property one_of: <dim> that dim's type

The map is one constant in duck.py, read wherever a column is typed. Date, Int32, Float32 and time zones are gone.

A dim that lists its labels has an ENUM column. add refuses a label outside the list, naming the list. Only a str dim lists its labels, as in mathspec.

A property one_of: <dim> takes its labels from that dim. It declares no dtype, and its column has the dim's type: an ENUM where the dim lists its labels, TIMESTAMP for a datetime dim. A stored value that is not NULL names a live label, checked where into is checked today. The property may be of a dim or of a group. This is datarecord's own spelling: #915 refuses a dimension reference on a parameter, but a datarecord property is a mathspec relation column, not a parameter.

An attribute takes no one_of, neither a list nor a dim, as a mathspec parameter has none.

Struct columns are derived, never declared. A group's column is a STRUCT with a field per key coordinate, each typed as its dim. An owner flag is a STRUCT of BOOLEAN. The fixed columns stay fixed: attribute VARCHAR, breakpoint DOUBLE, deleted BOOLEAN, breakpoints BOOLEAN.

docs.title: into goes
docs.text:
PropertySpec.into and GroupSpec.into are removed. bus.country into country becomes bus.country: {one_of: country}. A group bus_country over [bus, scenario] into country becomes the group over [bus, scenario] with a property country: {one_of: country}.

Lost from group into:

  • Exactly one label per tuple. The property may be NULL, so a tuple may carry none.
  • The column named after the dim. The property's name is free; country is a convention, not a rule.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Schema.categorizing(dim) today picks the Enum-typed properties of a dim in partial. Under this DEP it picks the properties of such a dim that are {one_of: <d>} where d lists its labels. A property taking its labels from a dim that lists none does not categorize: its labels are data a layer adds and removes.

PyPSA's ctype becomes a dim {dtype: str, one_of: [Generator, Line, ...]}, and entity.ctype becomes {one_of: ctype}. connection.role, an Enum of _ROLES today, becomes {one_of: role} on a dim role listing input, output and attached.

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
A dtype is written as its mathspec string, "dtype": "float". A dim lists its labels as "one_of": [...] beside its dtype, and a property takes its labels from a dim as "one_of": "<dim>" in place of its dtype.

An old manifest fails at load, naming the replacement:

dimension 'snapshot' declares dtype {"Datetime": "us"}, a narwhals name;
write "datetime" (one of float, int, str, datetime)

String, Float64, Int64, Boolean and Datetime map to str, float, int, bool and datetime. Enum names "one_of": [...] on a dim and "one_of": "<dim>" on a property. Date has no replacement and names datetime. A property or group declaring into fails at load, naming one_of: <dim>.

docs.title: The read API
docs.text:
The mappings stay; their values are relations. record.dims[name], record.properties[subject], record.groups[name] and record.attributes[name] are each a duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation on the record's connection.

today becomes Frames = Mapping[str, nw.LazyFrame] Relations = Mapping[str, DuckDBPyRelation] LazyFrames LazyRelations, built on __getitem__ as before layered/record.py's Record Record in record.py, the one resolver-backed record nw.from_native(resolver.attribute(name)) resolver.attribute(name) frame.to_native() in a caller gone

RecordLike is no longer engine-neutral. A tool's record builds its relations on the caller's connection. The PyPSA _NetworkSource scans its pandas frames with con.from_df.

docs.title: The write API
docs.text:
set, add and add_group take a DuckDB relation, or a pandas, polars or arrow frame. A frame reaches DuckDB through its own scanner, without collecting a relation; no scanner package becomes a dependency. A relation on another connection is refused, as today. A scalar stays a scalar.

A column is checked against the DuckDB type its dtype maps to. A lossless widening (INTEGER to BIGINT) is cast. Anything else is refused, naming the declared dtype. A frame with time-zone timestamps is refused, not converted to naive time.

check_group_columns takes a relation and runs in SQL. It reads rel.columns and rel.types. The partial-NULL check is one LIMIT 1 query.

docs.title: Snapshot timesteps
docs.text: A property declares no datetime dtype, since mathspec's ParameterDtype has none. So PyPSA's snapshot.timestep becomes {one_of: timestep} on a new datetime dim, timestep, PyPSA's own index level name. Its labels are the timesteps a multi-period network uses. snapshot.period becomes {one_of: period}.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
One engine, one representation. The resolver already returns relations. Handing them over bare removes a wrap per read and a conversion per write.

mathspec owns the vocabulary. A record feeds a mathspec model, which declares five dtypes and a dimension's labels. Storing those keeps the manifest and the model in one language. A wider vocabulary bought distinctions nobody read.

One spelling for "labels of a dim". into on a property, into on a group and an Enum property were three spellings of one idea. one_of: <dim> is one, and it is the relation column a mathspec model reads. A category is then a label that a dim lists, so ctype gets an axis file and an order like any dim.

A fixed map over a translation library. Seven entries replace a private narwhals import. They change only when mathspec does.

Struct columns derive from the schema. A group's struct follows from its key. Declaring it would state the key twice.

Costs. A caller reading record.attributes[...] with narwhals or polars expressions rewrites them as SQL or relation calls. A non-DuckDB backend for RecordLike is no longer possible. A record declaring Date, a number width, Enum or into is re-exported, breaking changes being free. A functional group loses its single-valuedness guarantee. PyPSA records gain timestep, ctype and role dims.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Before:

Dimension(dtype=nw.Datetime(), description="A snapshot.")
AttributeSpec(dtype=nw.Float64(), dims={"entity"})
PropertySpec(dtype=nw.Enum(["Generator", "Line"]))
PropertySpec(into="carrier")
Group(over=["bus", "scenario"], into="country")

p_nom = record.attributes["p_nom"]
p_nom.filter(nw.col("value") > 0).collect().to_pandas()
rel = p_nom.to_native()

After:

Dimension(dtype="datetime", description="A snapshot.")
Dimension(one_of=["Generator", "Line"])  # the ctype dim
AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity"})
PropertySpec(one_of="ctype")
PropertySpec(one_of="carrier")
Group(over=["bus", "scenario"])  # with property country: {"one_of": "country"}

p_nom = record.attributes["p_nom"]
p_nom.filter("value > 0").df()
w.set("p_nom", polars_frame)  # or pandas, arrow, a relation

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. pixi.toml (small): mathspec pinned at 9f18025; narwhals goes from it and pyproject.toml; pixi lock.
  2. schema.py (large): dtypes become mathspec strings, and dims and properties gain one_of; _BARE_DTYPES, _dump_dtype and _parse_dtype go; PropertySpec.into and GroupSpec.into go, with their checks; old names and into are refused at load; categorizing reads one_of; group_type and flag_type return DuckDB structs; check_group_columns runs in SQL.
  3. duck.py (small): the type map replaces DuckTypes' narwhals call; as_relation takes relations and pandas, polars or arrow frames.
  4. record.py and layered/record.py (medium): Relations and LazyRelations; Record moves into record.py, layered/record.py goes.
  5. layered/resolve.py, layered/write.py (small): defaults and empty columns read the type map; nw.from_native goes.
  6. mutable.py (medium): _incoming becomes as_relation; column checks compare DuckDB types; label and group selection are relation filters; add refuses a label outside a dim's one_of.
  7. tools/base.py (small): to_relation goes; to_datarecord returns relations on con.
  8. tools/pypsa.py (large): frames scanned on con; _DTYPES and _column_dtype return mathspec strings; ctype and role become dims; into becomes one_of; snapshot.timestep names a timestep dim.
  9. Tests (large): fixtures declare string dtypes; narwhals expressions become relation calls; tests/test_functional_groups.py moves from into to one_of, its group single-valuedness tests deleted; an old manifest and into are refused.
  10. Pages: schema (its into sections), format, record, read path, working record, writing, tools, module layout, the usage pages, CHANGELOG.md.

Checks: no narwhals in src/, pyproject.toml or pixi.toml; a manifest with "Float64" is refused naming float; one with into is refused naming one_of; every record.*[...] value is a DuckDBPyRelation; set takes a polars, pandas and arrow frame; a PyPSA network round-trips.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
• Keeping narwhals in tools only: two value types for one record, and the conversion stays.
  • DuckDB type names in the manifest: an engine's vocabulary where mathspec's is the consumer's.
  • A declared struct dtype: it would restate the group's key.
  • Keeping datetime on properties: mathspec's ParameterDtype refuses it, so the model could not read it.
  • A local Enum dtype on properties: mathspec puts the labels on a dimension; a property list would be a second vocabulary.
  • Keeping into beside one_of: two spellings of one declaration.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text: • Recovering single-valuedness for a functional group. A group property may be NULL, so a tuple may carry no label. Recommend nothing until a consumer needs it; a later required flag on a property would cover it.

docs.title: DEP 19: One Record and a package layout
DEP 19: one Record and a package layout
docs.text: DEP 19 Title one Record and a package layout Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-21) Requires DEP 18 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 5 (Record over a NodeCache), DEP 8 (a fold that is LayerData) Superseded-By DEP 20 (its re-added key introduced where it is re-added)

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Record absorbs Resolver: one class folds a record's layers and answers RecordLike, and a record with staged edits folds only its staged layer per read. The package splits into three subpackages, schema/, resolve/ and store/, under one dependency rule, which breaks the import cycle between store.py and layered/revision.py. The internal names that still say "inputs" take the owner map's vocabulary.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
DEP 8 split Resolver from Record so that the writer could read a Resolver directly as LayerData. Since WorkingRecord.commit was removed in a17bf6e, the writer no longer does: a whole record reaches it as a Record, through the adapter for a RecordLike. Each member of Record still forwards to one member of Resolver and turns its None into a KeyError, and code that needs the record has to carry both objects. Revision caches a Resolver in rev.resolver but builds a new Record around it on every access to rev.record, which throws away the cache of key sets that Record keeps. WorkingRecord builds its resolver with Resolver.with_source, which nothing else calls, and wraps that resolver in a Record once more.

When a working record is written as a whole, the writer has to fold its staged edits once for the duration of the write. _pinned does this by making a shallow copy of the Record and setting a PinnedResolver on the copy through object.__setattr__, since Record is a frozen dataclass, and release later reaches that PinnedResolver through two isinstance checks. Several members exist without a reader: nothing calls Resolver.axes() or Resolver.groups(), group_frame only calls group, and the writer never reads LayerData.frozen.

On a record with staged edits, every read of the axes, groups or dead labels folds them again from the deepest node cache on disk and opens the parquet files of every layer above it. Reading with pending edits says that the fold is materialised up to the staged layer and that only the staged step is folded per read, and the owner map already works that way.

store.py imports layered/revision.py lazily inside three methods, because revision.py imports store.py at the top. The page on the module layout no longer matches the tree: it lists no fold.py and says that files.py holds manifests. schema.py (1,554 lines) and layered/resolve.py (1,499 lines) each hold several parts that can stand on their own.

docs.title: One Record
docs.text:
Record is a frozen dataclass in resolve/record.py with the four fields Resolver has today:

field holds revision_id the node whose frozen layers are folded, as for Resolver today sources the layers, root first, truncated at the deepest materialised one workspace where the calling thread's cursor comes from schema the record's one manifest

A Record is read through one API, the RecordLike members (schema, dims, properties, groups, attributes, flags), and its public surface adds only its four fields, con and frozen. The Resolver methods that read the same rows a second way, returning None where a mapping raises KeyError, are deleted: axis, group, group_frame, attribute, the enumerators axes(), groups() and attributes(), with_source and inputs. What stays private is the fold the mappings answer from: _fold holds the owner map, _coords holds the folded axes, groups and dead labels (the Coords that Resolver.dims returns today), and _source_for and _relation resolve one attribute. _relation raises KeyError for an attribute that no layer owns, where attribute returned an empty relation; only a key set read before rollback() and used after it reaches that case. Record keeps its cache of key sets, which now checks self.frozen.

On a record with staged edits, _coords folds only the layers after the frozen prefix onto that prefix's coord tables. _frozen_coords already holds the prefix's folded axes, groups and dead labels as shared DuckDB tables (_coord_table), and resolve_coords already takes a folded seed when it starts from a node cache on disk. It now takes those tables as its seed, as _fold_map takes _frozen_table for the owner map, so a fold on a working record reads tables already in the database, opens no file, and does what reading with pending edits describes. The key set of groups comes from one such fold, not from one fold per declared group.

A label or group tuple that one layer removes and a later layer adds again is now introduced where it is added again, not where it was first introduced. The prefix's coord tables and the cache of a materialised node keep a tombstoned key at most as a dead label, which has no place in member order, so a fold seeded from either cannot put a re-added key where it was first introduced, as the old rule required. Under the new rule, fold_axis counts only the rows of a key that are deeper than its deepest tombstone, so the seeded fold, the fold over every layer and a fold over a materialised node agree.

WorkingRecord is the only caller of the deleted methods, and it reads through the mappings instead:

WorkingRecord today becomes resolver.axis(dim), to test for an axis or to check that labels exist self.dims.get(dim), read once per call resolver.axis(dim), to match property values self.properties.get(dim) resolver.axis(s) or resolver.dims.groups.get(s), for a referring property self.properties.get(s), for a dim and a group alike resolver.dims.groups.get(group) self.groups.get(group) _base.dims.groups.get(group) self._base.groups.get(group) _base.attributes() and _base.attribute(name) name in self._base.attributes and self._base.attributes[name] _base.dims.axes.get(dim), the full rows self._base.properties.get(dim), or self._base.dims.get(dim) for a dim without properties

The base axis rows that WorkingRecord unions into a layer owning the dim whole now come from properties, which adds each declared property that no layer stored as a typed NULL column. A written axis layer already holds those columns, because the staged axis table has a column for every declared property (_axis_columns) and _insert projects a staged row onto it, so the layer reads back as before.

PinnedRecord subclasses Record and replaces PinnedResolver: it folds the unfrozen tail once and keeps the owner map in a table until release() drops it. It creates that table on the first access to _fold, so a write that fails before write_layer enters its try leaves no table behind. layer_data builds a PinnedRecord from the four fields of any Record that is not frozen, and write_layer calls release() on it after the write. WorkingRecord calls Record.__init__ with the fields of its base and with [*base.sources, StagedSource(...)] as its sources, and keeps the base Record as _base.

Revision caches its Record instead of a Resolver, and materialise clears that cache. Revision.resolver is deleted, and Workspace.at and Store.layer construct a Record directly. A Record looks up workspace.con on each call, so one Record can be read from several threads, as one Resolver can today (a cursor per thread). A PinnedRecord keeps its relations on the cursor of the thread that built it, as PinnedResolver does.

DEP 5 made Record "the interface over one" NodeCache, which later became Resolver; with this DEP Record is the fold itself. DEP 8 made "a Resolver that is LayerData"; with this DEP the writer reads no fold as LayerData, and Record does not answer LayerData.

docs.title: LayerData
docs.text: LayerData stays separate from RecordLike. It loses frozen, which the writer never reads, and its enumerators return set[str] instead of Iterable[str], a type that existed only so that a Resolver could return an ordered list. A LayerSource keeps its own frozen, because the fold reads it.

docs.title: The package layout
docs.text:
datarecord/
├── __init__.py        # every public name, unchanged; where a user imports from
├── duck.py            # relation helpers
├── protocols.py       # RecordLike, LayerData, Relations, LazyRelations, EMPTY, Flags
├── schema/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Schema, Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec, Group
│   ├── dtypes.py      # DUCK_TYPES, enum_type, enum_labels, takes
│   ├── specs.py       # Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec, Group
│   ├── schema.py      # Schema, flag_type, LAYER_COLUMN, LONG_TAIL, DERIVED
│   └── categories.py  # which labels a NULL reaches on a categorized dim
├── resolve/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Record
│   ├── fold.py        # Fold
│   ├── sources.py     # LayerSource, ParquetLayer, DirectorySource
│   ├── coords.py      # resolve_coords, Coords, mortal, resolve_groups
│   ├── owner_map.py   # fold_attributes, the owner-map fold and its shared tables
│   └── record.py      # Record, PinnedRecord
├── mutable.py         # WorkingRecord, StagedSource
├── store/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Workspace, Store, Revision
│   ├── store.py       # Workspace, Store, Revision, ancestry
│   ├── files.py       # Files, LocalFiles, RemoteFiles
│   ├── cache.py       # materialised node caches
│   ├── manifest.py    # read_schema, reconcile_schema
│   └── write.py       # write_layer, layer_data
└── tools/             # unchanged

Runtime imports follow the order duck → schema → protocols → resolve → mutable → store → tools: a module imports at runtime only from modules earlier in that order, and nothing outside tools/ imports tools/. An import under TYPE_CHECKING may point the other way, as when resolve/ names Workspace in an annotation. A subpackage's __init__.py re-exports its user-facing names, and datarecord/__init__.py imports them from there. A user and the usage pages import only from datarecord. Code inside the package imports a name from the module that defines it, so no internal import runs through an __init__.py.

Workspace, Store and Revision share store/store.py because they need each other at runtime. Revision is a pydantic model with a field of type Store and calls Workspace.process() when it loads from its serialised form, while Store constructs Revisions, so in two modules one of them would need a lazy import.

The modules in resolve/ keep taking a Workspace rather than a connection, because they look up workspace.con on each call to reach the cursor of the calling thread. mutable.py stays one module, because StagedSource reads eight private members of WorkingRecord and the two cannot be separated.

docs.title: Renames
docs.text:
today becomes Schema.input_key Schema.owner_map_key the tool requirement "input_key" "owner_map_key" Schema.input_columns Schema.owner_map_columns Resolver.inputs deleted; the fold's owner_map resolve.fold_inputs owner_map.fold_attributes tests/fixtures.write_input write_attribute resolve.write_schema moves to tests/fixtures.py, its one caller

Schema.owner_map_key is partial_dims plus attribute, the columns that identify one row of the owner map, and Schema.owner_map_columns is that key plus _layer and the flag columns. The name "inputs" is left over from the inputs/ directory that DEP 17 replaced with attributes/. The design pages keep "fold key" for partial_dims alone.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Every caller of Resolver already holds the Record or the Revision beside it, so the second class adds an object to pass around without separating any concern: the fold and the RecordLike members that answer from it are one thing.

The protocols get their own module because they can no longer sit beside their implementation, where the module layout puts them today. Record now lives in resolve/, and a module holding both Flags and Record would import resolve/fold.py, which imports Flags back from it.

The path helpers stay on Store rather than move to a separate Layout object. The lower layers need the Workspace anyway, so a Layout would turn every store argument into two arguments to save five one-line methods.

This changes every internal import path, the monkeypatches that name a module, and the ::: paths in docs/api/. About 50 test lines that read rev.resolver or construct a Resolver move to rev.record and the new constructor. The 24 lines that test the owner map and the folded coords through .resolver.inputs and .resolver.dims read the private _fold and _coords instead, because no public member shows the owner map or an axis row before properties pads it. test_functional_groups.py:337, which checks that an attribute's value never becomes a column of the axis file, is one of them.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
A user, and every example on the usage pages, imports from datarecord, as today:

from datarecord import (
    Record,
    RecordLike,
    Revision,
    Schema,
    Store,
    WorkingRecord,
    Workspace,
)

Code inside the package, and a test reaching an internal name, imports from the defining module:

# before
from datarecord.layered.resolve import Resolver
from datarecord.layered.revision import Revision
from datarecord.record import Record, RecordLike

# after
from datarecord.protocols import RecordLike
from datarecord.resolve.record import Record
from datarecord.store.store import Revision

A caller that held the resolver holds the record:

# before
rev.resolver.sources
Record(rev.resolver)
Record(Resolver(layer_id, sources, ws, schema))

# after
rev.record.sources
rev.record
Record(layer_id, sources, ws, schema)

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Merge Resolver into Record and PinnedResolver into PinnedRecord. Delete axis, group, group_frame, attribute, the enumerators, with_source, inputs, Revision.resolver and _pinned, and move WorkingRecord onto the mappings. Seed the coord fold of a record with staged edits from the frozen prefix's coord tables. Trim LayerData. One commit.
  2. Move the modules into the tree above, break the store–revision cycle, and apply the renames. Point the ::: paths in docs/api/ at the new modules, rename the "Layered" API page to "Store" in mkdocs.yml, and update the paths that AGENTS.md cites (record.py and layered/resolve.py). One commit.
  3. Add to CHANGELOG.md under [Unreleased]: Revision.resolver is removed, Record is constructed from revision_id, sources, workspace and schema instead of from a Resolver, and the tool requirement "input_key" is now "owner_map_key".
  4. On landing, update these pages:
  5. module layout: the tree, the dependency rule, and where the protocols live.
  6. record: a LayerSource answers LayerData, and a Record reaches the writer through the adapter. The enumerators return set[str].
  7. writing: the same correction to the writer's input.
  8. read path: "one record over one fold" and "a cursor per thread" name Record, not Resolver. "The inputs key" and the inputs map become the owner-map key and the owner map, and fold_inputs becomes fold_attributes.
  9. layers: "the inputs key" becomes the owner-map key, and fold_inputs becomes fold_attributes. A Record takes its workspace from its fields, not from a Resolver.
  10. schema: the dtype map is schema/dtypes.py, and "the inputs key" becomes the owner-map key.
  11. format: "the inputs key" becomes the owner-map key.
  12. On implementation, DEP 5 and DEP 8 take Superseded-By this DEP, for the parts named under Replaces.

Checks: no module under src/datarecord imports layered, and no runtime import breaks the dependency rule. Resolver and input_key appear nowhere in src/, tests/ or docs/design/, except in DEPs. Folding the staged layer onto the frozen prefix's coord tables gives the same axes, groups and dead labels as folding over every layer, member order and tombstones included.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
Folding LayerData into RecordLike would remove the adapter, but a staged axis carries a deleted column that RecordLike.dims cannot hold, so the writer would have to split each axis and join it back together.

Moving Record next to Resolver without merging the two keeps the forwarding layer, the copy in _pinned and the duplicate members of Revision.

Sharing one _coords between the key set and the values of each mapping in Python would halve the folds per read of a working record, but each fold would still open every layer's files; seeding the fold from the tables in DuckDB removes the file reads themselves.

A format/ subpackage would be named after the format, which is the layer directory, yet write_layer and _FileLayer, the code that writes and reads that directory, would not be in it. An edit/ subpackage would hold only mutable.py.

Revision cannot import Store only under TYPE_CHECKING, because pydantic needs the type of the store field at runtime.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text: None.

docs.title: DEP 20: A layer restates an axis whole
DEP 20: a layer restates an axis whole
docs.text: DEP 20 Title a layer restates an axis whole Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-22) Requires DEP 19 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 1 (entity tombstones, and an order the fold generates), DEP 4 (the per-label axis fold, and partial as how many labels an axis layer carries), DEP 10 (group tombstones anti-joining the owner map), DEP 11 (removal by tombstone, and dead labels as winning tombstones), DEP 17 (a SubNetwork as an entity, and its tombstones), DEP 19 (a re-added key introduced where it is re-added)

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A layer that changes an axis or a group writes its file whole, in order, and the resolved axis or group is the deepest layer's file for it. A label is removed where a restatement of its axis omits it after the previous one held it, so no dims/ or groups/ file carries a deleted column. Attributes stay per-key patches under partial, which keeps one meaning, attribute ownership. A PyPSA SubNetwork becomes a label of its own dim.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
_fold_axis in resolve/coords.py folds an axis per label from every layer that touched it. A label takes its deepest row and is dropped where that row is a deleted = true tombstone. Its place is that of its first row deeper than its deepest tombstone. No single file says which labels a node's axis has or in which order.

That order is load-bearing, since _ordered_connections in tools/pypsa.py numbers a component's ports by connection order. DEP 19 had to reshape the order rule so that a cache holding a removed label only as a dead label agrees with a full fold. Every new seed or cache has to be checked against that rule again.

The per-label fold also hides a writer's mistakes. _axis_layer in mutable.py writes a non-partial axis with its staged rows first. A child adding z and then the existing label x thus stores ['z', 'x', 'y'], which the fold re-ranks to ['x', 'y', 'z']. A file holding label a twice reads as one a, with the properties of either row. On an axis, partial also says how much of it a layer writes (partial), a second meaning beside attribute ownership.

docs.title: An axis is its deepest file
docs.text:
A layer that adds or removes a label of a dim, or changes a property of one, writes dims/<dim>.parquet whole: every label the axis has at that node, with its properties, in order. A layer that changes a group's tuples or their properties writes groups/<group>.parquet whole the same way. A node's resolved axis or group is the deepest file for it on the path from the root, in that file's row order. attributes/<attr>.parquet still holds only the keys a layer sets, owned per key along the partial coordinates (the owner map).

A materialised node no longer caches a fold of its axes and groups. Its resolved/dims/ and resolved/groups/ hold copies of the deepest layer file at or below the node, so a read still stops there. resolved/dead/ and owner_map.parquet stay folds, since no layer file holds either.

docs.title: Removal
docs.text:
A label is removed at a layer whose restatement of its axis omits it while the previous restatement holds it. The previous restatement is the deepest file for the axis below that layer, or else a materialised base's resolved axis or the frozen prefix's shared table. A first restatement removes nothing.

For a partial dim or group, which the owner map keys, fold_attributes drops the parent rows naming a removed label. A mortal coordinate (resolve/coords.py) is one outside the owner-map key, or one a group's field ranges over or a property takes its labels from. Its dead labels (a label outside the key) are the labels some layer removed that the final axis lacks. The fold computes them as the base's dead set, the base's resolved axis and every restatement above the base, minus the final axis. _require_living_references takes the labels a layer kills from the same diff, its parent's axis minus its restatement.

In every case probed on a prototype, the rule gives today's answers. A keyed label's values from below its removal stay gone after it is added again, and an unkeyed coordinate's come back, as DEP 11 accepted. A label removed and added again in one staging area keeps its parent's values, and a broadcast reaches a label added after a restatement.

WorkingRecord.remove restates the axis without the label, and each group with a field over its dim without the tuples naming it (add / remove).

An attribute's value names only labels its dims' axes hold and tuples its groups hold. WorkingRecord.set refuses a label that the dim's axis, as staged, does not hold, for every dim, partial or not, naming the dim and up to three missing labels. It refuses a tuple that the group, as staged, does not hold the same way, naming the group. A group's tuple names only labels its fields' axes hold, and add_group refuses one naming a label that the axis, as staged, does not hold, naming the group, the field and up to three such labels. A staged value then names a label the staged axis lacks only where remove dropped the label after the set, in the same staging area. Such a label is in no restatement, so the fold marks it dead nowhere, and the staged attribute rows naming it are dropped as the staging area is read, which is the removal taking effect.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
An axis's order is its deepest file's row order. A label added again after its removal is a row of a later restatement and sits where that file puts it, which subsumes the rule DEP 19 landed.

WorkingRecord stages an axis or group as a whole table, as any layer holds it. The first edit of the axis copies the base's resolved axis into the table with a position column in base order, since a DuckDB table keeps no row order. add appends a new label at the next position and puts a label of the base back at its base position, remove deletes the label's row, and a property edit updates the row. StagedSource hands the table over in position order, so a read composes nothing. write_layer refuses a restatement whose order on its parent's labels differs from the parent's, naming the first label out of place.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
A dims/ or groups/ file with a deleted column is refused at read and by write_layer. A layer that WorkingRecord or the PyPSA tool wrote before this DEP thus fails instead of losing every label it did not touch:

dims/bus.parquet carries a `deleted` column; a layer removes a label by
restating its axis without it (.../design/layers/#deletion). Re-export the
record, or flatten it with `ws.write` under the previous release.

The fold and write_layer refuse a key that occurs twice in a dims/ or groups/ file, at one GROUP BY per file. A column that is neither the file's key nor a declared property of its subject is refused at read, as _refuse_extra in store/write.py refuses it at write today. A restatement composed from a base therefore never carries an undeclared column. deleted stays a reserved name, and no staging table carries it.

write_layer refuses an attribute row naming a label that the layer's final axis of that dim does not hold, for every dim, naming the dim and up to three such labels. It refuses an attribute row at a tuple that the layer's final group does not hold, naming the group. It refuses a group tuple naming a label that the layer's final axis of the field's dim does not hold, naming the group, the field and up to three such labels. The final axis or group is the layer's own file, else its parent's resolved one. The checks cover a layer written by hand or by a tool, as the reference check covers a group's tuples and a property's values.

Each of these checks, staged and at write, is one DuckDB query that anti-joins the rows against the resolved axis or group of every column it checks, and reads the first three labels of the first column with any. No label is iterated in Python.

docs.title: The reference check
docs.text: _require_living_references checks each subject a layer restates or whose rows name a label the layer removes, whole and in its final state, against the final dead labels. A reference an ancestor left dangling therefore fails the next write touching its subject, and that write can drop or repair the row, since it restates the subject whole. The promise of deletion that a reference an ancestor left dangling "fails no later write" goes, with its counterpart in that function's docstring.

docs.title: SubNetworks are a dim
docs.text:
_ResultsSource in tools/pypsa.py writes this solve's SubNetworks into the entity axis and tombstones the stale ones of base. Read as a restatement, that file removes every other entity. A SubNetwork becomes a label of the dim sub_network, which a results layer restates alone:

today becomes the entity label 0 SubNetwork, ctype="SubNetwork" the sub_network label 0 SubNetwork listed by ctype, a dim that lists its labels not listed, so flags(ctype="SubNetwork") is refused; _AXIS_TYPES maps SubNetwork to sub_network, as Bus to bus entity.carrier on a SubNetwork sub_network.carrier, which takes its labels from carrier slack_bus, an attribute over entity over sub_network a Line's sub_network value 0 SubNetwork 0, still an attribute over entity _SUB_NETWORK_SUFFIX, _record_name, _sub_network_named, _sub_network_unnamed deleted

sub_network stays outside partial, since a results layer writes every SubNetwork's values. A full export writes the axis beside bus and carrier, and build adds SubNetworks through _add_labels.

A solve without SubNetworks over a base with a sub_network axis restates that axis empty, so the record lists none of the base's SubNetworks. The empty axis's columns take the types the schema declares, not those pandas infers for an empty frame. Over a base without the axis, a results layer writes no sub_network axis.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
With one file per axis, no seed, cache or staged fold can disagree with a full fold about order or membership. A layer's axis file says what the axis is at that node. Groups follow the rule because port order is connection order.

Every timing and size in this DEP is a single DuckDB run at PyPSA-Eur scale, 60,000 entities and 150,000 connections, unless stated. With SubNetworks as a dim, a results layer restates only labels a solve derives. Its sub_network axis is 12 rows and 0.4 kB, or 18 kB where each of 4,000 buses is its own SubNetwork, as PyPSA makes one per connected component of lines and transformers. The schema change adds no migration of its own, since every record the tool wrote carries deleted columns and is re-exported anyway.

Storage grows with the axis rather than the edit. A one-entity property edit writes 0.30 MB where a one-row patch writes 0.8 kB today. Adding a connection writes 0.43 MB, and removing an entity restates both for 0.73 MB. A connection.role edit restates every tuple. A chain of 20 edit layers over 40,000 entities and 80,000 connections holds 5.57 MB against 10 kB today. The cost multiplies in scenario trees with many small leaves and on a remote store.

A prototype without the order and duplicate checks wrote that chain in 4.3 s against 5.7 s and read p_nom cold at its leaf in 1.07 s against 2.17 s. The entity fold drops from 80-95 ms, whatever the patch count, to a 50 ms read of the deepest file. Each restatement adds a diff to every fold, 6 ms for the entities and 18 ms for the connections. The dead set reads every restatement above the base, 23 ms over 20 of the entities, where today it reads tombstone rows. A duplicate check costs 5-11 ms per file. A WorkingRecord copies the base's resolved axis or group into its staging table at the first edit of it, about 15 ms for the entities and 41 ms for the connections, estimated from their write times, and a later read takes the table as it stands.

A tree the PyPSA tool did not write is refused where a dims/ or groups/ file carries a deleted column, as every axis or group edit of WorkingRecord writes. It is flattened with ws.write under the release before this one, losing its history. A full PyPSA export written as a child is refused where its parent's entity order interleaves types, as after a WorkingRecord adds a generator, since an export orders entities by type. It is written as a root instead. A foreign directory meets the same refusals, so not every standard parquet directory reads as a layer any more. A hand-written restatement that omits a property column blanks it for every label, where a patch blanked it only for the labels it held. A patch layer written before this DEP without a deleted column reads silently as a restatement removing every label it omits. Such a layer was written by hand, as write_axis does, or from a LayerData whose axis lacked the column. No format version detects it, since the project is pre-alpha and supports no earlier format. src grows, by an estimated 100-130 lines deleted and 135-235 added.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.add("bus", ["z"])
child = rev.child(w.edits)
rev.store.layer(child.id).dims["bus"]  # every bus of rev, in its order, then z

w = WorkingRecord(child.record)
w.remove("entity", ["old_coal"])  # entity.parquet without old_coal,
child.child(w.edits)  # connection.parquet without its tuples

A layer written by hand holds the whole axis, properties included:

# before: one row
pd.DataFrame({"bus": ["z"]}).to_parquet(f"{layer}/dims/bus.parquet")
# after: the parent's buses with their properties, in their order, then z
buses = parent.record.properties["bus"].df()
new = pd.DataFrame({"bus": ["z"]})
pd.concat([buses, new], ignore_index=True).to_parquet(f"{layer}/dims/bus.parquet")

A solve's SubNetworks are labels of their own dim:

solved = inputs.child(
    PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con, results_only=True, base=inputs.record)
)
solved.record.dims["sub_network"]  # this solve's; the entity axis is still inputs'
solved.record.attributes["slack_bus"]  # over sub_network

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Paths are under src/datarecord/.

  1. In resolve/coords.py, _fold_axis reads the deepest relation and refuses a duplicate key, and _dead_keys computes the dead set, dropping an empty one so that _living adds no join. resolve_coords and resolve_groups there take the deepest file, and _resolve_dead adds the base's resolved axis. In resolve/owner_map.py, the removed labels replace _deleted_relation in fold_attributes, _fold_map and _table. _FileLayer.axis and group in resolve/sources.py refuse a deleted column, then an undeclared one.
  2. In store/write.py, _validate_frame drops deleted from an axis or group file's columns. A duplicate check and the order check run on each written dims/ and groups/ file beside _refuse_unordered. _require_living_references derives the killed labels from the parent's axes, and _living goes.
  3. In mutable.py, the staging table of an axis or group takes the base's rows and a position column at its first edit, add, remove and property edits change its rows, _axis_layer and _collapsed_group lose their partial branches, and StagedSource hands the table over in position order.
  4. In tools/pypsa.py, _connection_rows, _NetworkSource.dims, _carriers, _entity_frame and _tagged stop writing deleted. _AXIS_TYPES and _PROPERTIES gain sub_network, whose carrier _registry declares explicitly, since it takes no property from an output. _ResultsSource writes the sub_network axis, _restated filters stale rows on sub_network instead of entity, and the suffix helpers go.
  5. In tests/fixtures.py, write_component, tombstone, write_connections, tombstone_connection, write_axis, write_scenarios and write_periods restate from the layer's parent, and write_connections stops writing the undeclared role and scenario. By a prototype's failures adjusted for this design, at least 18 tests change. Ten write a patch child through those fixtures, and two assert patch-shaped files. test_sub_networks_are_suffixed_off_the_lines and test_a_re_solve_leaves_no_stale_sub_network read sub_network, and four tests write or assert a deleted column. New tests pin the refusals, the order check, and one order across a materialised parent.
  6. CHANGELOG.md under [Unreleased]: a layer restates a changed axis or group whole, a deleted column is refused, and SubNetworks are labels of sub_network.
  7. On landing, update the design pages read path, layers, record, format, schema, working record, tools and writing, wherever they describe tombstones, per-label folding, first-introduced order or SubNetwork entities, and the usage pages on editing, tools and the schema.
  8. On implementation, DEP 1, 4, 10, 11, 17 and 19 take Superseded-By this DEP, for the parts named under Replaces.

Checks: a label removed and re-added reads in one order materialised or not, staged or committed, with connection in partial and out. No file write_layer writes under dims/ or groups/ has a deleted column.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
The 7-line fold fix, now in _fold_axis as the rule DEP 19 landed, fixes the order bug without a format change but keeps the per-label fold. With it stay the tombstones, partial's second meaning and an order derived from history.

A format version in manifest.json would also catch an old patch layer without a deleted column, at the cost of a second version beside schema.version.

Restating the entity axis in each results layer writes 0.30 MB per solve in 20 ms, plus 10 ms to check its order. That is small beside one marginal_price result over 4,000 buses and 8,760 snapshots, 301 MB with random values, an upper bound. It is rejected because every solve would rewrite an input axis it never changed and, under the reference check, fail on a reference an ancestor left dangling there.

Checking only the rows a restatement adds or changes and the rows naming a label the layer removes keeps the promise that an ancestor's dangling reference fails no later write. It costs one more anti-join against the parent per restated subject, and leaves the dangling row in every later restatement of its subject.

Sorting an out-of-order restatement into its parent's order, instead of refusing it, would bring the per-label fold back at write time.

Dropping undeclared columns when composing a restatement, instead of refusing them, would lose a foreign column silently at the first edit of its axis.

Pruning the owner map against each layer's restatement drops a broadcast's rows for labels added later. Pruning against the final axis alone brings back values from below a removal.

Dropping the dead cache and keeping the rows whose label is in the final axis makes series reads 4.4 times slower, 78 ms against 18 ms on 43.8M p_max_pu rows.

Recording in resolved/ which layer holds each axis and group, instead of copying the file, would save about 0.73 MB per materialised node. A read at that node would then open an ancestor's layer file, where materialised node caches has it stop at the node.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
The order check allows a new label before one of its parent's. In a group, a new tuple placed before an existing one of the same entity renumbers that entity's later ports. WorkingRecord appends, so only a layer written another way can do this.

DEP 14's open issue, extending a tree without restating its base, gets no easier.

docs.title: DEP 21: The owner map holds keys as written
DEP 21: the owner map holds keys as written
docs.text: DEP 21 Title the owner map holds keys as written Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-25) Requires DEP 20 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 1 (flags aggregated from expanded rows), DEP 8 (a fold that expands a broadcast against the resolved axes), DEP 10 (a NULL struct expanded in the fold), DEP 11 (a re-added label starts fresh), DEP 16 (a NULL row expanded over every label in the owner map), DEP 20 (a keyed label's broadcasts staying gone after it is added again)

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: The owner map holds each layer's attribute keys as the layer wrote them. Where a deeper layer's row crosses a parent row, that is where the two cover a common key and neither names every dim the other names, the parent row stays as written and the fold adds one overlap row, owned by the deeper layer, naming every label either row names. The fold thus reads no axis, and the persisted map grows with the rows layers write and the pairs that cross, not with the labels a broadcast reaches: 0.63 times today's rows on the first benchmark below, 0.01 times on the realistic case at five partial dims. A read returns the owned rows as written, NULL included, and a consumer settles each coordinate by the broadcast rule alone, the more specific row winning, with no depth and no list of partial dims. Every broadcast therefore reaches every label the record holds, and materialising a node no longer changes an answer.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
fold_attributes expands each row that leaves a partial coordinate NULL against the axis or group resolved over the whole path, and keeps one owner-map row per label. The owner map thus grows with the labels a broadcast reaches, not with the rows a layer writes: one broadcast over 60,000 entities and two scenarios takes 120,000 rows. A materialised node persists that expansion, and the frozen prefix of a WorkingRecord keeps it as a shared table.

A fold seeded from either does not expand again, so a broadcast also misses every label added after the seed.

A node holding q = 0.9 for every entity, with a child adding the entity n, reads n as 0.9 while the node is unmaterialised and as nothing once it is materialised. A label staged in a WorkingRecord over the node reads as nothing in both cases. Over 210 random six-layer records, materialising or staging changes one of today's answers in 95 to 128 records, depending on where. Materialised node caches promises that materialising changes no answer, and open questions lists the first two cases.

The expansion settles one thing only: which layer owns a key that rows of two layers cover. Within a layer the more specific row wins, and across layers the deeper one does. The two rules disagree only where two rows of different layers cross, and there a single row at their overlap, owned by the deeper layer, makes them agree. Everywhere else the rows can stay as written and the broadcast rule alone gives every answer.

docs.title: The owner map
docs.text:
The owner map holds one row per layer and per distinct key, with a NULL key column left NULL, and no depth:

# owner map
<partial dims>   -- the key: exactly the partial dims and groups, NULL included
attribute
layer_uuid
varies      STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)
broadcast   STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)
breakpoints BOOLEAN

A row is either a key a layer wrote or an overlap row. An overlap row names labels on dims where the owning layer's key holds NULL and carries that layer's varies and broadcast, so the layer's value row finds it by one NULL-safe hash join on the key as stored and takes the overlap row's labels.

docs.title: Crossing
docs.text: A row names a partial dim where its key holds a label, and any other dim where it varies along it, so a series over snapshot names snapshot. Only the dims the attribute uses count: its dims and the dims of its groups. Two rows cover a common key where, on each partial coordinate, they hold the same label or one of them holds NULL. They cross where they cover a common key and neither names every dim the other names.

docs.title: The fold
docs.text:
A layer is folded onto its parent's map in four steps, none of which reads an axis:

  1. The parent rows naming a label or tuple that the layer removes by DEP 20's diff are dropped, and a row NULL there never is.
  2. A parent row is dropped where a row of the layer covers it and names no partial dim the parent row leaves NULL.
  3. For each pair of a parent row and a layer's row crossing on partial dims, found by one equi-join per pair of named sets over the dims both name, the layer gains an overlap row naming every label either names. A parent row naming strictly fewer dims than the layer's row it overlaps stays as written, as does a crossed parent row.
  4. The layer's rows and its overlap rows are added.

An overlap row is an ordinary row to every later fold, which drops, crosses or removes it like any other.

With partial = {entity, scenario}, a root writing (gas, NULL) = 50 and (wind, NULL) = 100 and a child writing (NULL, high) = 999:

# today's owner map, one row per label
(gas,  low)  root    (gas,  high) child
(wind, low)  root    (wind, high) child

# this DEP
(gas,  NULL) root    # as written
(wind, NULL) root
(NULL, high) child   # as written
(gas,  high) child   # overlap rows, naming both dims
(wind, high) child

A child writing (gas, NULL) = 60 instead names no more than the root's (gas, NULL) and drops it. A child writing (gas, high) = 70 names more and leaves the root's rows as written, and the broadcast rule gives (gas, high) to the child.

docs.title: A dim outside partial
docs.text:
An overlap row cannot settle a crossing on a dim outside partial, since the key has no column to name its labels. A WorkingRecord therefore settles it as it stages: a staged row leaving such a dim NULL, over a base row naming it, is also written out along the base row's labels there, with the staged value. With partial = {entity}, a root writing a series over snapshot for every entity and a child writing (wind, NULL) = 0.9:

# root:  (NULL, 0) = 0.2   (NULL, 1) = 0.5
# child as staged: (wind, NULL) = 0.9
# child as written: (wind, NULL) = 0.9, (wind, 0) = 0.9, (wind, 1) = 0.9

The child's rows at wind name entity and snapshot, a strict superset of the root's, so nothing crosses and the root's series stays as written. This extends the completion a WorkingRecord already makes, which carries the base rows a staged key reaches so that a layer holds a key's whole extent along every dim outside partial. The fold refuses a layer written otherwise that leaves such a crossing, naming the attribute, the dim and the key.

docs.title: The read
docs.text:
A read of an attribute joins the value rows of the owning layers to the owner map's rows, as today, and returns the owned rows as written: a key NULL on a dim stays NULL, and an overlap row reads its labels. It expands no NULL and drops no row by depth. The anti-join against dead labels follows as today, and the row order stays unspecified.

A consumer settles a coordinate by the broadcast rule over the full coordinates, partial or not: a row's value applies to every combination of its NULL dims, and at each coordinate the row naming a strict superset of every other row reaching it wins. Wherever two rows cross, the fold or the staging has written a row naming both, so the rule finds one winner wherever a row reaches, and a consumer needs neither depth nor the list of partial dims.

docs.title: Reach
docs.text:
A NULL on a partial coordinate reaches every label of that coordinate's axis, or every tuple of its group, as resolved at the node read, since the read leaves it NULL and no row is split. A label added below a materialised node is reached, as is a label staged in a WorkingRecord and the first label of an axis empty when the broadcast was written. Adding the scenario mid below the child of the first example reads (gas, mid) as 50, and adding the entity solar below the child of the series example reads the root's series for it.

A row reaches every coordinate no more specific row covers, whichever layer wrote it. A deeper layer thus owns only the coordinates its rows reach, not the whole extent of a key along a dim outside partial. With partial = {entity, scenario} and x also over snapshot, a root writing (gas, NULL, 1) = 1.0 and a child writing (NULL, high, 0) = 2.0, (gas, high, 1) reads 1.0 from the root, where today it reads nothing. Likewise a root writing x = 1.0 with every coordinate NULL and a child writing (gas, NULL, 0) = 2.0 reads (gas, low, 1) as 1.0, where today it reads nothing.

A label removed and added again takes every broadcast covering it, whether written before or after the removal, and never a row that named it below the removal.

Materialising a node changes no answer, since its persisted map is the fold's result and the read expands nothing against the axes of the node read. A map persisted for another set of partial dims holds NULL in a column for a row varying along it, so the read ignores it and folds the node from its layers again.

docs.title: flags
docs.text:
flags() is today's aggregate run over the owner map's rows: per attribute, bool_or over each field of varies and broadcast and over breakpoints. Both structs report only the dims the attribute uses, so ctype no longer reads true in broadcast for an attribute not over it. flags() describes the dims used by the rows the fold keeps, and a broadcast that deeper layers shadow on every label still counts. In probe P7, a child of the root sets s = 0.9 with every coordinate NULL and its child sets s over snapshot for every entity, and flags()["s"].broadcast holds entity, where today it lacks it.

flags(**categories) aggregates the same way over the rows reaching the category, as today.

docs.title: Files and shared tables
docs.text: The frozen prefix keeps its owner map as the shared table owner_map_<key>_<rev>, <key> the hash of its key columns (a cursor per thread), onto which a WorkingRecord folds its staged layer per read. A materialised node writes its owner map as resolved/owner_map.parquet, last, which marks the node as materialised as today. An owner map written by an earlier release is unsupported and not detected, the project being pre-alpha.

docs.title: The change to DEP 20
docs.text:
On implementing this DEP, these sentences of DEP 20 change:

DEP 20, the sentence becomes "In every case probed on a prototype, …" In every case probed on a prototype, the rule gives today's answers, except that a label added again takes every broadcast covering it. "A keyed label's values from below its removal stay gone …" A keyed label's named values from below its removal stay gone after it is added again, while every broadcast covering it reaches it again. An unkeyed coordinate's values come back, as DEP 11 accepted.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The fold settles ownership across layers, so the map needs no depth and the read no anti-join. A depth would let the read or the consumer settle it instead, by taking the deepest covering layer first and the most specific row within it, but every way of doing so measured below costs each read more than the fold costs once, and a consumer would have to know about layers.

An overlap row settles a crossing without an axis. Its labels come from the two rows, so a later label reaches the crossed parent row unchanged, and its value from the deeper layer, whose value rows hold the dims the overlap row's key leaves NULL. Any parent row more specific than the overlap within the deeper row's reach is one that deeper row covers, and step 2 has dropped it.

Crossing is judged over every dim the attribute uses, not over partial alone, because the broadcast rule a consumer applies runs over the full coordinates. Left as written, the series example holds the root's (NULL, 0) beside the child's (wind, NULL), and at (wind, 0) the rule finds two rows, one naming snapshot and one naming entity, neither the winner. The key holds no snapshot, so that crossing is settled where the labels are, as the layer is staged.

A parent row that a deeper, more specific row covers stays as written, since there the two rules agree.

On a prototype on DEP 20, against today, each figure the median of three interleaved rounds run alone. The first benchmark holds 60,000 entities, 100 attributes and two scenarios over ten layers, with a materialised leaf and a child adding one entity, and the second a materialised child broadcasting 20 of 40 attributes. The scaling benchmark varies the number k of partial dims: entity with 20,000 labels and k - 1 further dims of three labels each, every attribute being over all of them. Its realistic case (R) holds nine layers and ten attributes, with at most four sets of named dims per attribute. Its worst case (W) holds 2^k layers, each naming the dims of its own set, in counting order, so most layers cross the ones below them. Its series case (S) holds 20,000 entities, two scenarios and 8,760 snapshots.

case map rows, today map rows first read, today first read repeated read, today repeated read 1 12.0 M 7.50 M 2.60 s 2.98 s 0.036 s 0.025 s 2 4.80 M 1.20 M 0.77 s 0.24 s 0.018 s 0.007 s R k3 1.80 M 223 k 0.70 s 0.69 s 0.019 s 0.013 s R k4 5.40 M 223 k 1.85 s 0.75 s 0.049 s 0.015 s R k5 16.2 M 223 k 6.25 s 0.81 s 0.147 s 0.017 s W k3 720 k 8.8 k 0.70 s 0.56 s 0.028 s 0.020 s W k4 2.16 M 35 k 2.30 s 3.02 s 0.107 s 0.049 s W k5 6.48 M 163 k 13.7 s 20.1 s 0.315 s 0.160 s S k2 120 k 124 materialise 25.7 s 0.22 s

The first read folds, and materialising follows it. The read returns rows as written, so its times leave out the consumer's expansion. A read of a record with two entities set in a staged layer over the materialised node takes 1.0 to 2.8 times today in the scaling benchmark, 0.11 times in the series case.

The first read is slowest in the worst case, at 1.3 to 1.5 times today for k = 4 and 5, since pairs of sets neither naming the other grow from 1 at k = 2 to 55 at k = 4 and 285 at k = 5, and the fold joins along each pair a parent row and a layer's row hold. This DEP accepts that cost: a record overriding one attribute along ever different sets of dims in a dozen layers is not one a workflow builds.

Over all 210 fuzzed records of six edit layers, with entity, scenario and the group connection as partial coordinates, reads and flags agree in all five ways: plain, materialised at depth 1 and 3, staged, and staged over a materialised parent. The plain read equals a plain-Python oracle of the broadcast rule over full coordinates, every row reaching the final axes, on 197 records. The 13 others hit the oracle's limits: 3 a group emptied of tuples, where the read keeps the NULL row; 2 a connection removed and added again within one layer, where DEP 20's diff sees no removal; and 5 a label new or added again in the layer writing a row over snapshot at it, where the shallower row reaches the other snapshot, as Reach accepts. A layer writing a full broadcast and a named row at once reads as the fold's step 2 gives, which an earlier oracle got wrong. Every probe reads the same materialised or not, staged or committed, and no fuzzed record triggers the refusal of a layer written without WorkingRecord.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
A read returns the rows as written, overlap rows included:

w.set("x", 50.0, entity="gas")  # the root
w.set("x", 100.0, entity="wind")
v.set("x", 999.0, scenario="high")  # its child
child.record.attributes["x"]
# (gas, NULL) 50, (wind, NULL) 100, (NULL, high) 999, (gas, high) 999, (wind, high) 999

A broadcast reaches a label added below a materialised node, committed or staged:

c = rev.child(w.edits)  # w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)
c.materialise()
w = WorkingRecord(c.record)
w.add("entity", ["n"], ctype="Generator")
w.attributes["p_max_pu"]  # (NULL) 0.9, which n takes by the broadcast rule

A constant override of a broadcast series is written out along the series' snapshots:

w.set("p_max_pu", [0.2, 0.5], snapshot=[0, 1])  # the root, every entity
v.set("p_max_pu", 0.9, entity="wind")  # its child
# the child holds (wind, NULL), (wind, 0) and (wind, 1) at 0.9

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Paths are under src/datarecord/.

  1. resolve/owner_map.py: fold_attributes drops the covered parent rows by _masks and _exactly, pairs crossing rows by _pair and adds the overlap rows by _overlaps, and refuses an unsettled crossing outside partial by _refuse_unfilled. It takes no axes.
  2. resolve/record.py: _as_stored returns the owned rows as written and reads the labels of an overlap row, and _owners returns each attribute's rows.
  3. resolve/fold.py folds without axes, and resolve/coords.py loses Coords.expand_dims.
  4. mutable.py: _complete_owned_whole also writes a staged row out along the base rows' labels on dims outside partial (_spread), and a staged layer folds onto the prefix's map the same way.
  5. Consumers: tools/pypsa.py's attribute and series reads, tools/base.py's Attr.resolve, and store/write.py's refusal of a pair neither more specific when it flattens a record into one layer apply the broadcast rule over rows as written.
  6. Tests asserting per-label reads assert rows as written instead. New tests and probes pin a deeper entity winning over a series it crosses, a broadcast reaching a label added below a crossing, a series reaching an entity added below an override, and the two coordinates a shallower row now reaches.
  7. CHANGELOG.md under [Unreleased]: a read returns rows as written, a broadcast reaches every label, a deeper layer owns only the coordinates its rows reach, a re-added label takes broadcasts again, and flags counts a shadowed broadcast and reports only an attribute's dims.
  8. On landing, update resolution, the layer tree, reading, writing, editing, the schema, the format, tools, the index, module layout and the usage page on layers where they describe the owner map, its expansion or what a layer owns. In open questions, close the item on a broadcast surviving materialisation.

Checks: every probe reads the same materialised or not, staged or committed, and the 210 fuzzed records read the same in all five ways: plain, materialised at two depths, staged, and staged over a materialised parent.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
Keeping keys as written with their depth and settling ownership at every read, by expanding the NULLs and one anti-join per named mask, reads at 1.55 to 2.1 times today in the realistic case from k = 2 on and at 31 times today in the worst case at k = 5, and runs out of memory at 24.6 GiB for k = 6. Caching each attribute's settled rows in a session file restores repeated reads to 0.15 to 0.90 times today, but moves the cost to the first read of each attribute in every session: a first sweep over the realistic case takes 2.5 to 3.6 times today, and 31 times in the worst case at k = 5. Picking the owner by a window, arg_max(depth), brings a repeated read of the worst case at k = 5 from 31 to 5.5 times today but takes the realistic case to 3.3 times.
