Building the file root to leaf halves the worst case's first read at k = 5 but slows the realistic case's by half, and disabling DuckDB's build_side_probe_side optimizer during a build takes it to 3.9 s against 9.3 s but holds for every concurrent cursor. A cache shared across sessions would pay the first pass once per revision, but needs a key covering the partial dims and a size cap, and keeps a per-label file per attribute.

Splitting a crossed parent row instead of adding an overlap row, expanding it along the dims the deeper row names against the axis as the crossing layer resolves it and dropping the pieces a deeper row reaches, reads the same as this DEP wherever no label is added below a crossing. Its pieces name the labels of that axis only, so a label added later reaches none of them: adding mid below the child of the first example reads (gas, mid) as nothing, and in 8 of the first 70 fuzzed records a label added below a crossing reads differently from the oracle. Its first read takes 65 s against 20 s for the worst case at k = 5, and its map holds 2.01 million rows against 163,000. Splitting every parent row a deeper row names a dim of, more specific or not, splits where the two rules agree as well, and dropping at the read the rows a deeper one shadows by an arg_max window over a depth reads at 2 to 8 times that.

Judging a crossing over the partial dims alone leaves the series example's rows crossing on snapshot, which the broadcast rule cannot order.

Keeping the per-label owner map, with a map of keys as written beside it to derive the labels it lacks, needs a delta over every seed and three kinds of shared table, and materialising took 2.5 times today in its own round, 8.5 s against 3.4 s.

Deciding flags per label, counting a row only where some label it covers has no deeper covering row, keeps today's flags exactly. On a flags benchmark of the first benchmark's size it took 3 to 24 times today, 1.016 s against 0.043 s for a repeated flags() at the materialised leaf.

Letting the more specific row win across layers keeps an earlier named value under a later broadcast, which the fold then cannot drop, so every read of its attribute expands it against the named rows, 0.045 s against 0.023 s on the second benchmark.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
The tools settle rows by one helper, settle(rel, labels, flags), which expands a NULL only on a coordinate in broadcast and picks a row only where a coordinate is also in varies; Attr.resolve and Schema.resolve take labels and flags. write_layer accepts two crossing rows where a row naming both is there, so a record of several layers flattens into one. The read of a staged layer refuses two rows crossing with no row naming both, as write_layer refuses them on commit.

No fuzzed record holds a series over more than one partial dim.

The worst case's first read stays at 1.3 to 1.5 times today for k = 4 and 5, which Rationale accepts.

docs.title: DEP 22: A layer restates membership whole
DEP 22: a layer restates membership whole
docs.text: DEP 22 Title a layer restates membership whole Author Jonas Hoersch Status On hold (2026-10-22) Requires DEP 19 Created 2026-10-22 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 1 (entity tombstones, and an order the fold generates), DEP 4 (the per-label axis fold, and partial as how many labels an axis layer carries), DEP 10 (group tombstones anti-joining the owner map), DEP 11 (removal by tombstone, and dead labels as winning tombstones), DEP 12 (every property of a dim as a column of dims/<dim>.parquet), DEP 17 (a SubNetwork as an entity, and its tombstones), DEP 19 (a re-added key introduced where it is re-added)

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: DEP 22 is an alternative to DEP 20, and only one of the two is implemented. A layer that adds or removes a label writes the label column of dims/<dim>.parquet whole and in order, and a layer that adds or removes a tuple writes the key column of groups/<group>.parquet the same way. Properties leave those files for properties/<subject>.<name>.parquet, one file per property holding the labels a layer sets it for, folded last writer wins per label and property. A property edit thus writes the rows it changes, and adding or removing a label writes the label column and the touched property rows, where DEP 20 writes every property of every label.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
DEP 20 replaces the per-label axis fold with one deepest file per axis or group, which settles order and membership and drops tombstones, and its motivation holds here unchanged. DEP 20 pays with storage that grows with the axis on every edit, properties included. A one-entity property edit writes 0.30 MB under DEP 20, and a connection.role edit restates 150,000 tuples.

A property can be bulky. A bus geometry of 64 vertices makes dims/bus.parquet 2.49 MB at 4,000 buses, against 17.5 kB for the labels alone, and DEP 20 writes all of it on every bus edit, a geometry fix to one bus included.

Only membership and order need a whole file, since only a whole file says which labels exist and in which order. A property is one value per label, and no read relates one label's value to another's. DEP 22 restates the label column and patches the properties.

docs.title: Membership is its deepest file
docs.text:
An axis is its deepest file holds with narrower files. dims/<dim>.parquet holds the label column alone, and groups/<group>.parquet the group's struct column alone. A layer that adds or removes a label writes its dim's file whole, every label the axis has at that node, in order, and a layer that adds or removes a tuple writes its group's file whole. A layer that changes only properties writes neither file. A node's membership and order are the deepest such file on the path from the root.

DEP 20's sections removal, order and SubNetworks are a dim apply unchanged, except for the staging table described below. A removal is still the diff of a restatement against the previous one, so DEP 20's owner-map pruning and dead labels carry over. DEP 21 uses that diff and works over DEP 22 as over DEP 20.

docs.title: A property is a file of patches
docs.text:
file holds dims/<dim>.parquet the label column, every label in order, written whole groups/<group>.parquet the struct column, every tuple in order, written whole properties/<subject>.<name>.parquet the subject's key column and the column <name>, one row per label the layer sets attributes/<attr>.parquet unchanged

The file name is the property's address (properties). bus.x lives in properties/bus.x.parquet, and connection.role in properties/connection.role.parquet, keyed by the connection struct. A row sets the property for its label, a row holding NULL sets it to NULL, and a label without a row keeps the value a shallower layer gave it. One property per file keeps an unset cell apart from a NULL one with no mask, since a file holds no cell its layer does not set.

A resolved property is, per label, the row of the deepest layer holding one. A resolved axis or group is the membership in its order with every property's fold joined on as a column, the shape Record.dims, Record.properties and Record.groups read today, so neither the API nor Coords changes shape. Properties of every subject fold per label, whether or not the subject is in partial.

docs.title: A removal cuts a label's properties
docs.text:
A property row counts only where it is deeper than every layer that removed its label. The fold takes, per label, the depth of the deepest layer whose diff removes it, from the diffs DEP 20 computes, and drops the label's property rows at that depth and shallower. A label added again after its removal therefore starts with no property and reads only the rows written with or after its re-add, as DEP 20 starts its keyed values empty.

A label removed and added again in one staging area is no removal, since its layer's restatement holds it. add stages a row of every declared property of each label it adds, NULL where no keyword names it, so the label reads the properties add gave it, as add restates a row whole today.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
DEP 20's refusals apply. In addition, a dims/ or groups/ file with any column beside its key is refused at read and by write_layer:

dims/bus.parquet carries columns ['x', 'y']; a property of bus is the file
properties/bus.<name>.parquet of the labels a layer sets it for
(.../design/format/#where-a-value-lives). Re-export the record.

A layer written before this DEP with properties in an axis or group file thus fails at read instead of reading as a restatement. DEP 20's silent case, an old patch file read as a restatement, narrows to an old axis file holding labels alone.

write_layer refuses a property file of an undeclared property, one with a column beside its key and its property, one holding a key twice, and a row naming a label or tuple outside the layer's resolved membership. A read refuses the first three, and a row naming a non-member falls out of the join onto the membership.

docs.title: The reference check
docs.text: DEP 20's check holds for group tuples, which a restatement holds whole. A property that takes its labels from a dim is checked whole, in its final state, against the final dead labels wherever the layer writes rows of that property or removes a label of the dim it takes its labels from. A layer repairs a dangling value an ancestor left by writing a row for its label, so the strict check costs nothing a patch cannot fix, and an edit of another property never meets the dangling value. _require_living_references reads the property's fold over the parents and the layer, instead of rows of the axis file.

docs.title: Caches and staging
docs.text:
A materialised node writes resolved/dims/<dim>.parquet and resolved/groups/<group>.parquet as today: the membership in order, with every property's fold as a column. DEP 20 copies the deepest file there instead. A fold above the node seeds the membership from the key column and each property from its column. A NULL cell there reads as a row holding NULL, which resolves the same as no row. resolved/dead/ and owner_map.parquet are as in DEP 20, and the frozen prefix's shared tables take the same shapes.

WorkingRecord stages membership in the table DEP 20's order describes, narrowed to the key and the position column. The first add or remove on a dim or group copies the base's resolved labels in, add appends a new label at the next position and puts a label of the base back at its base position, remove deletes the row, and StagedSource hands the table over in position order. A property edit stages one row per label in a table per property, replaced by key, and reads no base row, since no sibling property travels with it. remove also deletes the label's staged property rows. A read folds the staged property rows onto the frozen prefix's resolved properties as the deepest layer. No staging table carries deleted.

LayerSource and LayerData gain properties(), the (subject, name) pairs a layer has a file for, and property(subject, name). RecordLike.properties already holds a subject's properties apart from dims, so a write takes each of its columns as one property file, and a full export writes every property of every label.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Membership and order are facts about a whole axis, so DEP 20's case for a whole file holds for them. A property is a fact about one label, so a per-label patch loses nothing, and the last writer per label and property decides it as set already treats it. partial keeps the one meaning DEP 20 gives it, attribute ownership: a property never varies along another dim, so it cannot leave the hole partial guards against, and every subject's properties are patched per label.

docs.title: Added complexity
docs.text:
Every size and time below is a DuckDB run over synthetic data at DEP 20's scale, 60,000 entities with four properties and 150,000 connections with role, timed as the median of five, unless stated. Sizes for today and DEP 20 are DEP 20's.

edit today DEP 20 DEP 22 one entity's carrier 0.8 kB 0.30 MB 0.4 kB one connection's role one row 0.43 MB 0.4 kB add an entity one row 0.30 MB 0.30 MB, plus 4 rows remove an entity and its connections one row each 0.73 MB 0.72 MB edit one bus geometry, 4,000 buses of 64 vertices one row 2.49 MB one row add or remove a bus, same one row 2.49 MB 17.5 kB, plus a row per property chain of 20 edit layers, 40,000 entities, 80,000 connections 10 kB 5.57 MB 3.78 MB, estimated

Labels dominate the synthetic axes. The entity labels alone take 297 kB of the whole file's 303 kB, and the connection keys 424 kB of 426 kB. DEP 22 therefore saves nothing over DEP 20 on an add or a removal at this scale, and saves where a layer edits properties or a subject carries bulky ones. The chain alternates removals and property edits, and its DEP 22 figure sums file sizes, a method that gives 5.56 MB for DEP 20's measured 5.57 MB.

A read pays for the split. Assembling the entity axis from its label file and four property files, one of them folded over 20 patch layers, took 37 ms into a table, against 10.5 ms for reading one whole file as DEP 20 does. Folding the same 20 patches onto a materialised node's wide file took 19 ms. The connections with role from two files took 42 ms against 8 ms. The cut added 7 ms to a 25 ms fold of carrier, and the removal diff is DEP 20's, 6.8 ms for the entities. Today's entity fold takes 80-95 ms by DEP 20's measure, which fetched rows into Python, where the DEP 22 assembly took 89 ms and one whole file 64 ms.

Staging copies less than DEP 20 does. The first membership edit copies the labels and positions in 4.9 ms for the entities and 8.6 ms for the connections, against DEP 20's estimate of 15 ms and 41 ms for whole rows, and a property edit copies nothing. A read takes the membership table in position order, 5.6 ms and 9.8 ms, and composes no restatement, as under DEP 20.

A reader holds six fold rules where DEP 20 needs four and today six. DEP 20's four are the deepest file as membership and order, removal as a restatement's diff, the owner map dropping rows of a removed label, and dead labels as removed labels the final axis lacks. DEP 22 adds the deepest row per label and property, and the cut of a property row at or below its label's latest removal. Today's six are the last row per label, the tombstone, first-introduced order, the owner map's anti-join on tombstones, dead labels as winning tombstones, and partial deciding an axis layer's extent.

src/datarecord/ module beyond DEP 20 resolve/sources.py +30-40: properties() and property(), and the key-only refusal resolve/coords.py +50-80: a property fold seeded from a base column, the cut, and the join onto the membership store/write.py +40-60, −25-35: the property file checks, the reference check on the fold, one file per column mutable.py +20-40, −20-30: per-property staging tables, add's NULL rows, _patch_axis without siblings store/cache.py 0, −5-15: today's resolved files stay, where DEP 20 copies the deepest file

src thus grows by an estimated 140-220 lines and shrinks by 50-80 beyond DEP 20, or 275-455 added and 150-210 deleted against today, where DEP 20 adds 135-235 and deletes 100-130. On top of DEP 20's 18 or more changed tests, the fixtures write each property column as its own file, and the tests asserting a property column in dims/ or groups/ assert a property file instead. About eight new tests pin per-label-and-property ownership across two layers, NULL against no row, the cut on a re-add, materialised against unmaterialised properties, and the four property file refusals.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.set("bus.geometry", shape, bus="b7")
child = rev.child(w.edits)  # properties/bus.geometry.parquet, one row; no dims/

w = WorkingRecord(child.record)
w.add("bus", ["z"], x=1.0, y=2.0)
child.child(w.edits)  # dims/bus.parquet: every bus of child in order, then z;
# properties/bus.x.parquet and bus.y.parquet hold z, the other properties NULL rows

A layer written by hand holds the property's rows alone, or the whole label column:

pd.DataFrame({"bus": ["b7"], "x": [3.1]}).to_parquet(
    f"{layer}/properties/bus.x.parquet"
)
buses = parent.record.dims["bus"].df()
new = pd.DataFrame({"bus": ["z"]})
pd.concat([buses, new], ignore_index=True).to_parquet(f"{layer}/dims/bus.parquet")

A label added again reads none of its old properties, and bus.geometry above stands for a property a schema declares:

# the root sets bus.x = 1.0 on b; a child removes b; a grandchild adds b
grandchild.record.properties["bus"]  # b reads x as NULL

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Paths are under src/datarecord/.

  1. DEP 20's implementation notes 1, 2, 4 and 6 to 8, with _fold_axis reading the key column alone and keeping, per removed label, the depth of its deepest removal.
  2. In resolve/sources.py, LayerSource gains properties() and property(subject, name), and _FileLayer.axis and group refuse a column beside the key.
  3. In resolve/coords.py, a property fold takes the base's resolved column and each layer's property file, cut by the removal depths, keeps the deepest row per label, and resolve_coords and resolve_groups join each fold onto the membership.
  4. In store/write.py, write_layer writes and checks a properties kind, _require_living_references reads a property that takes its labels from a dim from the fold, and _RecordLikeAsLayerData.axis loses its join on properties.
  5. In mutable.py, DEP 20's note 3 with the staging table narrowed to the key and the position, a staging table per property, _patch_axis without the sibling carry, add staging NULL rows, and remove deleting the label's staged property rows.
  6. In tests/fixtures.py, DEP 20's note 5, with each property column written as its own file.
  7. CHANGELOG.md under [Unreleased]: DEP 20's entry, and a property is a file of per-label patches under properties/.
  8. On landing, DEP 20's page list, with where a value lives and properties placing a property in its own file. Whichever of DEP 20 and DEP 22 is implemented, the other takes Superseded with Superseded-By naming it.

Checks: DEP 20's checks; a property set by two layers on two labels reads per label; a label added again reads no property from below its removal, materialised or not, staged or committed.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
Keeping properties in the axis file beside the whole label column, NULL on labels a layer leaves alone, reads an untouched cell and a cell set to NULL alike. A mask column per property would tell them apart, at a column per property in every restatement.

One properties/<subject>.parquet per subject, holding the properties a layer sets as columns, makes a layer that sets x on one bus and country on another carry each bus's other value from the parent. A hand-written file of that shape blanks the cell it leaves NULL.

Declaring properties as attributes over their subject reuses the owner map, which keys them per label only where the subject is in partial, so carrier.color would be restated whole. DEP 12 separates properties from attributes for reasons this DEP leaves standing.

Keeping a re-added label's property rows from below its removal reads an old bus's carrier and geometry on a new bus of the same name.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
DEP 20's open issues apply unchanged.

A layer holds up to one file per declared property, about 14 for a full PyPSA export, which a remote store pays for in requests, and a read of properties["bus"] opens up to six files per layer holding them.

An old axis file holding labels alone, without a deleted column, still reads silently as a restatement.

docs.title: DEP 23: multi-dims replace groups
docs.text: DEP 23 Title multi-dims replace groups Author Bryn Pickering Status Implemented (2026-10-26) Requires DEP 10, DEP 12, DEP 13, DEP 18, DEP 20 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces the groups of DEP 2 and DEP 10

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A group becomes a multi-dim: a dim declared under dimensions with over, whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels. It has its own dimension table in dims/, its coordinates are addressed as connection.bus as properties are, and a functional group's property {one_of: <dim>} becomes a property of the multi-dim, unchanged. The groups section, and every public name with group in it, goes.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A group is a dim in all but name. DEP 10's amendment found it so in every way the fold sees: it is one struct column, it broadcasts, it is listed in partial or owned whole, it has a table of properties. DEP 20 made its file restated whole, as an axis file is. What still sets it apart is spelling, and the spelling costs:

a dim a group declared under dimensions under groups dims/bus.parquet groups/connection.parquet add, remove add_group, remove_group Schema.dimensions Schema.groups, group_columns, group_key, groups_of dims: [X] resolves a dim first …and a group if no dim is so named a property {one_of: <dim>} may categorize it never categorized

Every reader of a schema asks twice, and every rule that holds for both is stated twice.

docs.title: A multi-dim
docs.text:
A multi-dim is a dim whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels. It is declared under dimensions with over, as a group was, and has no dtype:

dimensions:
  entity: { dtype: str }
  bus: { dtype: str }
  snapshot: { dtype: datetime }
  role: { one_of: [input, output, attached] }
  connection: { over: { entity: entity, bus: bus } }
  corridor: { over: { from: bus, to: bus } }

properties:
  connection:
    role: { one_of: role }

attributes:
  efficiency: { dtype: float, dims: [connection, snapshot], default: 1 }

partial: [entity, bus, connection]
  • over is a list or a coordinate→dim map, as a group's was: over: [entity, bus] is over: {entity: entity, bus: bus}, and corridor draws two coordinates on bus. Each coordinate names a declared dim that is not a multi-dim.
  • over excludes dtype and one_of. A dim declaring over beside either is refused at load. A dim without over keeps its default dtype: str.
  • Its table is dims/connection.parquet, keyed by its struct column, with its properties as columns: connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role, what groups/connection.parquet was. dims/bus.parquet is keyed by bus the same way. A layer that changes its tuples or their properties writes it whole and in order, as DEP 20 has it write a group file today.
  • Dimension.over holds the map; Schema.dimensions holds every dim, multi or not.

docs.title: What DEP 10 settled carries over
docs.text:
• A row addresses it by one struct column named for it, a field per coordinate in over order.
  • It may be listed in partial, and is in the fold key there; owned whole otherwise.
  • A value is a whole tuple or NULL. A struct with some fields NULL is refused wherever a row comes in: set, add and the writer.
  • A NULL broadcasts over its live tuples, expanded against dims/connection.parquet as a NULL bus is against dims/bus.parquet.
  • An attribute may not name a multi-dim beside a dim that shares a name with one of its coordinates, since a keyword such as bus= would address both: dims: [connection, bus] is refused. A coordinate drawing on bus under another name, such as port, may sit beside bus, as a group's may today.
  • Removing a coordinate's label cascades: remove("bus", ["south"]) removes every tuple naming south, as it removed every group row.

docs.title: Coordinates are addressed as properties are
docs.text:
connection.bus names the bus of each tuple, wherever DEP 13 lets a dotted name stand: Schema.resolve among them. A coordinate is not a property column: it is part of the key, so set("connection.bus", …) is refused, naming remove and add. A default_by keyed on entity.ctype reaches entity through the coordinate already, as it reaches a group's field today.

  • A selector keyword stays bare: bus="north" on an attribute over connection selects the tuples whose bus is north, coordinate first, as today.
  • A property of a multi-dim named like one of its coordinates stays refused, as the schema refuses it for a group.
  • A multi-dim is never categorized. A property of it may refer to a dim with one_of, as role does, and still categorizes nothing, partial listing the multi-dim or not; a default_by keyed on one is refused. Whether that changes is left open.

docs.title: A functional group is a property of a multi-dim
docs.text:
A group property {one_of: <dim>}, which DEP 18 put in place of a group's into, becomes a property of the multi-dim, declared the same way:

# before
groups:
  plant_period: { over: [plant, period] }
properties:
  plant_period:
    zone: { one_of: zone }

# after
dimensions:
  plant_period: { over: [plant, period] }
properties:
  plant_period:
    zone: { one_of: zone }

One zone per tuple is what a property is: one value per label of its subject. The live-label check, the remove refusal and NULL meaning none are a property referring to a dim's.

docs.title: Groups go
docs.text:
With that, groups holds nothing and is removed. Group, Schema.groups, Schema.group_columns, Schema.groups_of, Schema.group_key, add_group, remove_group and the groups/ directory go. dims: [X] resolves a dim, and nothing else.

add and remove take a multi-dim's tuples as a frame, anything DuckDB scans, holding the struct column named for the multi-dim, which is what record.dims["connection"] reads, so a read goes back in as it stands. A frame may instead carry a column per coordinate, and a list of mappings from coordinate to label is made into that frame up front. Every form then takes the same path and the same type checks. A frame carrying both the struct column and a coordinate column is refused as ambiguous:

w.add("connection", other.dims["connection"])  # another record's tuples, as read
w.add("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}], role="output")
w.add("connection", pd.DataFrame({"entity": ["g2"], "bus": ["south"]}))
w.remove("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}])

A property is a keyword, as for any dim, or a further column of the frame. A tuple naming a label its coordinate's dim lacks is refused, as add_group refused it.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
A multi-dim, not a relation usable as a dim. A tuple set that may stand in dims when used there and is a relation otherwise is two kinds of thing decided by the caller. Declaring it under dimensions says once what it is, gives it a table for its properties, and lets add and remove treat it as any other dim.

A dim table, not a second directory. dims/ already holds one table per dim keyed by that dim's column, each restated whole; a multi-dim's is keyed by its struct column. A reader of the format looks in one place.

What breaks:

  • Every manifest with groups is rewritten, and every record re-exported: groups/ moves to dims/.
  • Every public name with group in it goes; callers of add_group and remove_group call add and remove.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
record.dims["connection"]  # connection STRUCT(entity, bus)
record.properties["connection"]  # connection | role
record.attributes[
    "efficiency"
]  # connection | snapshot | attribute | breakpoint | value

w.add("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}], role="output")
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="g1", bus="north")  # selector: the coordinates
w.set("connection.role", "input", entity="g1", bus="north")
w.set("connection.bus", "south", entity="g1")  # refused: a coordinate is the key
w.remove("bus", ["north"])  # and every connection at it

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Dimension.over, parsed as a group's was; over exclusive with dtype and one_of; groups an unknown key, refused as any other.
  2. The group struct-column machinery keyed on the dim: fold key, broadcast, whole-or-NULL, cascade, the coordinate-name clash.
  3. dims/<multi-dim>.parquet for its table, restated whole; groups/ and resolved/groups/ dropped from the writer and reader.
  4. add and remove take tuples, as a frame with the struct column or a column per coordinate, or as a list of mappings; add_group, remove_group removed.
  5. Schema.resolve resolves a coordinate.
  6. Group, Schema.groups, group_columns, groups_of, group_key removed; the PyPSA tool declares connection under dimensions.
  7. Pages, usage, changelog; fixtures re-exported.

Checks that hold once built:

  • A multi-dim behaves as a group did: the connection, broadcast, partial and cascade tests pass with connection declared under dimensions.
  • The word group appears in no public name, and no live page outside the DEPs.
  • A PyPSA network round-trips with connection a multi-dim and role its property.
  • A functional mapping is checked as a property is: a zone naming no live label is refused on set, and removing a named zone refused.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
A relation usable as a dim (dims: [connection] naming a relation). Makes a tuple set a relation or a dim depending on where it is used.

No multi-dims at all (dims: [entity, bus], validity by a condition). Loses the struct column, the whole-or-NULL broadcast and the table for role.

A surrogate port dim, one label per tuple with two properties {one_of: entity} and {one_of: bus}. A value is then written against a port label and its entity and bus looked up; the tuple stops being the address.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
• Whether a multi-dim may be over another multi-dim. Nothing needs it yet; it is refused until something does. Carried on as an open question.
  • Whether a functional mapping over two coordinates justifies a dim. plant_period exists only to carry zone; its labels must be written before the property can be. Carried on as an open question.
  • Whether a multi-dim in partial may be categorized. Once a group is a dim, the open question on a group's categories becomes whether the categories rule extends to a multi-dim. This DEP keeps a multi-dim uncategorized, as its specification says; a later DEP may lift that.

docs.title: DEP N: Title
docs.text:
DEP N Title Title Author Name Status Draft | Accepted | On hold | Implemented | Superseded, with its date Requires DEPs this one builds on, linked (omit if none) Created YYYY-MM-DD Version the datarecord release it ships in, Unreleased until then; omitted while a draft Replaces the DEP this one makes obsolete, linked (omit if none) Superseded-By the DEP that makes this one obsolete, linked (omit if none)

Once implemented, one sentence naming the design and usage pages it landed in, which are authoritative where the two disagree.

Keep it under about 2,000 words. State each rule once, in the section it belongs to, and cut what restates it, narrates how the design was found, or tours internals the reader can look up.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: What changes, in two or three sentences.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: The problem, in the terms of someone using datarecord today.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text: The design: what the schema, the format and the API become, as short statements or a table.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Why this design, only where the rule does not already say it, a short paragraph each; and what it costs: what breaks, what gets slower, what becomes harder to say.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: What a user writes with it, as short examples of what changes. These move to the usage pages on implementation.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text: The steps it is built in, in order, one line each, and the checks that hold once it is. On implementation, where the build departs from the text above.

docs.text: What else was considered, and why not, in a line or two each.

docs.title: Open Issues

docs.title: Threads, processes and concurrent writers
docs.text: Each thread reads through its own DuckDB cursor, and relations are the only objects bound to one. Fold results are shared tables keyed by the id of the layer they fold, so a fold that one thread builds serves every thread. A revision serialises as its location and id, so it resolves again in a fresh process. Two writers to one store meet only at the manifest. A bounded compare-and-swap settles that race and keeps both widenings.

docs.title: A cursor per thread
docs.text:
A DuckDB connection is unsafe to use from two threads at once, and DuckDB's answer is a cursor per thread. The workspace's con is the calling thread's cursor on the workspace's one database. A threading.local subclass makes it on first use in each thread. Its __init__ reruns in each new thread, so the lookup needs no existence check and no lock, and a cursor goes away with its thread. A dict keyed by thread id would reuse ids, and a ContextVar would be copied into a task runner's workers, which would then share the parent's cursor.

Tables are shared between cursors: the revisions cache, the staging tables and the folded caches. A DuckDBPyRelation is bound to the cursor that built it. The line between thread-bound and shared objects runs around relations alone.

A store, a revision, a Record and a layer source hold their workspace and look up workspace.con on each call. Every relation they build lands on the calling thread's cursor, so one Record serves any thread. Anything else they cache is plain data that every thread computes the same way. A relation and a WorkingRecord belong to the thread that built them. When one of them reaches another thread's write path, it is rejected as a relation from another connection is.

A fold caches its results as shared tables. The frozen prefix's folded axes are the tables dims_<dim>_<id>, a multi-dim's like any other, beside the owner map owner_map_<key>_<id>. A last table, coords_<id>, lists them and is created after them, so a reader that finds it finds them all. A dim's name is a caller's string, so the table name holds its hash, and <key> is the hash of the owner map's key columns. <id> is the node whose frozen layers were folded: a revision's id, the base's id for a WorkingRecord, or the id in the manifest for a standalone directory.

The schema is no part of the key beyond partial, so a fold made before the manifest widened is read as it is under the wider schema, while one made before a dim joined or left partial is folded again. A compatible widening only adds, and changes no column a table already has. The one addition a table can lack is the new dim's field in the flag structs. Each reader of a flag takes a missing field as unset, and decides this from the struct's type when it builds the query. A materialised owner map is cast to the declared types. These tables are left as the fold produced them, and each holds what the same fold returns uncached.

A fold that one thread builds serves every thread. When two threads miss at once, both fold and both create the table. DuckDB fails the second with a write-write conflict, and the miss path catches it and reads the winner's table. The duplicate fold wastes work and gives the same answer.

docs.title: A relation from another connection is rejected
docs.text: as_relation is the boundary that every frame crosses on its way to a write or an edit. It binds a relation to the target cursor first, which costs no read. The bind fails for a relation from another connection or from another thread's cursor. as_relation re-raises that failure as a ValueError that names the fix: build the frame on record.con in this thread, or hand over a pandas, polars or arrow frame to land. Copying the relation onto the target connection would collect it in full, which the caller never asked for, and fails anyway once that connection is closed.

docs.title: Crossing a process boundary
docs.text:
Revision serialises its store as its location: {"id": …, "parent": …, "store": "/data/a"}. It validates back through Workspace.process().store(uri).revision(id), which reads the revision file and each parent the process lacks, so ancestry() answers in a fresh process. Store pickles the same way.

Workspace.process() is the one default workspace, and only deserialisation reaches it implicitly. It is created on first use, on :memory:. Code that wants its own records to join with deserialised ones names it.

docs.title: The manifest's compare-and-swap
docs.text:
Two writers race on manifest.json when they create a location's first layers or widen its schema at once. The manifest is therefore written through a conditional write. A writer reads the manifest with its version, or Absent where there is none, checks compatibility, and writes only if the manifest is still at that version. A writer that loses re-reads and checks again. Two writers that widen at once end with both widenings, the later schema including the earlier, or with the later writer's incompatibility reported. No widening is silently lost.

The retry is bounded. A writer that loses ten times, with a jittered backoff in between, gives up with an error. A credential that can write manifest.json but cannot read it meets the same error, because a remote read answered 403 counts as missing and every create-only write then fails.

materialise() follows the same rule. owner_map.parquet marks a node as materialised, so it is written last, after the resolved dims. Locally each file is written under a temporary name and renamed. A parquet file appears at its final path before it is complete, and a reader that meets it mid-write fails. Two writers that materialise one node write the same content, so that race is harmless.

docs.title: A standalone directory
docs.text:
A standalone directory has no revision file, so its manifest is written last. ws.at requires a manifest, so a directory whose write failed reads as no record.

ws.write writes to a URI that does not exist yet and refuses one that does: locally the path, even an empty directory, and remotely any key under it. A whole-record write refuses an existing layer in the same way. The caller picks this URI, unlike a layer's UUID, and a write over an existing record would mix the two records under the old manifest. The check and the write are two steps, so two writers racing to one new URI can still mix. A standalone directory has one writer.

Each write gives the record a fresh id in its manifest. A record deleted and written again at one URI is therefore a new layer to every workspace, and no cached fold of the old record applies to it. ws.write and ws.at resolve a local path as ws.store does.

docs.title: The record format
docs.text:
A record on disk is a directory with manifest.json, dims/ and attributes/, and any parquet reader can open it. An axis file holds its key, then its properties, in order. An attribute file holds the attribute's own coordinates, then attribute, breakpoint and value. The section in which a name is declared decides the file its values go in.

A write produces the directory, and Workspace.at(uri) reads it. A record that is never written has no directory and answers the protocol all the same.

record/
├── manifest.json                   # the schema, and the record's id
├── dims/<dim>.parquet              # one axis per declared dim, multi-dims included: labels and properties
└── attributes/<attr>.parquet       # one attribute per file, results included

Each file is named for what it holds: dims/scenario.parquet holds the scenario axis, and attributes/p_nom.parquet holds p_nom. A file takes the declared name unchanged, so the dim bus lives in dims/bus.parquet.

docs.title: Axis files
docs.text:
dims/<dim>.parquet holds the labels of the dim that exist at the layer's node, in order, with the properties that describe each.

<dim> | <property> ...

In the running example dims/entity.parquet is entity | ctype | carrier | sign | type. A Record hands an axis file over as dims[dim], and the writer writes it.

A label exists at a node when the deepest dims/<dim>.parquet on its path has a row for it. That file's row order is the axis order. A layer removes a label by writing the file without it (removal). Each property is one column, NULL where no layer wrote a value, so a category's frame is a filter on its property column.

docs.title: Where a value lives
docs.text:
The section that declares a name decides its file. One name is one spec in one file. A property belongs to its subject and is a column of that subject's file alone, so bus.x and an attribute x live in two places.

declared as lands in property of a dim dims/<dim>.parquet, a column of the axis file property of a multi-dim dims/<multi-dim>.parquet, likewise attribute, any dims attributes/<attr>.parquet, long rows

attributes/p_nom.parquet holds entity | attribute | breakpoint | value, one row per entity. Widening p_nom over scenario adds a scenario column to the same file. That column is NULL in every row written before, and the broadcast rule reads those rows unchanged. A scenario weight over scenario alone is long rows too.

An axis file therefore carries its key and its subject's properties, and no attribute values. A framework's constant frame per category joins the category's properties with the coordinate-only rows of its attributes, and the tool builds it.

A multi-dim's tuples live in dims/<multi-dim>.parquet: every tuple the multi-dim has at the layer's node, in order. The file is keyed by one struct column named for the multi-dim, as a plain dim's file is keyed by the column named for it. For the connection multi-dim over (entity, bus), dims/connection.parquet is connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role, where role is a property of connection. An attribute row carries the multi-dim in the same struct column, so no read or write converts between two shapes. A record with no file for a multi-dim has no tuples of it.

A multi-dim's property that refers to a dim is a plain column of its file beside the key: dims/bus_country.parquet is bus_country STRUCT(bus, scenario) | country. A classification of one coordinate is a property of the dim, so bus.country is a column of dims/bus.parquet. A property that refers to a dim is stored like any other property, and nothing in the layout depends on it.

docs.title: The long schema
docs.text:
Every attributes/ file carries its attribute's own coordinates, then the columns every row has:

<coordinate> ... | attribute | breakpoint | value

The coordinates are what the attribute's dims declare, multi-dims first. A multi-dim is one struct column named for it, with a field per coordinate. attributes/efficiency.parquet over the connection multi-dim carries connection STRUCT(entity, bus). attributes/p_max_pu.parquet over entity and snapshot carries entity | snapshot and no bus. The writer refuses a multi-dim's column that is not a struct of exactly its coordinates. DuckDB casts a struct by field name, so a missing field would turn NULL, an extra field would be dropped, and every row would silently change its key.

Each attribute file has its own column set. A fixed prefix such as entity | bus would put an all-NULL entity on a record-level weighting, which has no entity. UNION ALL BY NAME supplies NULL for a column a file does not carry, so the differing shapes cost nothing. The same rule reads a file written before a dim was declared (resolving a relation). The fold's key is uniform across files: partial_dims plus attribute, one fixed tuple over every attribute. A coordinate that an attribute does not carry reads as NULL in that key. The owner map holds each key as its layer wrote it, so a NULL there means every label, as it does in the file.

Each file holds one attribute, so value carries that attribute's dtype.

docs.title: A label is unique within its dim
docs.text:
An axis has one row per label, and a label's properties are columns of that row. In the example, two entities both called north collide, whatever their ctype. A bus called north is a label of another dim and collides with neither. add of a label already there restates its row (add / remove).

An attributes/ row addresses a label by the label alone, so set("p_nom", 150.0, entity="wind1") names no ctype (set). A consumer that wants the p_max_pu of one ctype joins the resolved attribute to the resolved entity axis on entity.

A modelling framework that scopes names per class reconciles them before it writes, and its tool's verify reports a collision. The record layer never renames a label. A label is the framework's own name, and a renamed label would come back as one the framework cannot find.

docs.title: Workspaces and stores
docs.text: A Workspace holds the DuckDB database and the means to read and write files. A Store holds one location with its manifest, revision tree and layers. The location holds the record, and the database holds caches. Revision files sit beside the layers, one per revision, and are written create-only. Files go through a small Files protocol with conditional writes, backed by the local filesystem or by S3.

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
Several stores share one workspace, so records from them join. A standalone directory needs the workspace alone.

ws = Workspace()  # ":memory:" by default
store = ws.store("/data/a")  # one Store per normalised location
rev = store.revision(rid)  # look one up
record = ws.at("out/")  # a standalone directory, read under its own manifest
layer = store.layer(rid)  # one layer read alone, under the store's manifest

A call takes the workspace explicitly only where nothing in hand carries one: ws.store, ws.at, and the con that a tool receives when it converts a framework object. Everything else takes its workspace from what built it. A revision takes it from its store, a Record from the revision or workspace that builds it, and a WorkingRecord from its base record.

The location is required and absolute. ws.store("") raises. A local path is resolved on the call, so a later chdir or a process with another working directory reaches the same location. layer_dir, resolved_dir and the manifest's location derive from the location alone.

The location is authoritative, and the database is disposable. Deleting a workspace's database loses at most uncommitted edits. A file-backed database keeps staged edits across a crash and the revisions cache across runs, and it gives DuckDB room to spill. A location is written once. Every cache keyed by id assumes that an id always names the same content. A fresh UUID over write-once files guarantees this, and a location wiped and written again breaks it.

docs.title: The tree beside the layers
docs.text:
<location>/
├── manifest.json
├── revisions/<id>.json        # {"id": ..., "parent": ...}
└── layers/<id>/

The revision files sit beside layers/, so a layer directory holds exactly what the layer wrote, and listing the tree is one listing over small files. Each revision has its own file, named by a fresh UUID, so the file is write-once like a layer. Two processes that create revisions in one location never write the same object. The file is written create-only through files, which enforces this.

The workspace's revisions table caches those files for every store on the workspace, keyed by (location, id). A revision's parent never changes, so the cache can be incomplete but never stale, and rows are only ever added. revisions() lists revisions/ once and reads only the files the table lacks. revision(id) on a miss reads that file and each parent the table lacks, and raises KeyError when the first file is absent. Two cursors that add the same row at once conflict. The row is the same whoever wins, so the loser moves on.

docs.title: Files, local and remote
docs.text:
Tables go through DuckDB. The manifest, the revision files and their listing go through the workspace's Files, which the URI's scheme selects. A URI without :// is local, an s3:// URI is remote, and any other scheme raises.

class Files(Protocol):
    def read_text(self, uri: str) -> tuple[str, Version] | None: ...  # None on a miss
    def write_text(
        self, uri: str, text: str, *, expect: Version | Absent | None
    ) -> Version: ...
    def list(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]: ...  # names directly under prefix
    def exists(self, uri: str) -> bool: ...

expect is the precondition of a write. Absent writes only if nothing is there. A Version writes only if the object is unchanged since it was read. None writes unconditionally.

Locally every write lands under a temporary name and moves into place, so a reader meets a whole file or none. Absent moves the file with a hard link, which the OS refuses over an existing file. A local Version is the content's SHA-256. The writer checks it and replaces the file while it holds a lock on a sibling <name>.lock, which makes the check and the write one step.

Remotely, Files runs on boto3, behind the optional extra datarecord[remote]. expect maps to the conditional headers of put_object: IfNoneMatch="*" for Absent, and IfMatch for a Version, which is the object's ETag. A refused write (412, or 409 for a racing one) raises PreconditionFailedError. The conditions guard the revision files, which the server then keeps create-only, and the manifest's compare-and-swap. DuckDB's httpfs writes a layer's parquet unconditionally, under a fresh UUID. The conditions hold only as far as the server honours them. SeaweedFS checks them atomically from 4.18, and AWS S3 since November 2024.

The configuration is the AWS environment and config files, and datarecord adds no settings of its own. boto3 reads them itself. DuckDB gets CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, PROVIDER credential_chain). When AWS_ENDPOINT_URL is set, the secret adds its ENDPOINT, URL_STYLE 'path', USE_SSL per its scheme and CHAIN 'env;config', because a self-hosted server has no bucket-subdomain DNS and no instance-metadata service to probe. The workspace sets both up on the first s3:// URI it receives, so a purely local workspace pays for neither.

docs.title: A revision exists only by its file
docs.text:
A tree write runs in three steps: the layer, then the manifest, then revisions/<id>.json. The revision file comes last, and its existence makes the layer real. revision(), revisions() and ancestry() reach a layer only through its revision file.

Locally a failed write leaves nothing, since the layer is staged and renamed. Remotely there is no rename, so a failed write can leave part of a layer behind. That part is unreachable, so every reader sees a remote write as atomic. Removing such leftovers is a separate cleanup task.

The manifest check comes after the layer. A layer whose schema is incompatible, or whose write fails, leaves the manifest untouched and the layer unreachable. The manifest widens only for a layer that exists.

A standalone directory has no revision file and orders its write by the manifest (a standalone directory).

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
A tool translates between a record and one modelling framework, in both directions. build reads any record. to_datarecord presents a framework object as relations on a connection the caller provides. verify reports what the framework cannot take. A tool holds its framework's vocabulary, including which attributes are results and which attributes each type takes.

The PyPSA tool is the one tool today, and its page covers results on connections, writing results, a value its type does not take and geometry.

class Tool(Protocol):
    name: str
    schema: Schema  # attribute mapping

    def requires(self, record: RecordLike) -> Requirements: ...
    def verify(self, record: RecordLike) -> Requirements: ...  # falsy when usable
    def build(self, record: RecordLike) -> Any: ...
    def to_datarecord(
        self,
        model: Any,
        con: DuckDBPyConnection,
        *,
        results_only: bool = False,
        base: RecordLike | None = None,
    ) -> RecordLike: ...

A record is the input to a translation and owns none. A tool is a module-level singleton reached by importing it, with no registry and no name dispatch. build returns the framework's own type, and nothing in the record layer imports a tool (the package). build takes a RecordLike, so a tool builds from a standalone directory as readily as from a tree of layers and needs no knowledge of layering. It reads record.con for its queries.

verify reports what the framework cannot take and the record layer cannot check, such as an entity type the framework does not know. It returns a Requirements, falsy when the record is usable. build raises UnsupportedRecordError for a record that verify finds unusable.

docs.title: Presenting a framework object
docs.text:
to_datarecord is the inverse of build. It requires the connection to plan its relations on, and in practice that is ws.con of the workspace that writes them. A tool plans relations and has no business with directories, locations or the tree, so it receives a connection alone. A relation planned on another connection is rejected at the boundary, so a tool that picked its own connection would fail on the first write.

root = store.root(PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con))

The result presents Relations keyed by attribute, each in the long schema, so they go straight to a write. The PyPSA tool scans its pandas frames on con with con.from_df.

A framework holds its values per entity type, so each attribute's relation concatenates its types. The relations are lazy, so the concatenation is a plan, and nothing materialises until a caller fetches. The tool builds and hands over relations one entity type at a time, so peak memory is one type's frames.

The protocol asks for lazy relations, and an implementation may be eager. A tool that reshapes a solved model's in-memory containers has nothing to defer and scans its eager frames. A tool that can fetch an attribute from a solver on demand may do so, and a caller who wants three attributes of forty then pays for three. This is the Relations argument on the write side.

A framework's per-port results are stored on connections, like its per-port inputs. A solve's results are written as a thin layer.

docs.title: The tool's schema
docs.text: The schema declares a record's attribute names, so a tool maps one declared vocabulary to another. The tool's own Schema holds that mapping per entity type. An entry names the record attribute that a tool attribute is renamed from, or the several attributes it is computed from. An attribute without an entry is read under its own name.

docs.title: Settling rows
docs.text:
A tool settles each attribute it reads with settle. The PyPSA build passes filter=False, since its own joins on entity drop a row naming another type's member anyway.

Attr.resolve(record, labels, flags) and Schema.resolve(record, ctype, name, labels, flags) settle each source before a rename or a computation, so a computed attribute combines one row per coordinate of each. The PyPSA tool passes a type's members as entity, their connections as connection, and the scenarios of a stochastic network, so a NULL entity reaches each member of the type it builds.

docs.title: PyPSA
docs.text: The PyPSA tool maps components to entity labels with ctype as a category, and buses and carriers to dims of their own. Each port of a component is a connection tuple, and per-port inputs and results are attributes over that multi-dim. Multi-period snapshots are one flat axis with a period property. A solve writes its results as a thin child layer.

docs.title: Entities and their properties
docs.text:
PyPSA's registry decides what is a property and what is an attribute. The properties of entity are exactly ctype, carrier, sign and type, and role is a property of connection. Every other input, every number among them, is an attribute, so p_nom is long rows of attributes/p_nom.parquet (where a value lives).

entity.ctype is {one_of: ctype}, where ctype is a dim with one_of that holds the types exported as entities. connection.role is {one_of: role}, where role is a dim with one_of that holds input, output and attached. to_datarecord writes both axes whole, with every label in one_of, those the network leaves unused included. This is the tool's convention, since the axis of a dim with one_of holds only the labels that layers added.

A default that differs per component, such as sign, p_min_pu or p_set, is a default_by on entity.ctype. build applies it when it builds a component's static frame from the type's entities and the entity-only rows of its attributes.

The PyPSA schema declares partial={"entity", "bus", "scenario", "connection"}. A layer then patches one link's efficiency series, or one bus's v_nom, and inherits every other value from its parent (partial). entity is in partial also because ctype categorizes it. carrier is outside partial, so a layer restates every carrier's co2_emissions, a few dozen rows.

docs.title: What verify reports
docs.text:
verify catches what the record layer cannot: an entity type that PyPSA has no registry entry for, a connection role it cannot place, and a partial set that breaks PyPSA's split between constant and varying data. The record checks a category against the one_of of its dim, and the tool checks it against PyPSA's registry.

verify is also where PyPSA's names per type meet names unique across the record. PyPSA permits a Generator and a Load both called north, and to_datarecord reports such a network as unbuildable. A record cannot hold two entities under one key. Collisions are within a dim. A bus is a label of bus, so a Bus and a Load called north, as in every clustered pypsa-eur network, do not collide. SubNetworks, which PyPSA names 0, 1, … on every topology pass as it numbers Lines, are labels of their own dim sub_network (writing results).

The tool reports a collision and repairs none. A renamed Generator:north would come back as a component that PyPSA cannot find by its own name, and the framework's vocabulary belongs to the framework. PyPSA itself is moving to names unique across the network, which removes the constraint.

docs.title: Buses and carriers are dims
docs.text:
Bus and Carrier are no entity types. A bus is a label of bus, and a carrier is a label of carrier. The properties rule places what PyPSA stores on either, and every name stays PyPSA's:

PyPSA record Bus.type, Bus.carrier, Bus.x, Bus.y, Bus.unit, Bus.location properties of bus Bus.v_nom, Bus.v_mag_pu_min, Bus.v_mag_pu_max, Bus.v_mag_pu_set attributes over bus (and the varying dims) Bus.marginal_price, Bus.v_mag_pu, Bus.v_ang result attributes over bus and the varying dims Bus.p, Bus.q, Bus.control, Bus.generator, Bus.sub_network not written: derived from the connections Line.v_nom, ShuntImpedance.v_nom not written: derived from the bus a custom Bus or Carrier column attribute over its dim, as a custom entity column is Carrier.color, Carrier.nice_name properties of carrier Carrier.co2_emissions, max_growth, max_relative_growth attributes over carrier a component's carrier entity.carrier, {one_of: carrier}

So x is a line's reactance and bus.x is a bus's coordinate, each addressed by its own name. entity.carrier and bus.carrier refer to carrier, and bus.carrier defaults to AC. to_datarecord writes both axes in PyPSA's order. It adds every carrier that a component or bus names and n.carriers lacks, and it stores PyPSA's "" carrier as NULL, which names no carrier. build rebuilds n.buses and n.carriers from the axis, the properties with their defaults and the attribute rows, each series by its flags, the bus results among them.

PyPSA's calculate_dependent_values copies Line.v_nom and ShuntImpedance.v_nom from the bus. The tool does not write them, and build gets them back when PyPSA recomputes them.

remove("bus", …) is the cascade every dim has. An entity that it leaves attached to no bus is verify's to report, as its type's missing bus. remove("carrier", …) is refused while a stored carrier names the label.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Each port of a component is a connection tuple (entity, bus). The schema declares connection under dimensions as the multi-dim Dimension(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}), and its tuples live in dims/connection.parquet with role beside them. A per-connection input follows its connection's position: efficiency on a Link's bus2 connection is PyPSA's efficiency2, static or per snapshot. The tool collapses bus-keyed connections back to PyPSA's positional encoding, ordered by the connection order. It translates a curve or reports it unbuildable.

A Process's rate0, rate1, rate2, … are likewise the one input rate. They are numbered from 0 because PyPSA registers rate0 and leaves port 1's efficiency unsuffixed. A Process's ports default differently, -1 at the input end and 1 at the others, so rate declares no default, and a port with no row keeps PyPSA's own.

The tool reads which stems are per port off PyPSA's registry: a name that ends in a port index, plus a Link's unsuffixed efficiency, delay and cyclic_delay. Every per-port input, delay and cyclic_delay included, is long rows of attributes/ over connection, since a number is an attribute whatever its dims.

docs.title: Results on connections
docs.text:
A per-port result is stored like a per-port input: one attribute over the connection multi-dim, one row per (entity, bus), carried as the one connection struct column. to_datarecord packs the struct, and build unpacks it back to entity and bus where it places ports. PyPSA's p0, p1, p2, … on a Line, Transformer, Link or Process and the one-port p on a Generator, Load, Store, StorageUnit or ShuntImpedance are all the result p. Each row sits on the connection its port attaches to and keeps PyPSA's sign for that port. q0, q1 and the one-port q are q. A third port needs no declaration of its own: a Link's p2 is p on its bus2 connection, which the schema built from the bare registry already declares.

The tool names the two results that follow another rule. Bus.p, Bus.q, Bus.control, Bus.generator and Bus.sub_network are not written. p and q are the signed sum of the connection p and q at that bus, so they are derivable, and a bus-level p would collide with the connection-level one. The other three follow from the connections and the topology. Link.p and Process.p are written as p_internal. PyPSA's internal power sits at no bus, so it is a result over entity, and it takes another name because one name holds one spec across the record.

The schema's attributes and the frames that to_datarecord presents follow one rule, so every result is written under a name the schema declares. build turns p back into PyPSA's per-port columns as it does a per-port input, and p_internal into Link.p.

docs.title: Custom columns
docs.text: A static column that PyPSA's registry lacks is an attribute over its type's dim. Where that dim is entity, build puts it onto that type alone (below). One name is one spec, so a custom Bus.country beside a custom Generator.country would be one country with two dims. Carrier.efficiency likewise meets the per-port efficiency. to_datarecord reports either clash in Requirements.columns. A custom column clashes only with an attribute of the same name, so a custom Generator.location is an attribute beside the property bus.location.

docs.title: A value its type does not take
docs.text:
A NULL entity reaches every entity (the broadcast rule), so set("p_max_pu", 0.9) stores a value that a load reaches. PyPSA's registry says which attributes and entity properties each type takes, and the tool keeps that knowledge. build hands a type only the names it takes, so it leaves the load's value out.

A type takes its registry inputs and results and the custom columns its network was exported with. to_datarecord records those per type in the schema's meta. A name that no type claims, such as an attribute a record adds, reaches every type. So a custom Generator.e_nom is built onto generators, though the registry gives e_nom to stores.

verify reports each (type, attribute) whose stored value is left out in Requirements.ignored. An entity property left out goes unreported, since its column exists on every entity whatever its type. The ignored report is informational: it leaves the result falsy, and build does not raise for it. A value meant for the types that take it is written per label, as in set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator").

docs.title: Snapshots and weightings
docs.text:
PyPSA's multi-period (period, timestep) snapshots are one flat snapshot axis. Each snapshot carries its period as snapshot.period, a property that refers to period, and period is an axis of its own beside it. A snapshot is labelled by its timestep where no timestep repeats across periods. Otherwise it is labelled by its position, 0 to n-1 across every period in the network's order, and its timestep becomes the property snapshot.timestep. That property refers to the datetime dim timestep, PyPSA's own index level name, whose axis holds each timestep once. The pd.MultiIndex.from_product of set_investment_periods repeats every timestep, so its snapshots are positions.

A multi-period network declares its attributes over snapshot as a single-period network does, and a single-period network's schema declares no property of snapshot. build rebuilds the (period, timestep) index from the axis order, snapshot.period, and the label or snapshot.timestep. A period is selected like any property of a dim that an attribute reaches: set("p_max_pu", 0.5, entity="wind", period=2030) stages the snapshots of 2030 alone (set).

A weighting is an attribute over its axis. PyPSA's weighting frames become scenario_weight over scenario, snapshot_weighting_objective, snapshot_weighting_stores and snapshot_weighting_generators over snapshot, and period_weighting_objective and period_weighting_years over period. The tool writes them for each axis the network holds, and a multi-period network's snapshot weightings are over its flat snapshot like any other. build sets them back, and a label that no row reaches keeps PyPSA's own default, an equal share for a scenario.

docs.title: Writing results
docs.text:
A framework's outputs are attributes. to_datarecord writes them with every other attribute, so a solved network round-trips its results through attributes/. build copies every attribute the record holds into the network, a solved bus's marginal_price included. Only the tool knows which attributes are outputs, from PyPSA's registry status "Output". It reads that status on import alone, and the status decides only what results_only presents. A full export leaves out a result still at its default, so an unsolved network writes none.

With results_only=True, to_datarecord presents only what the solve produced. It is a thin layer written as a child of base, the record the model was built from. base is required with results_only and refused without it.

inputs = rev.child(w.edits)  # edited inputs are committed first
n = PyPSA.build(inputs.record)
n.optimize()
solved = inputs.child(
    PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con, results_only=True, base=inputs.record)
)

The results layer goes straight to a write, and no WorkingRecord stages it. It holds the result attributes and the intermediate results they need, since a solve derives structure as well as values. A result at its default is written too, so a re-solve's value stands over its parent's. base's inputs are never written.

A result row that base holds and the solve does not write again, such as the mu_* duals under assign_all_duals=False, is restated as NULL, so no stale value is inherited. NULL reads as no value, where a marginal_price at its default 0.0 would read as a price, and build leaves PyPSA its own default there. A layer removes a label or a tuple by restating its axis without it, a multi-dim's included, and has no way to remove a value, so restating is how a value is replaced.

A PyPSA SubNetwork is a label of the dim sub_network, 0, 1, … as PyPSA names it. sub_network.carrier is a property that refers to carrier, slack_bus is an attribute over sub_network, and a line's sub_network is an attribute over entity that holds the plain label. sub_network stays outside partial, since a results layer writes every SubNetwork's values. A results layer restates the sub_network axis alone and leaves the entity axis to base. A re-solve that numbers SubNetworks differently therefore leaves no stale label behind and rewrites no input axis. A solve without SubNetworks over a record with a sub_network axis restates the axis empty, its columns typed as the schema declares them, so the record holds none of the earlier SubNetworks. Over a record without that axis, it writes no sub_network axis. A full export writes the axis beside bus and carrier, and build adds the SubNetworks from it. A results layer meets full validation, so it carries the labels its results name.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
A geometry is text. PyPSA's Shape.geometry, the column its registry types geometry, is an attribute like idx and component beside it. Its values are WKT in attributes/geometry.parquet, declared String. A network has one coordinate reference system, so the CRS is crs in the schema's meta, as the CRS's authority string (EPSG:3035) where it has one. The tool does not write PyPSA's srid network attribute, that CRS's EPSG code.

build sets the network's CRS from crs before it adds any component, and parses each geometry back into a GeoSeries in that CRS. A record without crs builds in PyPSA's default, EPSG:4326.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord stages edits over a base record and reads back as that record with the edits applied. Each edit is already a row of the layer it will become. set writes attribute rows or patches a property, and add and remove change an axis, a multi-dim's tuples included. Each edit is checked when it is staged. The staged rows live in DuckDB tables shaped like the files they become. The caller writes edits as a child layer to keep them.

class WorkingRecord(Record):
    """A `Record` whose last source is a staging area, plus the edit surface."""

    def __init__(self, base: Record) -> None: ...

    def set(
        self,
        attribute: str,  # an attribute or a property
        value: Any,  # scalar | sequence | mapping | series | relation or frame
        **coords: Any,  # coordinates, a multi-dim's included, properties of a dim reached
    ) -> None: ...

    def add(self, dim: str, labels: Any, **columns: Any) -> None: ...
    def remove(self, dim: str, labels: Any) -> None: ...

    @property
    def edits(self) -> LayerData: ...  # the staged layer alone
    def rollback(self) -> None: ...

WorkingRecord(revision.record) stages on the base's connection, record.con. The base must be a Record. Any other RecordLike is refused, since a framework object has no layer layout to fold the edits over.

WorkingRecord is a subclass of Record. Its sources are the base's sources plus one staged source, so it reads as a record one layer deeper than its base. Every read member is inherited unchanged, so an edit reads back through the same code path a written layer would. A caller can read an edit back, or hand the record to something that only reads, before anything is written. RecordLike is the protocol, and WorkingRecord is a class, since there is one way to edit a record.

Edits accumulate and are written at once:

  • An edit costs a row in a staging table. A hundred edits to one attribute are a hundred rows, collapsed once when written. The first edit of an axis copies the base's resolved one into its table.
  • Nothing touches the record until edits is written as a child. A caller that fails halfway leaves no layer, and a caller that changes its mind calls rollback().

docs.title: The shape of an edit
docs.text:
Each edit maps onto exactly one part of the format:

edit writes key it targets set an attribute attributes/<attr>.parquet rows the attribute's coordinates set a property the whole dims/<dim>.parquet, one column of a row changed the dim's axis key set a multi-dim's property the whole dims/<multi-dim>.parquet, one column of a row changed the multi-dim's struct add labels or tuples the whole dims/<dim>.parquet, their rows added the dim's axis key remove labels or tuples the whole dims/<dim>.parquet without them, each multi-dim without its tuples the dim's axis key, the multi-dim's key

add and remove take any dim, a multi-dim among them, and an attribute's dims decide which coordinates its rows carry.

An edit is expressed in the format's own terms. Setting p_nom on twenty entities stages twenty attributes/p_nom.parquet rows, which is what a patch layer holds. A staged edit is already the row it will be written as, so writing edits is a concatenation.

docs.title: set
docs.text:
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # broadcast
w.set("p_nom", [150.0, 80.0], entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # per label
w.set("p_nom", {"wind1": 150.0, "wind2": 80.0})  # per label, keyed
w.set("p_max_pu", frame, entity=["wind1"])  # long frame
w.set("p_max_pu", series.rename_axis("snapshot"), entity=["wind1"])  # a series
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)  # every entity, loads included, now and later
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, ctype="Generator", carrier="wind")  # selected now
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="dc", bus="north")  # a connection
w.set("p_nom", 200.0, entity="wind1", scenario="high")  # scoped
w.set("entity.carrier", "solar", entity="g2")  # a property, by its subject
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")  # a property; `x` alone names an attribute

Every coordinate is a keyword, a multi-dim's coordinates included: entity=, snapshot=, bus="north" for one connection, from= and to= for one corridor. The schema declares which coordinates exist, so none has a parameter of its own. A keyword holds one label, which fixes that coordinate, or a list of labels, at each of which the value is staged.

A coordinate that no keyword names is NULL. By the broadcast rule, NULL is every label of the coordinate. So set("p_max_pu", 0.9) is one row that reaches every entity, loads and entities added in a later layer included. set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator") is one row per generator that exists now.

A later set replaces what it covers. It drops each row of the attribute that an earlier call staged and that one of its own rows covers. A new row covers an old one when, at every coordinate, it names the same label or is NULL, counting labels selected by a property keyword or a multi-dim's coordinates. So set("p_nom", 0.9, entity=["a"]) followed by set("p_nom", 0.95) stages one row, and a reads 0.95. The other order keeps both rows, and a reads 0.9, since within one layer the more specific row wins. A default set first keeps the exceptions set after it.

set packs a multi-dim's coordinates into its struct column, so entity="dc", bus="north" stages connection = {entity: dc, bus: north}. A multi-dim's value is a whole tuple or NULL, so every coordinate must be given or none. Omitting bus alone is refused, since {entity: dc, bus: NULL} names no tuple. Naming no coordinate stages the NULL struct, which is every tuple. A coordinate is named by its own name: a contract (from, to) over entity is addressed as from="plant", to="mill". entity= beside those coordinates is refused, since it could name either party.

A property as a keyword selects labels when set is called. A keyword is bare. It names a coordinate of the attribute first, else any property of a dim the attribute reaches, categorizing or not. So bus="north" on a connection attribute is the coordinate even where entity has a property bus. carrier="gas" on an attribute over the carrier dim is that dim, and on p_max_pu it is entity.carrier. A dotted keyword is refused, and so is a name that several dims the attribute reaches declare a property of. ctype="Generator", carrier="wind" resolves to the labels that match every keyword on the record as staged, and set writes one row per label. The filter itself is not stored, so a label added later is not reached. A plain NULL and default_by are the two ways a value reaches labels not yet added. The property's dim must be one the attribute reaches through exactly one coordinate, and the keyword is refused beside that coordinate's own keyword.

set writes a property too, a category included, when attribute names one as subject.name. A plain name is an attribute. Setting a property patches one column of its subject's axis rows and keeps the other columns. Its value is a mapping or series from label to value, a scalar with a dim= keyword naming the labels, or a scalar for every label the axis has. A multi-dim's property takes a scalar, with its coordinates as keywords selecting the tuples, none selecting every tuple: set("connection.role", "input", entity="g1", bus="north"). A coordinate is part of the key, not a property, so set("connection.bus", ...) is refused; the caller removes the tuples and adds them again. Changing a category is such a patch: set("entity.ctype", "Load", entity="g1"). Every value g1 holds stays stored and read, and the per-category reads of ctype="Load" now include those values.

value takes five forms, since assigning one value to many labels and a different value to each are equally ordinary:

value meaning keywords scalar staged at every listed combination an omitted coordinate broadcasts sequence aligned positionally exactly one list keyword, same length mapping keys are labels of one coordinate the one coordinate no keyword names series index is labels of one coordinate the index's own name, else the one coordinate no keyword names frame supplies its own keys single labels completing it

A frame is a DuckDB relation, or a pandas, polars or arrow frame. It reaches DuckDB through DuckDB's own scanner, and no scanner package is a dependency, so a frame of a library never imported is no frame. A relation on another connection is refused.

Each column is checked against the DuckDB type its dtype maps to (dtypes). A widening is cast: a smaller integer to BIGINT, a number to DOUBLE, a timestamp of any precision to TIMESTAMP, and text to the ENUM of a dim with one_of and back. The cast keeps the kind of value, though an integer past 2^53 rounds and a nanosecond truncates to the microsecond. Any other type is refused, naming the declared type, unless the column holds only NULLs. A column of timestamps with a time zone is refused.

A mapping's keys and a series' index may hold labels of any of the attribute's coordinates, since an axis label is a string like any other. The caller says which coordinate, by naming the series' index after it or by naming every other coordinate as a keyword. Where neither settles it, the call is refused. set never infers the coordinate from the labels. A test against the axis would make one call mean different things in two records: a scenario labelled wind1 would capture a series meant per entity, and a partial overlap would pick a reading silently.

A frame over a multi-dim carries it as the struct column, connection STRUCT(entity, bus). A frame that carries a coordinate flat, entity or bus, is refused with the struct to pass. So is a struct whose fields differ from the multi-dim's coordinates, which a cast would silently re-key. A struct with some fields NULL is refused too. A NULL struct broadcasts over every tuple.

The first four forms become a long frame before staging, so there is one staging path. A sequence whose length differs from its keyword's is an error at the call.

Every form is checked against the labels the record resolves, the frame included. A frame decides where the labels come from, and those labels must still exist.

docs.title: add / remove
docs.text:
w.add("carrier", ["wind", "H2"])
w.add("bus", ["north", "south"])
w.add("bus", ["north H2"], carrier="H2", x=10.1)  # bare: the dim's own
w.add("entity", ["g1", "g2"], ctype="Generator", carrier="wind")
w.remove("entity", ["old_coal"])
