w.remove("carrier", ["gas"])  # refused while entity.carrier holds it
w.add("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}], role="output")
w.add("connection", other.dims["connection"])  # the struct column `connection`
w.add("connection", frame)  # an `entity` and a `bus` column, `role` beside them
w.remove("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}])

add(dim, labels, **columns) stages whole axis rows. columns are the other columns of dims/<dim>.parquet: the dim's properties, bare since the subject is dim. Each is a scalar for every label or a sequence aligned to labels. A column no keyword names is NULL on these rows, since add restates a label's row whole. A new label goes after the axis's last, and a removed label of the base goes back to its base position. A label of a dim with one_of must be one of those it lists, both in add(dim, ...) and as the value of a property that refers to the dim. The axis of such a dim holds only the labels added. A property value that one_of lists and the axis lacks is refused as any unknown label is, and remove takes such a label as it takes any other. An attribute keyword is refused with a pointer to set, since an attribute's values are long rows whatever its dims. A column the schema does not declare is refused. A staging table is shaped like the file it becomes, so it has no dtype for such a column. A tool that grows a column declares it first, which schema versioning accepts as a widening.

A label exists by virtue of its axis row, so add is an edit of its own. Validation refuses a value for a label no layer declares. Adding a bus with no properties is an edit with nothing to set. One axis row holds each label, so an add of a label the record already resolves restates its row.

A multi-dim's labels are tuples, which add and remove take as a frame or a list. A frame, anything DuckDB scans, holds the multi-dim's struct column, connection STRUCT(entity, bus), which is what dims["connection"] reads, so a read goes back in as it stands. A frame may instead carry one column per coordinate, entity and bus. A frame carrying both the struct column and a coordinate column is refused, since it gives each tuple twice. Either frame may carry property columns beside the tuples, and beside a frame a keyword property must be a scalar. A list of mappings from coordinate to label, such as {"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}, takes its properties as keywords, each a scalar or a sequence aligned to the list. The list is made into a frame with a column per coordinate up front, and the struct column is unpacked to the same, so every form takes the same path and the same type checks. The coordinates are packed into the multi-dim's struct column, and each tuple is staged as one row of dims/<multi-dim>.parquet, placed as any label is. A tuple with a coordinate missing or NULL is refused, since it names no tuple. A tuple naming a label that its coordinate's axis, as staged, lacks is refused (validation). A multi-dim's attributes are long rows, set through set with its coordinates as keywords.

Adding a component with its connections and varying values is add of the entity, then add of its connections, then a set per attribute.

remove(dim, labels) deletes each label's row from the staged axis. It need not list what it deletes. Where dim is partial, the fold drops every value keyed by the label, and a multi-dim attribute's value through the label inside its struct (the owner map). remove also deletes every tuple, of any multi-dim, with a coordinate drawing on dim that names one of labels. It reads those tuples from the record as it resolves with pending edits, so the writer never meets a dangling tuple. An add of the same label brings back the label alone, and its tuples come back through an add of each multi-dim.

remove is refused while a property that refers to dim stores one of the labels, read from the record as staged. A tuple goes with its label, and a property's row belongs to its subject and outlives the label. The caller sets such a property to another label or None first.

docs.title: Edits
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord does not write. It holds two things that the writers take:

w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.set("p_nom", 100.0, entity=["gen1"])
edited = rev.child(w.edits)  # the delta, as a child layer
ws.write(w, "out/")  # base plus edits, flattened
w.rollback()
  • w.edits is the staged layer alone, the LayerData it already is. Written as a child of the revision w was built over, it holds only the edits: the attribute rows it set, and each axis it changed, a multi-dim's included, restated whole. The fold resolves the rest from the parent. The layer lands in the child, so the revision that child returns reads the edits back.
  • w itself is what is staged plus what the record already reads: the whole resolved record. It is written as a standalone directory, where there is no parent to resolve against.

The writer has one contract for both: enumerate what the source holds and hand each part over. The caller chooses the rows to write, w.edits or w. The caller names the parent, which is the revision w was built from. rollback() clears the staging area. A write clears nothing, so a WorkingRecord that still holds its edits reads exactly what it did before.

other.child(w.edits), with w built over a different revision, would write a delta computed against the wrong parent, since an axis edit restates its base's whole axis. child therefore compares the edits' base revision with its own id and raises on a mismatch. Edits over a directory have no revision as their base, so they are a child of none. rev.child(w) writes the whole resolved record as a child layer. That layer reads back correctly and is larger than the delta, so edits is the name to use.

An edited axis, a multi-dim's included, is restated whole, whatever partial says. The layer holds every label the axis has with the edits applied, with its properties, in axis order. A layer's axis file then says what the axis is there, and reads without its parent (removing labels). A standalone write of w writes the resolved axis whole as well, and an axis nothing touched is written by neither.

An edit replaces the rows it names. It deletes the rows at the coordinate it writes and inserts the new ones, so a staging table holds one row per coordinate and reads without a fold. The coordinate it replaces on is the one a read would have collapsed, so the delete removes at least what a last-writer-wins fold would have discarded. An attribute's set also deletes every earlier row it covers. A property of an axis, a multi-dim's included, differs in mechanism and has the same effect. A row's columns are independently editable, so a property set patches its one column in place (UPDATE), which keeps a sibling property that another set wrote.

An edit replaces per coordinate. The ownership key leaves out the dims an attribute is not owned per, so replacing on it would collapse a whole staged series to one row. Two edits at different snapshots are two coordinates. The same distinction governs the read overlay and the fill below, and it is the easiest thing here to get wrong.

Three interactions go beyond replacing by coordinate:

  • remove after set on the same label: the removal wins, since a removed label has no values. A removal reaches another file's rows, so it stays an anti-join at read and at write. Attribute rows are keyed by coordinate, and the axis by label. A layer's removals apply only to its parents in the fold, so the staged collapse drops its own rows itself. It drops a row that names a label the staged axis removed, and a row whose multi-dim column names a tuple the staged multi-dim removed, by remove of the tuple or by the cascade of remove on a label. set refuses a label the staged axis lacks (validation), so a removal after the set is the only way a staged row comes to name one.
  • add after remove of the same label: the label exists again, at its base position. The staged axis then holds it as the base does, so the parent's values for it come back. Its tuples stay removed.
  • set on a label this record also added: the attribute rows live in attributes/, and a property patches the staged row.

Along an axis outside partial, a layer must carry a label's whole extent. So a set of one value along such an axis reads the resolved series for that key and stages the untouched coordinates beside the edit. That is the one read of parent data an edit makes. It happens when the rows are staged, so the staging table already holds what the layer will hold, and a write of edits has no completion step.

The fill covers the key the edit named. A label no edit mentioned keeps its rows in the parent, since a layer that carried them would claim an extent it was never given. A multi-dim outside partial is owned whole the same way. A set on one connection's efficiency stages every other connection's resolved value beside it. A connection attribute's key names no label of a partial dim, so the key the edit named is (attribute) alone. A staged row that leaves the axis NULL needs no fill, since the broadcast rule already makes it cover every label, and a carried row beside it would overlap. Where a base row names a label of that axis and the staged row reaches it, the staged row is also written out along the base row's labels there, with the staged value. The two rows would otherwise cross on a dim the owner map has no column for, which no overlap row settles. Carried rows go in only where no edit holds the coordinate, so a later set on a carried coordinate replaces the fill. The anti-join that keeps a fill off an occupied coordinate is the whole of what orders the two.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The writer validates structure, so writing edits inherits its checks. Editing adds checks at the edit, caught when the edit is staged, so a caller learns about a typo at the line that typed it:

  • an undeclared attribute, property or keyword, or a keyword the attribute does not vary over; a plain name that only properties carry is refused naming their dotted forms, so set("carrier", …) suggests bus.carrier and entity.carrier;
  • a label that its dim's axis, as staged, lacks, for every dim, partial or not; add the label first;
  • a tuple that its multi-dim, as staged, lacks, in set; add the tuple first;
  • a tuple that names a label which its coordinate's axis, as staged, lacks, in add or set, naming the multi-dim, the coordinate and up to three such labels; set checks this before the tuple itself, so a set at a connection with an unknown bus names the bus;
  • a label that a dim with one_of does not list, in add or set;
  • a frame column whose type does not fit its dtype, timestamps with a time zone among them; by the same rule a label given to set, add or remove, or a value of a property that refers to a dim, so a string is not parsed into a datetime dim's label;
  • a value of a property that refers to a dim that is no label of the dim as staged, in add or set, such as set("entity.carrier", "coal", entity="g1") with no carrier label coal; NULL names no label and passes;
  • an add that names an attribute.

Each label and tuple check is one DuckDB query that anti-joins the staged rows against the axis as staged, for every checked column at once.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
Staged rows live in DuckDB tables on the record's own connection:

CREATE TABLE staged_attributes_<attr digest>_<id> (<that attribute's long columns>);
CREATE TABLE staged_axis_<dim digest>_<id>        (<the axis key>, <the dim's properties>, <position>);

<id> is the staged layer's own id, so two WorkingRecords on one connection share no table. An attribute or dim name is a caller's string, so the table name carries a digest of it.

Every table is shaped like the file it becomes. An axis table adds only a position column, since a DuckDB table keeps no row order. No table unions columns that the format keeps apart, so a column the schema does not declare has no table to go in, and add refuses it.

There is one table per staged attribute, since that is the file it becomes. Its columns are the attribute's own coordinates, and value has the attribute's declared type. A shared table would have to widen value to text and carry every declared dim. The value would then need casting back on the way out. A NULL in a dim column would also be ambiguous between an attribute without that axis and the broadcast rule's every value. Per attribute, the table's shape answers both questions.

There is one table per staged axis, a multi-dim's keyed by its struct column, holding it whole as a layer restates it: its key, its properties and a position column. The first edit copies the base's resolved axis into it in base order. add appends a new label at the next position and puts a label of the base back at its base position. remove deletes the label's row, and a property set patches one column in place. The writer and the reads take each table in position order.

These tables are the only place a staged row exists, and the reads fold them directly.

DuckDB holds the staged rows for three reasons. The reads are already a fold, and staging elsewhere would marshal every edit into a relation on every read. A large edit is a bulk insert. A write of edits hands each table to the writer as the file it already is.

The tables live in the workspace's database, like the folded caches, so on :memory: they vanish with the workspace and never reach disk. A record whose edits must survive a process boundary is written as a child.

An edit replaces what it names, so a table holds one row per key and reads as a scan. An attribute's table has no ordering column, and edit order is which edit ran last.

docs.title: Reading with pending edits
docs.text:
The read members reflect the edits, so a set followed by a read returns the new value.

A set of pending edits is a layer that is not yet written. The reads compose it the same way: the staged rows are the last layer, resolved over whatever the record read before.

resolved = fold(parent layers..., staged rows)

This is one more fold step over the same owner-map machinery, with the staging tables in place of a layer directory. A broadcast of the base reaches a label staged here, since the fold keeps it NULL (what a row reaches). A staged layer has met no writer, so the read refuses two staged rows that cross with no staged row naming both, as the write of edits would. It works over a layered base and a plain directory alike, since a directory is a layer laid out like any other. It costs what one more layer costs, on every read. A written layer is folded once and cached, and the staged layer cannot be, since it is the only one that can still change. So the fold is materialised up to the last layer that cannot change under the reader, and the staged step on top stays a relation. An edit then needs no invalidation, since nothing that depends on it is cached.

flags come from the map rows the staged layer folds to, as for any layer. A staged row that sets a dim adds it to varies, one that leaves it NULL adds it to broadcast, and a staged curve sets breakpoints. Properties are read from properties, staged edits included.

A staged axis is read as its table stands, in position order. The table already holds the base's rows with the edits applied, so a read composes nothing. Two set calls for two properties of one label compose, each patching its own column of the row.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
RecordLike is the protocol that a reader codes against, and a framework object can satisfy it structurally. Record is the class that implements it. A record hands back DuckDB relations for dims, properties and attributes, built lazily so that listing them costs no I/O. flags reports which axes an attribute's rows set or leave NULL, so a consumer can plan containers before fetching anything. DuckDB is the one engine from fold to consumer.

@runtime_checkable
class RecordLike(Protocol):
    """Dimensioned attribute data with a declared schema."""

    @property
    def schema(self) -> Schema: ...  # dims, properties, attributes, partial

    @property
    def dims(self) -> Relations: ...  # axis key columns, keyed by dim
    @property
    def properties(self) -> Relations: ...  # stored property values, keyed by subject
    @property
    def attributes(self) -> Relations: ...  # long relations, keyed by attribute

    def flags(self, **categories: str | Sequence[str]) -> dict[str, Flags]: ...

A signature annotates against RecordLike, and a framework object satisfies it without depending on this package. Record is the interface over one fold, and Revision.record and Workspace.at(uri) both return one. The class has the short name because a caller constructs and holds it. The protocol is read-only. Writing goes through store.root(source), rev.child(source) or ws.write(source, uri), and the record format is how a record is stored.

Each accessor holds one section of the schema: dims the labels, properties the metadata of those labels, and attributes the data. What a name is declared as decides where its values are read.

A multi-dim reads as any dim does. dims["connection"] is its key column alone, the struct connection STRUCT(entity, bus), one row per tuple in member order. Its properties are in properties["connection"], connection | role.

docs.title: Properties and categories
docs.text:
A property holds one value per label of its subject, a dim or a multi-dim, as a column of the subject's file.

properties[subject] is the subject's key with every property declared for it, as stored. It is a record-wide view, NULL wherever no layer wrote a value. It has a key for each subject that declares properties, and its columns are the properties' plain names, since the relation already names the subject.

A property of a dim in partial that refers to a dim with one_of categorizes its dim. One category's labels are properties[dim] filtered on it, with every property of the dim. Schema.default_for gives a property's default: default_by per category, else default. A framework's static frame, such as PyPSA's n.generators, is that frame with defaults applied, joined with the entity-only rows of its attributes. A per-category read that applies the defaults itself waits until a caller needs one.

A category selects labels. A label whose category changes keeps what it held, and a per-category read judges it by its current categories.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Relations = Mapping[str, DuckDBPyRelation]

A Record hands back bare DuckDB relations, each a plan on the record's connection. Every record is DuckDB underneath, so a value handed over as itself costs no wrapping per read, and a caller who wants SQL needs no unwrapping. A consumer filters, joins and aggregates with relation calls or SQL, and fetches with .df(), .pl() or .to_arrow_table().

An attribute's relation holds its rows as written, in no promised order. A NULL coordinate stays NULL, and two rows may cover one coordinate, of one layer or of two. The consumer settles each coordinate by the broadcast rule: the row naming every dim the others there name wins, as settle does. The record guarantees such a row wherever two rows cross (resolution), so a consumer needs no knowledge of layers or of partial.

LazyRelations builds each relation on first access. Building a relation is itself I/O: read_parquet opens the file to read the footer that binds the relation's columns. Locally that is a page-cache hit. Against a remote record it is a round trip per attribute, so a consumer that wants three of forty attributes pays for three, and listing the keys pays for none.

Laziness saves I/O. An unmaterialised relation is a query plan, so holding every attribute's relation at once costs little memory either way. Fetching is the expense, and the consumer decides when to fetch.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flags say which axes an attribute's rows use, so a consumer can plan its reads before opening a file.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Flags:
    varies: frozenset[str]  # dims some row of this attribute sets
    broadcast: frozenset[str]  # dims some row leaves NULL, i.e. "all values"
    breakpoints: bool  # any row carries a breakpoint

flags() answers for the whole record in one query, keyed by attribute. Only attributes with rows are present, so set(record.flags()) also says which attributes the record has.

flags(**categories) answers for one category. The keywords are categorizing properties of one dim by their plain names, such as ctype="Generator", each with one category or a list (categories). Only rows that reach a matching label count: a row naming it through the dim's own column or a multi-dim's single coordinate drawing on the dim, and a row leaving that column NULL, which reaches every label or tuple. An attribute is present where such a row exists. Keywords that categorize several dims are refused, and so is a multi-dim that draws on the dim through two coordinates, since a row would then count towards no single label.

The sets name dims, so a consumer asks about a named axis: "timestep" in flags["p_max_pu"].varies. breakpoints is a boolean, since a breakpoint is an abscissa within one row's value and no axis (wide and long rows).

varies and broadcast can overlap. An attribute may have per-timestep rows for one entity and a single NULL-timestep row for another, so timestep is in both. That tells the consumer to use both containers. timestep in broadcast selects the NULL-timestep rows into a constant frame, and timestep in varies selects the rest into a series frame. For one label the two sets would be complements, and the union over many labels is what makes the pair informative. For the same reason a framework asks per category: a Generator's per-timestep rows and a Link's single row, unioned, describe neither.

varies | broadcast tests whether an attribute touches a dim at all. Both sets empty for a dim means the attribute has no values along it, so the consumer builds no container there.

Both sets cover only the dims an attribute is addressed by, multi-dims included. A dim outside its dims is in neither set. The source the flags aggregate, such as the owner map, a scan of attributes/ or a staging table, is one relation over every attribute. A dim one attribute uses reads NULL in the rows of another attribute that lacks it, and that NULL means the axis does not exist for that attribute. Counting it as broadcast would mislead every consumer into building a constant container along an axis with no values.

p_nom set per entity puts entity in varies, and a single entity = NULL row puts it in broadcast. The flags describe the rows the record holds, so a broadcast that more specific rows shadow at every label still puts its dim in broadcast.

flags covers attributes alone. Properties are columns of their subject's file, read from properties.

docs.title: Settling rows
docs.text:
settle(rel, labels, flags), exported as from datarecord import settle, settles an attribute's rows as written by the broadcast rule, one row per coordinate. A row NULL on a coordinate in labels takes each label there, and a row naming a label outside labels, or reaching none, is dropped. At each coordinate the row naming every coordinate in labels that the other rows there name is kept, and where none does the query fails, naming the coordinate. A coordinate outside labels is kept as written, a NULL there being one more label, so a constant p_max_pu stays one row with snapshot NULL. filter=False keeps a row naming a label outside labels as written, for a caller whose own joins on the labels drop it anyway.

flags spares the work a record does not need, and flags overstating the rows change no value. Only a coordinate in broadcast is expanded, and rows are picked only where one is in varies as well. Elsewhere every row names the same coordinates, one row per key, and settle keeps those naming a passed label.

The rule needs no knowledge of layers, so settle lives in core and reads a plain directory as it reads a tree.

docs.title: One engine
docs.text:
The protocol names DuckDB: a RecordLike answers DuckDBPyRelations. A tool's record builds them on the caller's connection, as the PyPSA tool scans its pandas frames with con.from_df. A RecordLike therefore needs DuckDB, which is the cost of one representation from fold to consumer.

The resolution engine has no abstraction layer either. The owner-map fold is relational algebra of real complexity, and an engine interface with one implementation behind it costs effort for a second engine that does not exist.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
There are three ways to write: store.root, rev.child and ws.write. Each one writes one layer from a LayerData source and returns what it made. The writer casts every column to its declared type. It refuses rows that do not fit the schema or that name labels the layer's axes lack, and it refuses an axis whose order differs from its parent's. A tree write puts the revision file last, so a layer becomes reachable only once it is complete. A standalone directory gets its manifest last for the same reason.

store.root(source) -> Revision  # a new root with this layer
rev.child(source) -> Revision  # a new child of rev with this layer
ws.write(source, uri) -> Record  # a standalone directory, read back

There is one call per destination, and each is named for what it returns. A tree write needs the location and the tree, a directory write needs only a connection, and the two return different things. child lives on the parent, so the call names the store once. Its name says that it makes something new, since layers are write-once and rev itself never changes.

docs.title: A write makes a new layer
docs.text:
Each call writes source as a new layer. An existing layer directory is an error, so a write never half-replaces what a record holds. ws.write refuses anything that already exists at uri: locally the path, even an empty directory, and remotely any key under it.

The writer looks up keys one at a time and writes each file before it builds the next. A lazily-building source therefore does one read per file written. Locally, the layer is staged into a sibling directory and renamed on success, so a frame that fails validation leaves no layer. Remotely, a failed write can leave part of a layer, which nothing reaches without the revision file or the manifest written after it.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: The writer casts every column that the schema declares a type for, so a record's files carry the schema's types and a reader can trust them. It holds each column to its dtype as set holds a frame's. A wider type of the same kind is cast. A column of only NULLs passes, whatever type its dataframe library guessed. Any other type is refused, naming the attribute, property or dim and its dtype.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
Each attribute file is checked against its AttributeSpec. An attribute that the schema does not declare is refused. Its dims say which columns its file carries, so an undeclared attribute has no shape to write it in. A frame must carry its attribute's own coordinates, and the writer refuses one that lacks any of them. It also refuses a frame that carries a coordinate the attribute is not addressed by. The read path projects only the attribute's own coordinates, so such a column would be written and never read. A source that emits one disagrees with the schema about the attribute, and the error reports that disagreement. A multi-dim's column must be its struct, with exactly its coordinates as fields. Two rows of one attribute that cover one coordinate are refused when both name the same dims, or when each names a dim the other leaves NULL and no row there names both, naming the attribute and the coordinate. A record holding rows of several layers, written whole by ws.write(w, uri), passes: wherever two of its rows cross, it holds the row naming both (crossing rows). A child layer that leaves a dim outside partial NULL over a parent row naming it, with no row naming the dim there, is refused by the fold rather than the writer (a dim outside partial).

A dims/ file of a declared dim must carry the dim's key column, the struct column named for it for a multi-dim.

docs.title: Axes and labels
docs.text:
A dims/ file is the whole axis at the new revision, a multi-dim's tuples included, in order (removing labels). The writer refuses a file that holds a key twice, or that carries a column other than its key and its subject's declared properties. It refuses a file that orders its parent's labels differently from the parent, naming the first label out of place, since a consumer numbers ports by that order.

Every row must name labels and tuples that the layer keeps:

  • an attribute row that names a label which the layer's final axis of its dim lacks is refused, naming the dim and up to three such labels;
  • an attribute row at a tuple which the layer's final multi-dim lacks is refused the same way, naming the multi-dim;
  • a multi-dim's tuple that names a label which the layer's final axis of its coordinate's dim lacks is refused, naming the multi-dim, the coordinate and up to three such labels.

The final axis is the layer's own file, else its parent's resolved one. One DuckDB query per file anti-joins its rows against the final axis of every column it names. A layer written by hand or by a tool therefore holds values only at labels and tuples some axis holds, as set holds a staged one. The checks on properties that refer to a dim, and on labels a layer removes, are on removing labels.

docs.title: LayerData
docs.text:
The writer reads one protocol, LayerData: the rows of one layer, enumerated and read.

@runtime_checkable
class LayerData(Protocol):
    @property
    def schema(self) -> Schema: ...

    def axes(self) -> set[str]: ...
    def axis(self, dim: str) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...
    def attributes(self) -> set[str]: ...
    def attribute(self, name: str) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...

Each pair is an enumerator of the keys of one kind and a read for one key. An axis is the rows of its file: every label the axis has at the layer's revision, in order, with the dim's properties. A multi-dim's axis is every tuple it has there, keyed by its struct column.

schema decides which of the other pairs are populated: axes and axis answer only for the dims it declares. An enumerator answers the empty set where the schema declares nothing of that kind. Rows are DuckDBPyRelations, as a RecordLike's are, so the write path runs on one engine throughout.

A LayerSource answers axis and attribute for its own layer's rows. A staged layer's own rows, w.edits, are such a source, so a WorkingRecord hands its edits to the writer as they are.

A RecordLike is no LayerData. This holds for a Record, a WorkingRecord among them, and for a framework object such as Tool.to_datarecord returns. The writer wraps a RecordLike in a thin adapter that reads its Relations mappings through the same enumerate-and-read pairs, so the writer has one code path. The adapter takes each value as set does: a relation on the writer's connection, or a pandas, polars or arrow frame that DuckDB scans. A WorkingRecord is read through a pinned copy that folds its staged edits once for the write.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
These pages show how to use the package, organised by task. Design states what a record is and why. API Reference holds the generated signatures.

page what it covers Reading a record the RecordLike protocol, properties, flags Declaring a schema dims, multi-dims, properties and attributes Editing WorkingRecord: set, add, edits Branching and layers revisions, branching, materialising, writing a layer Storage workspaces, stores, files local and remote, processes The PyPSA tool consuming a record from PyPSA and writing results back

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord is a record plus pending edits, held in DuckDB tables and not yet written anywhere. It is a Record, so it reads as the data with its pending edits applied. You can read an edit back, or hand the record to something that only reads, before writing it (design).

from datarecord import WorkingRecord

w = WorkingRecord(root.record)

docs.title: set
docs.text:
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # broadcast
w.set("p_nom", [150.0, 80.0], entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # per label, positional
w.set("p_nom", {"wind1": 150.0, "wind2": 80.0})  # per label, keyed
w.set(
    "p_max_pu", frame, entity=["wind1"]
)  # a long frame: pandas, polars, arrow, a relation
w.set("p_max_pu", series.rename_axis("snapshot"), entity="wind1")  # a series
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)  # every entity, loads included, now and later
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator")  # every generator there is now
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, ctype="Generator", carrier="wind")  # the ones there are now
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="dc", bus="north")  # a connection
w.set("p_nom", 200.0, entity="wind1", scenario="high")  # scoped to one scenario
w.set("entity.carrier", "solar", entity="g2")  # a property, by its subject
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")  # a property; `x` alone names an attribute

Every coordinate is a keyword, a multi-dim's coordinates included. bus="north" with entity="dc" addresses one connection, and from= with to= one corridor. A coordinate that no keyword names is NULL, which means every label of it: every entity, loads included, and entities added later. A multi-dim value is a whole tuple, so you give all of its coordinates or none (design).

A property as a keyword selects labels at call time. A keyword is bare: it names a coordinate of the attribute first, else any property of a dim the attribute reaches. ctype="Generator", carrier="wind" stages one row per label that matches both, on the record as staged. A label added later is not reached, and a plain NULL is how a value reaches such labels. A name that several reached dims declare a property of is refused, so set it per dim.

A multi-period snapshot carries its period as snapshot.period, which names a label of period. It carries its timestep as snapshot.timestep, which names a label of the datetime dim timestep (design).

w.add("period", [2030, 2040])
w.add("timestep", [t0, t1])
w.add(
    "snapshot", [0, 1, 2, 3], period=[2030, 2030, 2040, 2040], timestep=[t0, t1, t0, t1]
)
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, entity="g1", period=2030)  # snapshots 0 and 1
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.5, entity="g1", timestep=t0)  # snapshots 0 and 2
w.set("snapshot.period", {3: 2030})
w.remove("period", [2040])  # refused while a snapshot.period names it

A mapping's keys or a series' index are labels of the one coordinate that no keyword names, unless the series' index is named after a coordinate. Where neither says which coordinate, the call is refused.

set writes properties too, a category included, each named by its subject. set("entity.ctype", "Load", entity="g1") patches one column of g1's axis row. A plain name is an attribute. set("carrier", ...) in a schema where only properties are called carrier is refused, and the error suggests bus.carrier and entity.carrier.

A multi-dim's property takes a scalar, and its coordinates as keywords select the tuples it patches, none selecting every tuple. A coordinate is part of the key, so set("connection.bus", ...) is refused: remove the tuple and add it anew.

w.set("connection.role", "input", entity="dc", bus="north")
w.set("connection.bus", "south", entity="dc")  # refused: a coordinate is the key

docs.title: add / remove
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

w.add("carrier", ["wind"])
w.add("bus", ["north", "south"])
w.add("ctype", ["Generator", "Link"])
w.add("entity", ["wind1", "wind2"], ctype="Generator", carrier="wind")
w.add("entity", ["dc"], ctype="Link")
w.set("p_nom", [100.0, 80.0], entity=["wind1", "wind2"])

w.remove("entity", ["old_coal"])

w.add(
    "connection",
    [{"entity": "dc", "bus": "north"}, {"entity": "dc", "bus": "south"}],
    role=["bus0", "bus1"],
)
w.add("connection", pd.DataFrame({"entity": ["wind1"], "bus": ["north"]}))
w.add("connection", other.dims["connection"])  # another record's tuples, as read
w.remove("connection", [{"entity": "dc", "bus": "south"}])

add(dim, labels, **columns) works on any dim. The keywords are the axis file's other columns, the dim's properties, bare. Each is a scalar or a sequence aligned to labels. An attribute keyword is refused, since attributes go through set whatever their dims (design). A label exists by virtue of its axis row, so add is an edit of its own: adding a bus with no properties sets nothing.

remove(dim, labels) takes the labels out of the staged axis. It need not list what it deletes. The fold applies it to every value keyed by the label, and remove also takes every tuple that names one of the labels out of its multi-dim, with the tuple's values (design). remove("bus", ["north"]) removes every connection at north.

A layer restates each axis it changes whole, a multi-dim's included: every label the base has, with the edits applied, in the base's order, then the labels it adds. An add of a label that remove took out puts it back where the base has it. remove is refused while a property that refers to the dim still stores one of the labels, such as entity.carrier naming gas. That row belongs to its subject and outlives the label, so set it to another label or None first (design).

On a multi-dim, add and remove take tuples. A frame DuckDB scans gives them in the struct column named for the multi-dim, as dims["connection"] reads it, or with one column per coordinate instead, but not both; it may carry a column per property, and beside it a property keyword must be a scalar. A tuple is also a mapping from coordinate to label, and a list of them takes each property keyword as a scalar or a sequence aligned to the list. A tuple with a coordinate missing or NULL is refused, as is one naming a label its coordinate's dim lacks, so add the label first (design).

docs.title: Inspecting and rolling back
docs.text:
w.attributes["p_nom"]  # the edit applied, over the base's rows
w.properties["entity"]  # additions in, removals out
w.rollback()  # discard everything staged

You read what you staged from the record itself, which answers with the edits applied (design). Staged rows live in DuckDB tables on the record's connection, so they vanish with it and never touch disk (design).

docs.title: Writing the edits
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord does not write. The record stays unchanged until you hand its edits to a writer (design):

new = root.child(w.edits)  # a patch layer under a new child of the base
ws.write(w, "out/")  # a standalone record, flattened
w.rollback()  # clear the staging area, if you are done

w.edits holds only the edits: the attribute rows set, and each axis changed, restated whole. The fold resolves the rest from the parent. w itself is the resolved result, what is staged plus what the record already reads. A standalone directory needs that, since it has no parent to resolve against.

The edits are a delta against the revision w was built over, so child raises if you write them under another one. Layers are write-once, so the layer lands in the new child (design). The returned revision reads the edits back:

new.record.attributes["p_nom"].df()

Writing clears nothing: a WorkingRecord that still holds its edits reads exactly what it did before, until rollback().

An edit replaces the rows it names, so restating a coordinate overwrites it and the last write stands. A remove after a set wins regardless of order, since a removed label has no values. An add after a remove brings the label back with its parent's values and without the multi-dim tuples that named it.

A base's results are attributes and carry like any other. A child written from edits inherits them, though an edited input may no longer support them. The tool writes a solve's results as a layer of its own (tools).

Edit-level mistakes are caught when the edit is staged, so a typo is reported at the line that typed it (design).

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
A Revision is a node in a tree of layers. Each revision adds one layer, and it reads as that layer over its ancestors' layers, a deeper layer's row winning where it crosses a shallower one (design).

from datarecord import Workspace

store = Workspace().store("/data/my-record")

root = store.root(source)  # a new revision, with `source` as its layer
child = root.child(patch)  # branch off it, with `patch` as its layer
record = child.record  # the resolved tree, as a `Record`

A revision exists only by writing its layer, so there is no empty revision.

Each revision is a file under revisions/ beside layers/, so a location alone is enough to find the tree. A Revision serialises as its id, its parent and its store's location (design).

A layer's data is write-once, so any revision may be a parent and no cache needs invalidating (design). Branching is several children that share a parent by pointing at it.

docs.title: Reading across layers
docs.text:
An attribute reads as its rows as written, and the more specific row wins at each coordinate. Where a child's row crosses a parent's, the child also holds a row naming both, so that row wins there (design):

w.set("x", 50.0, entity="gas")  # the root
w.set("x", 100.0, entity="wind")
v.set("x", 999.0, scenario="high")  # its child
child.record.attributes["x"]
# (gas, NULL) 50, (wind, NULL) 100, (NULL, high) 999, (gas, high) 999, (wind, high) 999

A broadcast reaches every label the record holds, including one added below a materialised revision or staged in a WorkingRecord:

c = rev.child(w.edits)  # w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)
c.materialise()
w = WorkingRecord(c.record)
w.add("entity", ["n"], ctype="Generator")
w.attributes["p_max_pu"]  # (NULL) 0.9, which n takes by the broadcast rule

A constant set over a parent's series is written out along the series' snapshots, so it wins at each of them (design):

w.set("p_max_pu", [0.2, 0.5], snapshot=[0, 1])  # the root, every entity
v.set("p_max_pu", 0.9, entity="wind")  # its child
# the child holds (wind, NULL), (wind, 0) and (wind, 1) at 0.9

docs.title: Materialising
docs.text:
materialise() writes a revision's owner map and resolved axes under layers/<id>/resolved/. A descendant's read then stops there and walks no further towards the root. Materialising is a policy that you apply when you choose. It changes no answer, only how many layers a read touches (design):

child.materialise()

docs.title: Navigating
docs.text:
revision = store.revision(uuid)  # load one by id
store.revisions()  # every revision, unordered
revision.ancestry()  # the ids from the root to this revision
store.layer(uuid)  # one layer read alone

docs.title: Writing a whole record
docs.text:
root = store.root(source)  # a new root revision with this layer
child = root.child(source)  # a new child of root with this layer
record = ws.write(source, "out/")  # a standalone directory, read back

source is a LayerData or anything satisfying RecordLike, including a framework object that presents itself as a record. Read and write therefore meet at one interface (design). An existing layer directory is an error. Locally, the writer stages the layer into a sibling path and renames it on success, so a source that fails validation leaves no layer (design).

The writer casts every column the schema declares a type for, so a record's files carry the schema's types and a reader can trust them. Each attribute file must carry exactly its attribute's own coordinates. An attribute the schema does not declare is refused, and so is a column the attribute is not addressed by. Each row must name labels and tuples that the layer's final axes hold, a multi-dim's tuples included.

docs.title: The Record protocol
docs.text:
A consumer codes against the read-only RecordLike protocol. A plain directory, a hundred-layer tree, a record with pending edits and a framework's own object all satisfy it, and a consumer cannot tell which it holds (design).

record.schema  # what may exist: the axes, the properties, the attributes
record.dims["entity"]  # axis labels, keyed by dim
record.dims["connection"]  # a multi-dim's tuples, as one struct column
record.properties["entity"]  # stored property values, keyed by dim
record.attributes["p_max_pu"]  # long relations, results included, keyed by attribute
record.flags(ctype="Generator")  # which axes each attribute actually uses

Every value is a duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation on record.con, which is a query plan. Nothing is read until you fetch it with .df(), .pl() or .to_arrow_table(), and listing the keys reads nothing (design).

entities = record.properties["entity"]
gens = entities.filter("ctype = 'Generator'").df()
p_nom = record.attributes["p_nom"].filter("value > 0").df()

docs.title: Labels and properties
docs.text:
dims[dim] is the axis's label column alone, in axis order. A multi-period snapshot's period is a property of the snapshot (design):

record.dims["snapshot"]  # snapshot
record.properties["snapshot"]  # snapshot | period | timestep

A multi-dim's labels are its tuples, so dims["connection"] is the one struct column connection STRUCT(entity, bus), in its own order (design):

record.dims["connection"]  # connection
record.properties["connection"]  # connection | role

properties[subject] is a dim's key with every property declared for it, as stored. A NULL there is a value no layer wrote.

A categorizing property is a property of a partial dim that refers to a dim with one_of. One category's labels are properties[dim] filtered on that property, with every property of the dim. Schema.default_for("entity.sign", **categories) gives an unset property's default, default_by per category included. It names the property by its subject and the categories by their plain names, as the frame's columns are (design).

docs.title: Wide and long
docs.text:
dims and properties are wide, with one row per label or tuple. attributes are long, with one row per value:

<coordinate> ... | attribute | breakpoint | value

attributes holds every attribute in long rows, whatever its dims, so p_nom over entity alone has the same layout as p_max_pu. The coordinates are the attribute's own (design). p_nom has entity, a connection attribute such as efficiency has one connection struct column, and an attribute addressed by another axis alone has no entity column.

A NULL in a coordinate column means every label of that dim (design). A constant p_max_pu is one row with timestep = NULL, and a varying one is a row per timestep. One p_max_pu row with entity = NULL reaches every entity, loads included. A multi-dim's struct column broadcasts the same way: a NULL connection means every connection. breakpoint carries the abscissa of a piecewise-linear value.

attributes shows stored rows only, in no promised order. Two rows may cover one coordinate, of one layer or of two, and the row naming every dim the others there name gives its value. A consumer settles them with settle, as settling rows shows. A coordinate that no row covers takes the attribute's default, which Schema.default_for(name, **categories) gives per category.

An attribute row holds no property, so attributes["p_max_pu"] holds every entity's rows together. To scope it to one category, join properties["entity"], filtered on the category, on entity.

docs.title: flags
docs.text:
flags() says which axes each attribute's rows use, across the record in one query, so a consumer can plan its reads before opening a file. flags(**categories) answers for one category of one dim, and counts only rows that reach a matching label:

flags = record.flags(ctype="Generator")
set(flags)  # which attributes generators have at all
"timestep" in flags["p_max_pu"].varies  # some row sets it
"timestep" in flags["p_max_pu"].broadcast  # some row leaves it NULL
flags["marginal_cost"].breakpoints  # some row carries a curve

A dim can be in both sets. Then some labels carry a per-timestep series and others a single constant row, and the consumer uses both containers (design).

docs.title: Settling rows
docs.text:
attributes gives rows as written, so a consumer applies the broadcast rule itself. settle(rel, labels, flags) does it in one query, and flags tells it how little it needs to do (design):

from datarecord import settle

flags = record.flags(ctype="Generator")
gens = record.properties["entity"].filter("ctype = 'Generator'").select("entity")
p_max_pu = settle(record.attributes["p_max_pu"], {"entity": gens}, flags["p_max_pu"])

labels names the coordinates to settle, each with a relation of its labels in a column of the coordinate's name. A NULL there becomes one row per label, a row naming a label not passed is dropped, and at each coordinate the most specific row is kept. So the rows of other categories need no filter first. A coordinate left out of labels stays as written, so a constant p_max_pu stays one row with snapshot NULL rather than one row per snapshot. Leave out every coordinate your container can hold a broadcast for.

flags decides, per coordinate in labels, how much work the query does:

the coordinate is in the rows settle varies only all name it keeps the rows naming a passed label broadcast only all leave it NULL expands each row over the labels varies and broadcast some name it, some leave it NULL expands, then picks the most specific row

The pick is a window over every coordinate and the costly step, so it runs only where a coordinate is in both sets. flags(**categories) counts only the rows reaching that category, which often takes a coordinate out of one set and spares the pick. Flags of a wider scope overstate the rows and give the same answer, only more slowly.

flags also chooses the container before any value is read:

f = flags["p_max_pu"]
if "snapshot" not in f.varies:
    ...  # one value per generator
elif "snapshot" not in f.broadcast:
    ...  # one series per generator
else:
    ...  # constants for some generators, series for others

docs.title: Reading a directory
docs.text:
A parquet directory is a record, and reading one involves no layers:

from datarecord import Workspace

ws = Workspace()
record = ws.at("s3://bucket/my-record/")
record.attributes["p_nom"].df()

The layout is the whole format (design):

record/
├── manifest.json            # the schema, and the record's id
├── dims/<dim>.parquet       # one axis per declared dim, multi-dims included: labels and their properties
└── attributes/<attr>.parquet  # one attribute per file, whatever its dims, results included

docs.title: Declaring a schema
docs.text:
A record has one schema, written as manifest.json (design). The schema declares the dims, the properties of their labels and the attributes. This example declares a small network:

from datarecord import Schema, Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec

schema = Schema(
    version=1,
    dimensions={
        "entity": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "ctype": Dimension(one_of=["Generator", "Link", "Load", "StorageUnit"]),
        "bus": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "carrier": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "country": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "scenario": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "timestep": Dimension(dtype="datetime"),
        "connection": Dimension(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}),
    },
    properties={
        "entity": {
            "ctype": PropertySpec(one_of="ctype"),
            "carrier": PropertySpec(one_of="carrier"),
            "sign": PropertySpec(
                dtype="float",
                default=1.0,
                default_by={"entity.ctype": {"Load": -1.0}},
            ),
        },
        "bus": {
            "carrier": PropertySpec(one_of="carrier", default="AC"),
            "x": PropertySpec(dtype="float", default=0.0),
            "country": PropertySpec(one_of="country"),
        },
        "connection": {"role": PropertySpec(dtype="str")},
    },
    attributes={
        "p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity"}, default=0.0, unit="MW"),
        "x": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity"}, default=0.0),
        "co2_emissions": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"carrier"}, default=0.0),
        "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype="float", dims={"entity", "scenario", "timestep"}, default=1.0
        ),
        "p_min_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype="float",
            dims={"entity", "timestep"},
            default=0.0,
            default_by={"entity.ctype": {"StorageUnit": -1.0}},
        ),
        "efficiency": AttributeSpec(
            dtype="float", dims={"connection", "timestep"}, default=1.0
        ),
    },
    partial={"entity", "bus", "scenario", "connection"},
)

docs.title: Dims
docs.text:
A Dimension declares one axis. Its dtype is a mathspec dtype: "float", "int", "str" or "datetime". A "str" dim may take one_of=[...], the labels it allows, and add then refuses a label outside the list (design).

A multi-period snapshot is a label of snapshot with a property that refers to its period, snapshot.period: {"one_of": "period"} (design).

docs.title: Multi-dims
docs.text:
A Dimension with over is a multi-dim: its labels are tuples of other dims' labels, and it declares which tuples exist. over maps each coordinate name to a dim, and a list is short for the case where the two coincide. A multi-dim has no dtype and no one_of. Above, connection is a multi-dim over (entity, bus). Schema.dimensions holds every dim, Schema.multi_dims the multi-dims and Schema.dims the others (design).

connection.bus names a coordinate wherever a dotted subject.name stands, and Schema.resolve("connection.bus") answers connection and the dim bus (design).

A multi-dim's property may refer to a dim, such as bus_country.country: {"one_of": "country"} on the multi-dim bus_country over ["bus", "scenario"], for a bus's country per scenario. A multi-dim is never categorized, and no property refers to a multi-dim (design).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
properties declares, per subject, the values that identify, classify or describe one of its labels. A subject is a dim, multi-dims included. A property holds one value per label and does not vary along another axis. Each property is a column of its subject's own file, dims/entity.parquet or dims/connection.parquet. A caller addresses it as subject.name, such as entity.carrier, bus.carrier or connection.role (design).

A property name belongs to its subject. It may match an attribute, a dim or another subject's property: bus.x and the attribute x are two names, as are entity.carrier and the dim carrier. The schema refuses a property named like its subject's key or like one of a multi-dim's coordinates.

A property declares exactly one of dtype and one_of. Its dtype is "float", "int", "bool" or "str". With one_of="<dim>" it refers to that dim, and its values are typed as the dim. Above, entity.carrier and bus.carrier refer to carrier, and bus.country to country. set and add refuse a label the record lacks, and NULL means no label. remove("country", ...) is refused while a bus still holds the label (design).

w.add("country", ["DE"])
w.add("bus", ["north"], country="DE")
w.set("bus.country", "FR", bus="north")  # refused: no `country` label FR

docs.title: Categories and defaults
docs.text:
A property of a dim in partial that refers to a dim with one_of categorizes its subject. Its values are the subject's categories. default_by keys on them by the property's dotted name, and a set or flags keyword selects by them. Above, entity.ctype refers to ctype, which has one_of, so it categorizes entity. A dim may have several categorizing properties. entity.carrier refers to carrier, which has no one_of, so its labels are data and it categorizes nothing. Schema.categorizing("entity") lists the categorizing properties (design).

default_by overrides default per category, on properties and attributes alike. The first key whose map holds the label's category wins. Schema.default_for("p_min_pu", ctype="StorageUnit") answers -1.0 (design).

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
attributes holds the data. One name is one spec, record-wide. Schema.resolve tells the attribute x from the property bus.x.

A NULL coordinate reaches every label of its dim, so a value set with no entity reaches every entity. A property keyword scopes a value to some labels, one row per label. Which labels a framework reads a name for is the tool's business (design):

w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator")  # one row per generator
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype=["Generator", "StorageUnit"])
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)  # every entity; PyPSA reads no load's

AttributeSpec.dims is the only addressing mechanism, and it names multi-dims as it names any dim. efficiency names the multi-dim connection in its dims, and its rows carry it as one struct column (design). dims makes a scenario-varying p_nom a schema violation. Every attribute lands in attributes/, whatever its dims, so widening dims is a compatible change that moves no file.

docs.title: partial
docs.text:
partial names the dims that a layer may patch value by value, and it is the fold key. entity in partial lets a layer patch one entity, and its categories need it to key defaults. Above, bus and scenario are patchable, and a layer restates carrier whole, which is a few rows. timestep is not patchable, so a patch to one hour restates that entity's whole series (design). A multi-dim follows the same rule. With connection in partial a layer patches one connection's efficiency, and without it the layer restates every connection's.

partial applies to attribute values. A layer that changes an axis, a multi-dim's included, restates it whole either way (design).

docs.title: unit and description
docs.text: unit and description are stored and never interpreted. The package does no unit conversion and no dimensional analysis. None means undeclared, and "" means the quantity has no unit (design).

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
schema.compatible_with(other) answers whether layers written under other still read under self. It returns one reason per incompatibility, and an empty list when the change is compatible (design).

reasons = new_schema.compatible_with(old_schema)
if reasons:
    raise ValueError("\n".join(reasons))

docs.title: Workspaces and stores
docs.text:
A Workspace holds the DuckDB database and reaches files. A Store is one location with its schema, its revisions and its layers. Several stores share one workspace, so their records join (design).

from datarecord import Workspace

ws = Workspace()  # ":memory:" by default
store = ws.store("/data/my-record")  # absolute; never empty
record = ws.at("out/")  # a standalone directory

A revision's file is written after its layer and the manifest, so a write that fails leaves no revision behind (design).

docs.title: A standalone directory
docs.text:
record = ws.write(source, "out/")  # a new directory, read back
record = ws.at("out/")  # read it again later

ws.write refuses a URI where anything exists, even an empty local directory. It writes the manifest last, so a write that fails leaves no record behind (design).

docs.title: On S3
docs.text:
store = ws.store("s3://bucket/my-record")
record = ws.at("s3://bucket/out/")

An s3:// URI needs the optional extra datarecord[remote]. Credentials and the endpoint come from the AWS environment and config files. Set AWS_ENDPOINT_URL to reach a self-hosted server. The server has to honour conditional writes, as AWS S3 does and SeaweedFS does from 4.18 (design).

docs.title: Threads and processes
docs.text:
ws.con is the calling thread's DuckDB cursor, so one workspace serves every thread. A relation belongs to the thread that built it (design).

A Revision serialises as its id, its parent and its store's location, and pickles the same way. In a fresh process it loads back onto Workspace.process() (design):

payload = rev.model_dump_json()  # in one process
rev = Revision.model_validate_json(payload)  # in another
rev.ancestry()

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
A tool is one modelling framework's view of a record. Tools live under datarecord/tools/, and a caller reaches one by importing it. Nothing in the core imports a tool, so importing the record layer pulls in no framework (design, the package).

from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSA

missing = PyPSA.verify(record)
if missing:
    raise RuntimeError(missing.describe())

n = PyPSA.build(record)  # a pypsa.Network
n.optimize()

record_back = PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con)  # the inverse, results included

to_datarecord plans its relations on the connection it receives, the one of the workspace that writes them, so they reach the write path with no copy. build reads record.con itself.

verify catches what the record layer cannot: an entity type the framework has no registry entry for, a connection role it cannot place, and a partial set that breaks the framework's split between constant and varying data. It returns a Requirements that is falsy when the record is usable. A stored attribute that a type does not take, such as p_max_pu on a load, is left out of the build and listed in ignored, and the result stays falsy. build raises UnsupportedRecordError for a record it cannot build in full.

docs.title: Buses and carriers
docs.text:
PyPSA's buses and carriers are dims. A bus is a label of bus, and a carrier is a label of carrier. What PyPSA stores on either is a property of the label or an attribute over the dim, and every name stays PyPSA's (design).

record.dims["carrier"]  # carrier
record.properties["bus"]  # bus | carrier | type | x | y | unit | location
record.properties["entity"]  # entity | ctype | carrier | sign | type
record.attributes["v_nom"]  # bus | attribute | breakpoint | value
record.attributes["marginal_price"]  # bus | snapshot | scenario | ..., a result

A property is named by its subject, so x is a line's reactance and bus.x is a bus's coordinate. entity.carrier and bus.carrier are {"one_of": "carrier"}, so they refer to carrier:

w.add("carrier", ["H2"], color="#f0f")
w.add("bus", ["north H2"], carrier="H2", x=10.1, y=52.0)  # bare: the dim's own
w.set("v_nom", 380.0, bus="north")
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")  # `x` alone is a Line's reactance
w.set("entity.ctype", "Load", entity="g1")
w.set("entity.carrier", "coal", entity="g1")  # refused: no label `coal`
w.set("carrier", "AC")  # refused, naming `bus.carrier` and `entity.carrier`
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, ctype="Generator")  # selector: `entity.ctype`
w.remove("bus", ["south"])  # and every connection at it
w.remove("carrier", ["gas"])  # refused while a carrier names it

A bus and a load may share a name, since they are labels of two dims. to_datarecord adds every carrier that a component or bus names and n.carriers lacks, and it stores PyPSA's "" carrier as NULL. verify reports an entity attached to no bus.

docs.title: Solving and writing results back
docs.text:
A result is an attribute. With results_only=True, to_datarecord presents only what the solve produced, as a thin layer over base, the record the network was built from:

w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, entity=["wind1"])
inputs = rev.child(w.edits)  # edited inputs are committed first
n = PyPSA.build(inputs.record)
n.optimize()
solved = inputs.child(
    PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con, results_only=True, base=inputs.record)
)
solved.record.attributes["marginal_price"]  # a child of solved reads it too
PyPSA.build(solved.record)  # marginal_price is in the network

base is required with results_only and refused without it. A SubNetwork is a label of the dim sub_network, 0, 1, … as PyPSA names it. The results layer restates that axis with this solve's SubNetworks and leaves the entity axis to base, so a re-solve leaves none stale (design).
